## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_018\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_018\auto

# Programming language policy

We will do demos in Python (Jupyter Lab).   
You’re welcome to use any language you like (that your TAs can read) for homework or project.   
TAs will only support Python.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_019\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_019\auto

# Collaboration policy

Project: yes of course! Clarify the contributions of each member.

Give credit to the people who have helped you: write on your report the names of the people you worked with.   
Give credit to the other resources that have helped you: please write on your report the GenAI tools, textbooks, notes, or web pages you found useful.

Midterm/Final: Figure out your solutions by yourself.

All of the text that you submit should be done by you. No collaboration/discussion here!

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_033\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_033\auto

# Definition of Machine Learning

Prof. Tom M. Mitchell from CMU (Samuel, 1959):

A computer program is said to learn from experience E with respect to some class of tasks T and performance measure P, if its performance at tasks in T, as measured by P, improves with experience E.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_039\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_039\auto

# Taxonomy of Machine Learning

# Supervised Learning

# Unsupervised Learning

# Reinforcement Learning

Has outcome information ("labels")

No outcome information available

Makes decisions based on trial and error

Finds patterns that relate to those outcomes

Analyzes or identifies groups without labels or human instruction

Decision-making algorithm is constantly refined based on "rewards"

Uses patterns to predict outcomes not yet known

Offers insights into characteristics that define groups

Excels in complex stuations

# ! Pecan

(Source: Web)

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_048\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_048\auto

Linear regression (polynomial regression with degree 1): Assume $y = p _ { 1 } ( x ) = a x + b$ and guess the values of a and $b$ .

If a residence has $x = 3 2 0$ square kilometers, we predict its price as $y = 8 6 1 . 2 9 \mathrm { ~ C N Y }$ .

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_075\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_075\auto

A set $S$ is an unordered collection of objects.   
• $S = \{ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 \}$ is the possible outcomes of the toss of a die.   
$S = [ a , b ] = \{ x \in \mathbb { R } : a \leq x \leq b \}$ is the set of all numbers from a to $b$ inclusive.   
$S = ( a , b ] = \{ x \in \mathbb { R } : a < x \leq b \}$ is the set of all numbers from a to $b$ , excluding including $b$ .   
$\mathbb { R }$ is the set of all real numbers.   
• $\mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ is the set of all real vectors of length $d$ .

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_076\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_076\auto

# Functions

A function $f$ is a map from a set $X$ to another set Y . We write this as

$$
f : X \to Y .
$$

For example, the function $f : \mathbb { R } \to [ 0 , \infty )$ could be given by the recipe $f ( x ) = x ^ { 2 }$ . The set of inputs is called the domain; the set of possible outputs is called the codomain; the set $\{ f ( x ) : x \in X \}$ is called the range (or image). • For example $f : \{ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 \}  \{ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 \}$ given by the recipe $f ( x ) = x + 2$ has codomain $\{ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 \}$ and range $\{ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 \}$ .

![](images/8ece3e031d0d9d36b3913c7df8fb8041e05d48fafff4d87beb58428934d47eda.jpg)

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_077\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_077\auto

# Functions

# Definition 3.1

Let $f ( x )$ be a continuous function defined on domain $\mathbb { R }$ .

$f ( x )$ is differentiable if $\begin{array} { r } { f ^ { \prime } ( x ) = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { x  c } \frac { f ( x ) - f ( c ) } { x - c } } \end{array}$ c f (x)−f (c) exists for all x ∈ R.   
$f ( x )$ is convex if $f ( \lambda a + ( 1 - \lambda ) b ) \leq \lambda f ( a ) + ( 1 - \lambda ) f ( b )$ for all a, $b \in \mathbb { R }$ ;   
$f ( x )$ is strictly convex if $f ( \lambda a + ( 1 - \lambda ) b ) < \lambda f ( a ) + ( 1 - \lambda ) f ( b )$ for all a, $b \in \mathbb { R }$ ;   
• $f ( x )$ is concave if $f ( \lambda a + ( 1 - \lambda ) b ) \geq \lambda f ( a ) + ( 1 - \lambda ) f ( b )$ for all a, $b \in \mathbb { R }$ ;   
• $f ( x )$ is strictly concave if $f ( \lambda a + ( 1 - \lambda ) b ) > \lambda f ( a ) + ( 1 - \lambda ) f ( b )$ for all a, $b \in \mathbb { R }$ ;

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_078\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_078\auto

# Functions

# Definition 3.1

Let $f ( x )$ be a continuous function defined on domain $\mathbb { R }$ .

$f ( x )$ is differentiable if $\begin{array} { r } { f ^ { \prime } ( x ) = \mathsf { l i m } _ { x  c } \frac { f ( x ) - f ( c ) } { x - c } } \end{array}$ c f (x)−f (c) exists for all x ∈ R.   
• $f ( x )$ is convex if $f ( \lambda a + ( 1 - \lambda ) b ) \leq \lambda f ( a ) + ( 1 - \lambda ) f ( b )$ for all a, $b \in \mathbb { R }$ ;   
$f ( x )$ is strictly convex if $f ( \lambda a + ( 1 - \lambda ) b ) < \lambda f ( a ) + ( 1 - \lambda ) f ( b )$ for all a, $b \in \mathbb { R }$ ;   
• $f ( x )$ is concave if $f ( \lambda a + ( 1 - \lambda ) b ) \geq \lambda f ( a ) + ( 1 - \lambda ) f ( b )$ for all a, $b \in \mathbb { R }$ ;   
• $f ( x )$ is strictly concave if $f ( \lambda a + ( 1 - \lambda ) b ) > \lambda f ( a ) + ( 1 - \lambda ) f ( b )$ for all a, $b \in \mathbb { R }$ ;

$f ( x )$ is differentiable and convex: $x _ { 0 }$ such that $f ^ { \prime } ( x _ { 0 } ) = 0$ minimize function $f$ . $f ( x )$ is differentiable and concave: $x _ { 0 }$ such that $f ^ { \prime } ( x _ { 0 } ) = 0$ maximize function $f$

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_079\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_079\auto

# Linear functions

A function $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { d }  \mathbb { R }$ is linear if it satisfies

(Homogeneity) For any vector $\mathbf { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ and scalar $\mathsf { a } \in \mathbb { R }$ ,

$$
f ( a \ { \pmb { x } } ) = a \ f ( { \pmb { x } } )
$$

(Additivity) For any two vectors $\pmb { x } , \pmb { y } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ ,

$$
f ( \mathbf { x } + \mathbf { y } ) = f ( \mathbf { x } ) + f ( \mathbf { y } )
$$

Note that a linear function $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { d }  \mathbb { R }$ must pass through the origin, i.e., $f ( { \bf 0 } ) = 0$ where $\pmb { 0 } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ is the zero vector in $d$ dimensions. Why?

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_080\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_080\auto

# Affine functions

An affine function $f$ is a linear function plus possibly a constant.

More precisely, a function $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { d }  \mathbb { R }$ is affine if it can be expressed as

$$
f ( { \pmb x } ) = { \pmb a } ^ { \top } { \pmb x } + b
$$

for some vector $\mathbf { a } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ and some scalar $b \in \mathbb { R }$

The scalar $b$ is called the bias or offset.

Example: The following function $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }  \mathbb { R }$ is affine. Why?

$$
f ( \mathbf { x } ) = f ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } ) = - x _ { 1 } + 3 x _ { 2 } + 7 .
$$

Exercise: Is a linear function affine? Is an affine function linear?

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_082\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_082\auto

# Local and global extrema

Consider a function $f : [ a , b ]  \mathbb { R }$ .   
The function $f$ has a local minimum at $c \in \mathbb { R }$ if $f ( x ) \geq f ( c )$ for all $x$ in an open neighborhood of $c$ .   
● The function $f$ has a global minimum at $c \in \mathbb { R }$ if $f ( x ) \geq f ( c )$ for all $x \in [ a , b ]$ .

Exercise: If $c$ is a local minimum of $f$ , is it a global minimum? If $c$ is a global minimum of $f$ , is it a local minimum?

Exercise: How would you define local maximum and global maximum?

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_084\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_084\auto

# min and arg min

• For a function $f : X \to Y$ , the minimum $\mathrm { m i n } _ { x \in X } f ( x )$ returns the smallest value among all elements in the set $\{ f ( x ) : x \in X \}$ .

For a function $f : X \to Y$ , the argmin $x ^ { * } = \arg \operatorname* { m i n } _ { x \in X } f ( x )$ returns the value of $x \in X$ that minimizes $f ( x )$ , i.e.,

$$
f ( x ^ { * } ) = \operatorname* { m i n } _ { x \in X } f ( x )
$$

arg min returns a value from the domain of the function $X$ and min returns from the range (codomain) $Y$ of the function.

Let $X = \{ 0 , 1 \}$ and $f ( 0 ) = \pi$ and $f ( 1 ) = e$ . Then

$$
\operatorname* { a r g m i n } _ { x \in X } f ( x ) = 1
$$

$$
\operatorname* { m i n } _ { x \in X } f ( x ) = e ,
$$

and

$$
\underset { x \in X } { \mathrm { a r g } } \underset { x } { \mathrm { m a x } } f ( x ) = 0 \qquad \underset { x \in X } { \mathrm { m a x } } f ( x ) = \pi .
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_086\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_086\auto

For a multivariable function $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { d }  \mathbb { R }$ , its gradient vector or derivative at $\mathbf { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ is the column vector

$$
\nabla _ { \mathbf { x } } \ : f ( \mathbf { x } ) = \frac { \mathrm { d } f } { \mathrm { d } \mathbf { x } } = \left[ \frac { \partial f } { \partial x _ { 1 } } \quad \frac { \partial f } { \partial x _ { 2 } } \quad . . . \quad \frac { \partial f } { \partial x _ { d } } \right] ^ { \intercal }
$$

Recall that $\frac { \partial f } { \partial x _ { i } }$ is the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to the scalar variable $x _ { j }$

For example, if $f ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } ) = 2 x _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + 5 x _ { 1 } x _ { 2 } + 3 x _ { 2 } ^ { 3 }$ , then

$$
\frac { \partial f } { \partial x _ { 1 } } = 4 x _ { 1 } + 5 x _ { 2 } \quad \mathsf { a n d } \quad \frac { \partial f } { \partial x _ { 2 } } = 5 x _ { 1 } + 9 x _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } .
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_087\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_087\auto

# Important derivatives

There are only two derivatives for functions $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { d }  \mathbb { R }$ that take vectors to scalars you need to know for now.

For a fixed vector $\mathbf { a } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , consider $\pmb { f } ( \pmb { x } ) = \mathbf { a } ^ { \top } \mathbf { x }$ (known as the inner or dot product). Then

$$
\nabla _ { \mathbf { x } } \operatorname { f } ( \mathbf { x } ) = \mathbf { a } .
$$

For a fixed matrix $\pmb { \mathsf { A } } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d \times d }$ , consider $f ( \mathbf { x } ) = \mathbf { x } ^ { \top } \mathbf { A } \mathbf { x }$ (known as the quadratic form). Then

$$
\nabla _ { \mathbf x } \mathfrak f ( \mathbf x ) = ( \mathbf A + \mathbf A ^ { \top } ) \mathbf x .
$$

In most applications, A is a symmetric matrix (i.e., $\pmb { \mathsf { A } } = \pmb { \mathsf { A } } ^ { \top }$ ) so

$$
\nabla _ { \mathbf { x } } \operatorname { f } ( \mathbf { x } ) = 2 \mathbf { A } \mathbf { x } .
$$

This generalizes the basic fact that if $f ( x ) = a x ^ { 2 }$ , then $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { \mathrm { d } f } { \mathrm { d } x } = 2 a x } \end{array}$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_092\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_092\auto

# Discrete random variables

# Random variables $X$ and Y :

$X$ can only take values in the finite set ${ \mathcal { X } } = \{ x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } . . . . , x _ { M } \} .$ .   
$Y$ can only take values in the finite set $\mathcal { Y } = \{ y _ { 1 } , y _ { 2 } . . . . , y _ { L } \}$ .

A random variable is said to be discrete if the set of values it can take has a finite number of values.

$$
\sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { M } \mathsf { P r } ( X = x _ { i } ) = 1 , \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { L } \mathsf { P r } ( Y = y _ { i } ) = 1 .
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_093\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_093\auto

Consider $m$ trials (of sampling $X$ and $Y$ ) and let the number of trials for which $X = x _ { I }$ and $Y = y _ { j }$ be $m _ { i j }$ . Then, if $m$ is large, we can assume that

$$
\mathsf { P r } ( X = x _ { i } , \ Y = y _ { j } ) = \frac { m _ { i j } } { m } .
$$

The argument of $\mathsf { P r } ( \cdot )$ is known as an event.   
◦ Event: A set in which a r.v. (or multiples r.v.s) assume some value(s) in some set. e.g., $\{ X = x _ { i }$ , $Y = y _ { j } \}$ .

# Sum rule and product rule

• Sum rule:

$$
\digamma = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { L } \mathsf { P r } ( X = x _ { i } , Y = y _ { j } ) , \quad \mathsf { P r } ( Y = y _ { j } ) = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { M } \mathsf { P r } ( .
$$

C Product rule:

$$
{ \mathrm { ' } } = x _ { i } , Y = y _ { j } ) = \mathsf { P r } ( X = x _ { i } | Y = y _ { j } ) \cdot \mathsf { P r } ( Y = y _ { j } ) .
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_096\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_096\auto

# Bayes’ rule

Probability mass function (pmf): p(x) := Pr(X = x), $p ( x , y ) : = \mathsf { P r } ( X = x , Y = y ) , \mathsf { \ } p ( x | y ) : = \mathsf { P r } ( X = x$ |Y = y ).

Bayes’ rule/Bayes’ Theorem:

$$
| x ) = { \frac { p ( x , y ) } { p ( x ) } } = { \frac { p ( x | y ) p ( y ) } { p ( x ) } } = { \frac { p ( x | y ) p ( y ) } { \sum _ { y ^ { \prime } \in { \mathcal { V } } } p ( x | y ^ { \prime } ) p ( y ^ { \prime } } }
$$

▶ ‘Invert the casucal relationship’ between $X$ and $Y$ .   
$p ( x | y ) \propto p ( y | x ) p ( x ) .$ likelihood $\times$ prior   
▶ posterior = ∝ likelihood $\times$ prior. model evidence

# Continuous random variables

Cumulative distribution function (cdf): $x \in \mathbb { R } \mapsto F _ { X } ( x ) = \mathsf { P r } ( X \leq x )$ is differentiable on $\mathbb { R }$ .

Probability density function (pdf):

fX $\mathbf { \Psi } : ( x ) = \frac { \mathrm { d } } { \mathrm { d } x } F _ { X } ( x ) , \quad x \in \mathbb { R } ; \quad f _ { X } ( x ) \geq 0 \quad \forall x \in \mathbb { R } \ \hat { \mathbf { \Psi } }$ nd $\int _ { \mathbb { R } } f _ { X } ( x ) \mathrm { d } x = 1 .$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_098\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_098\auto

# Continuous random variables

Cumulative distribution function (cdf): $x \in \mathbb { R } \mapsto F _ { X } ( x ) = \mathsf { P r } ( X \leq x )$ is differentiable on $\mathbb { R }$ .

Probability density function (pdf):

fX $\mathbf { \Psi } : ( x ) = \frac { \mathrm { d } } { \mathrm { d } x } F _ { X } ( x ) , \quad x \in \mathbb { R } ; \quad f _ { X } ( x ) \geq 0 \quad \forall x \in \mathbb { R } \ \widehat { \mathbf { \Psi } }$ nd $\int _ { \mathbb { R } } f _ { X } ( x ) \mathrm { d } x = 1 .$

Joint probability density function of continuous r.v.s.:

$$
f _ { X , Y } ( x , y ) = \frac { \partial ^ { 2 } } { \partial x \partial y } F _ { X , Y } ( x , y ) , ( x , y ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } .
$$

• Conditional probability and independence can be defined analogously to the discrete case:

$$
a < X \leq b , \ c < Y \leq d ) = \int _ { c } ^ { d } \int _ { a } ^ { b } f _ { X , Y } ( x , y ) \mathrm { d } x \mathrm { d } y
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_099\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_099\auto

# Definition 3.2 (Independence)

Two random variables $X$ and $Y$ are independent if $p _ { X , Y } ( x , y ) = p _ { X } ( x ) p _ { Y } ( y )$ for all $x \in \mathcal { X }$ and $y \in \mathcal { V }$ .

• $X$ and $Y$ are independent if $p _ { X | Y } ( x | y ) = p _ { X } ( x )$ for all $x \in \mathcal { X }$ and $y \in \mathcal { V }$ such that $p _ { Y } ( y ) > 0$ (what if $p _ { Y } ( y ) = 0 ? )$ .

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_100\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_100\auto

# Expectation and variance

● Expectation:

Discrete r.v.: $\begin{array} { r l } & { \mathbb { E } X = \displaystyle \sum _ { x \in \mathcal { X } } x p _ { X } ( x ) . } \\ & { \mathrm { ~ } \mathrm { ~ v . ~ } \mathbb { E } X = \displaystyle \int _ { \mathbb { R } } x f _ { X } ( x ) \mathrm { d } x . } \end{array}$   
Continuous r.   
If $\boldsymbol { g }$ is a function from the domain of $X$ to $\mathbb { R }$ , we can obtain the expectation of $Y = g ( X )$ in the same way:

$$
\mathbb { E } Y = \mathbb { E } [ g ( X ) ] = \int _ { \mathbb { R } } y f _ { Y } ( y ) \mathrm { d } y = \int _ { \mathbb { R } } g ( x ) f _ { X } ( x ) \mathrm { d } x .
$$

Linearity of expectation: if $g ( X ) = a X + b$ (for constants $^ { a }$ , $b \in \mathbb { R }$ ), then $\mathbb { E } [ g ( X ) ] = a \mathbb { E } [ X ] + b = g ( \mathbb { E } [ X ] )$ .

# ● Variance:

$$
\begin{array} { r l } { \mathrm { ~ \displaystyle ~ \mathbb ~ { \ P } ^ \mathrm { ~ } ~ D i s c r e t e ~ r . v . : ~ V a r } ( X ) = \displaystyle \sum _ { x \in \mathcal { X } } ( x - \mathbb { E } X ) ^ { 2 } p _ { X } ( x ) . } \\ { \mathrm { ~ \displaystyle ~ \mathbb ~ { \ P } ^ \mathrm { ~ } ~ C o n t i n u o u s ~ r . v . : ~ V a r } ( X ) = \displaystyle \int _ { \mathbb R } ( x - \mathbb { E } X ) ^ { 2 } f _ { X } ( x ) \mathrm { d } x . } \end{array}
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_101\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_101\auto

# Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)

C In machine learning, we almost always do NOT have access to the underlying distributions that the data are generated from.   
Rather, we have access to sample data and we would like to use it to estimate some parameters.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_102\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_102\auto

# Maximum likelihood estimation: Gaussian distribution

If samples in $\mathcal { D } = \{ X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { m } \}$ are independently drawn from the univariate Gaussian distribution

$$
\mathfrak { N } \left( x ; \mu , \sigma ^ { 2 } \right) = \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 2 \pi \sigma ^ { 2 } } } \exp \left( - \frac { 1 } { 2 \sigma ^ { 2 } } ( x - \mu ) ^ { 2 } \right)
$$

we can use the samples in $\mathcal { D }$ to estimate the parameter vector $\theta = \left( \mu , \sigma ^ { 2 } \right)$ .

Note: notation $f _ { X } \left( x ; \mu , \sigma ^ { 2 } \right)$ or $f _ { X } ( x ; \theta )$ emphasize that the density is parametrized by the parameters $( \mu , \sigma ^ { 2 } )$ or $\theta$ .

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_103\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_103\auto

# Maximum likelihood estimation: Gaussian distribution

If samples in $\mathcal { D } = \{ X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { m } \}$ are independently drawn from the univariate Gaussian distribution

$$
\mathfrak { N } \left( x ; \mu , \sigma ^ { 2 } \right) = \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 2 \pi \sigma ^ { 2 } } } \exp \left( - \frac { 1 } { 2 \sigma ^ { 2 } } ( x - \mu ) ^ { 2 } \right)
$$

we can use the samples in $\mathcal { D }$ to estimate the parameter vector $\theta = \left( \mu , \sigma ^ { 2 } \right)$ .

Note: notation $f _ { X } \left( x ; \mu , \sigma ^ { 2 } \right)$ or $f _ { X } ( x ; \theta )$ emphasize that the density is parametrized by the parameters $( \mu , \sigma ^ { 2 } )$ or $\theta$ .

$\circledcirc$ Maximum likelihood estimates for the mean and variance:

$$
{ \hat { \mu } } _ { \mathrm { M L } } = { \frac { 1 } { m } } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } X _ { i } \quad \mathrm { ~ a n d ~ } \quad { \hat { \sigma } } _ { \mathrm { M L } } ^ { 2 } = { \frac { 1 } { m } } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } ( X _ { i } - { \hat { \mu } } ) ^ { 2 }
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_108\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_108\auto

# Maximum likelihood estimation: Bernoulli distribution

Samples in $\mathcal { D } = \{ X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { m } \}$ are generated independently from the Bernoulli (coin toss) distribution

$$
p _ { X } ( x ; \theta ) = \left\{ \begin{array} { c c } { { 1 - \theta } } & { { x = 0 } } \\ { { \theta } } & { { x = 1 } } \end{array} \right.
$$

or

$$
p _ { X } ( x ; \theta ) = ( 1 - \theta ) ^ { 1 - x } \theta ^ { x } , \quad x \in \{ 0 , 1 \} .
$$

How would we estimate $\theta$ from samples?

# Maximum likelihood estimation: Bernoulli distribution

$\begin{array} { r } { M _ { 1 } : = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } X _ { i } } \end{array}$ denote the total number of ones in $\mathcal { D }$ . Consider

$$
\hat { \theta } _ { \mathrm { M L } } = \underset { \theta \in ( 0 , 1 ) } { \arg \operatorname* { m a x } } \ \prod _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } p x \left( X _ { i } ; \theta \right)
$$

$$

# Maximum likelihood estimation: Bernoulli distribution

$\begin{array} { r } { M _ { 1 } : = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } X _ { i } } \end{array}$ denote the total number of ones in $\mathcal { D }$ . Consider

$$
\hat { \theta } _ { \mathrm { M L } } = \underset { \theta \in ( 0 , 1 ) } { \arg \operatorname* { m a x } } ~ \underset { \mathrm { O b j e c t i v e ~ f u n c t i o n } } { \underbrace { ( m - M _ { 1 } ) \log ( 1 - \theta ) + M _ { 1 } \log \theta } } .
$$

・ $g ( \theta )$ is strictly concave $\Rightarrow$ differentiating and setting to zero yields the (unique) maximum:

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \displaystyle \boldsymbol { g } ^ { \prime } ( \boldsymbol { \theta } ) = - \frac { m - M _ { 1 } } { 1 - \theta } + \frac { M _ { 1 } } { \theta } , } \\ & { \displaystyle \hat { \theta } _ { \mathrm { M L } } = \arg \operatorname* { m a x } _ { \boldsymbol { \theta } \in ( 0 , 1 ) } \Longrightarrow \boldsymbol { g } ^ { \prime } ( \hat { \theta } _ { \mathrm { M L } } ) = 0 \Longrightarrow \hat { \theta } _ { \mathrm { M L } } } \end{array}
$$

$\circledcirc$ Mean $\theta$ is estimated by the empirical mean $M _ { 1 } / m$ : agrees with common sense!

# Maximum likelihood estimation: exponential distribution

Samples in $\mathcal { D } = \{ X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { m } \}$ are generated independently from the exponential distribution (memory-less)

$$
\begin{array} { r } { f _ { X } ( x ; \theta ) = \left\{ \begin{array} { c c } { \theta \exp ( - \theta x ) } & { x \ge 0 } \\ { 0 } & { x < 0 } \end{array} . \right. } \end{array}
$$

$\theta > 0$ is the unknown (rate) parameter. In fact, $\mathbb { E } [ X ] = 1 / \theta$ . ◦ Case: network request arrival time

$$
\begin{array} { r } { F _ { X } ( x ; \theta ) = \left\{ \begin{array} { c c } { 1 - \exp ( - \theta x ) } & { x \ge 0 } \\ { 0 } & { x < 0 } \end{array} . \right. } \end{array}
$$

How would we estimate $\theta$ from samples?

\begin{array} { r } { \hat { \theta } _ { \mathrm { M L } } = \underset { \theta > 0 } { \mathrm { a r g } } \underset { i = 1 } { \mathrm { m a x } } \ \underset { i = 1 } { \overset { m } { \prod } } f _ { X } \left( X _ { i } ; \theta \right) = \underset { \theta > 0 } { \mathrm { a r g } } \underset { i = 1 } { \mathrm { m a x } } \ \underset { i = 1 } { \overset { m } { \sum } } \log f _ { X } } \\ { = \underset { \theta > 0 } { \mathrm { a r g } } \underset { i = 1 } { \mathrm { m a x } } \ \underset { i = 1 } { \overset { m } { \sum } } \left( \log \theta - \theta X _ { i } \right) = \underset { \theta > 0 } { \mathrm { a r g } } \underset { \theta > 0 } { \mathrm { m a x } } \ \underset { i = 1 } { \overset { m } { \sum } } \underset { \theta \_ { 0 } } { \mathrm { l o g } } \underset { i = 1 } { \overset { \theta } { \prod } } } \end{array}
$$

• $\begin{array} { r } { g ( \theta ) = m \log \theta - \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } \theta X _ { i } } \end{array}$ is strictly concave $\Rightarrow$ differentiating and setting to zero yields the (unique) maximum:

$$
\begin{array} { r l r } {  { = \frac { m } { \hat { \theta } _ { \mathrm { M L } } } - \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } X _ { i } , } } \\ & { \cdot ) = 0 \implies \hat { \theta } _ { \mathrm { M L } } = \hat { \theta } _ { \mathrm { M L } } = \frac { m } { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } X _ { i } } = ( \frac { 1 } { m } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } X _ { i } ) } & \end{array}
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_124\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_124\auto

# Maximum likelihood estimation: exponential distribution

Exponential distribution (memoryless distribution)

$$
\begin{array} { r } { f _ { X } ( x ; \theta ) = \left\{ \begin{array} { c c } { \theta \exp ( - \theta x ) } & { x \ge 0 } \\ { 0 } & { x < 0 } \end{array} . \right. } \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \mathbb { E } [ X ] = 1 / \theta , \ \hat { \theta } _ { \mathrm { M L } } = \big ( \frac { 1 } { m } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } X _ { i } \big ) ^ { - 1 } . } \end{array}
$$

⊚ $\textstyle { \frac { 1 } { m } } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } X _ { i }$ is the empirical mean: it seems plausible that $m / ( \textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } X _ { i } )$ is a “good” estimate of $\theta$

Why would it not be “good”?

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_126\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_126\auto

# Systems of linear equations

# Definition 3.3 (Rules)

A vector space over the reals consists of a set $\nu$ , a vector sum operation $+ : \mathcal { V } \times \mathcal { V } \to \mathcal { V }$ and a scalar multiplication operation · $: \mathbb { R } \times \mathcal { V }  \mathcal { V }$ satisfying the following properties.

Commutativity: ${ \pmb x } + { \pmb y } = { \pmb y } + { \pmb x }$ for all $\mathbf { \boldsymbol { x } } , \mathbf { \boldsymbol { y } } \in \mathcal { V }$ ;   
Associativity: $( x + y ) + z = x + ( y + z )$ for all $\pmb { x } , \pmb { y } , \pmb { z } \in \mathcal { V }$ ;   
Identity element of addition: $\pmb { x } + \pmb { 0 } = \pmb { x }$ for all $\pmb { x } \in \mathcal { V }$ ; Inverse element of addition: For every $\pmb { x } \in \mathcal { V }$ , there exists an element $- x \in \mathcal { V }$ such that ${ \pmb x } + ( - { \pmb x } ) = { \pmb 0 }$ ; Associativity of scalar multiplication: For all a, $b \in \mathbb { R }$ and $x \in \mathcal V$ , $a ( b x ) = ( a b ) x$ ;   
Identity element of scalar multiplication: $1 x = x$ for $\pmb { x } \in \mathcal { V }$ ;   
Distributivity of scalar multiplication with respect to vector addition: $a ( { \pmb x } + { \pmb y } ) = a { \pmb x } + a { \pmb y }$ for all $a \in \mathbb { R }$ and $\pmb { x } , \pmb { y } \in \mathcal { V }$ ; Distributivity of scalar multiplication with respect to addition in $\mathbb { R }$ $: ( a + b ) \pmb { x } = a \pmb { x } + b \pmb { x }$ for all a, $b \in \mathbb { R }$ and $\pmb { x } \in \mathcal { V }$ .

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_127\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_127\auto

# Definition 3.4 (Linear independence)

A set of vectors $\{ \pmb { x } _ { 1 } , \pmb { x } _ { 2 } , \dots , \pmb { x } _ { k } \}$ from a vector space $\nu$ is linearly independent if

$$
\beta _ { 1 } \pmb { x } _ { 1 } + \beta _ { 2 } \pmb { x } _ { 2 } + . . . + \beta _ { k } \pmb { x } _ { k } = \mathbf { 0 }
$$

implies that $\beta _ { 1 } = \beta _ { 2 } = . . . = \beta _ { k } = 0 .$

• $\{ \pmb { x } _ { 1 } , \pmb { x } _ { 2 } , \dots , \pmb { x } _ { k } \}$ are linearly independent $\Longleftrightarrow$ no vector $x _ { j }$ can be expressed as a linear combination of the other vectors $\left\{ { { x } _ { 1 } } , \dotsc , { { x } _ { i - 1 } } , { { x } _ { i + 1 } } , \dotsc , { { x } _ { k } } \right\}$ .

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_128\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_128\auto

# Definition 3.5 (Basis of vector space)

A set of vectors $\{ \pmb { x } _ { 1 } , \pmb { x } _ { 2 } , \dots , \pmb { x } _ { k } \}$ is a basis for a vector space $\nu$ if

• $\mathcal { V } = \operatorname { s p a n } \{ \pmb { x } _ { 1 } , \pmb { x } _ { 2 } , \dots , \pmb { x } _ { k } \}$ ;   
$\{ \pmb { x } _ { 1 } , \pmb { x } _ { 2 } , \dots , \pmb { x } _ { k } \}$ is a linearly independent set of vectors.

Equivalently, every $\pmb { x } \in \mathcal { V }$ can be uniquely written as $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } \beta _ { i } \pmb { x } _ { i }$ for some $\{ \beta _ { i } \} _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } \subset \mathbb { R }$ . The number of vectors in any basis of $\vee$ is called the dimension of $\nu$ , written as $\dim ( \nu )$ .

# Definition 3.6 (nullspace and range of matrix)

The nullspace (also called kernel) of a matrix $\pmb { A } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m \times d }$ is defined as $\mathcal { N } ( \dot { \pmb { A } } ) = \{ \pmb { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } : \pmb { A } \pmb { x } = 0 \}$ .

The range or column space of $\pmb { A }$ is defined as

$$
\mathcal { R } ( \pmb { A } ) = \{ \pmb { A } \pmb { x } : \pmb { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { f } \} \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m } .
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_129\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_129\auto

# Matrix

# Definition 3.7 (Rank of matrix)

The column rank or rank of a matrix $\pmb { A } \in R ^ { m \times d }$ is defined as

$$
\operatorname { r a n k } ( \pmb { A } ) = \dim ( \mathcal { R } ( \pmb { A } ) ) .
$$

In other words, the column rank of $\pmb { A }$ is the dimension of the column space of A.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_130\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_130\auto

The column rank or rank of a matrix $\pmb { A } \in R ^ { m \times d }$ is defined as

$$
\operatorname { r a n k } ( \pmb { A } ) = \dim ( \mathcal { R } ( \pmb { A } ) ) .
$$

In other words, the column rank of $\pmb { A }$ is the dimension of the column space of A.

$\circledcirc$ Rank-nullity: $\operatorname { r a n k } ( \pmb { A } ) + \dim ( \mathcal { N } ( \pmb { A } ) ) = d .$   
It is always true that ra $\operatorname { n k } ( \pmb { A } ) \leq \operatorname* { m i n } \{ m , d \} .$ .   
A matrix is full rank i $\operatorname { r a n k } ( \pmb { A } ) = \operatorname* { m i n } \{ m , d \} .$   
A matrix is full column rank (resp. full row rank) if the set of columns (resp. rows) of the matrix is linearly independent.   
If the matrix A is square (i.e., $m = d$ ) and it is full rank, then the inverse $\pmb { A } ^ { - 1 }$ exists.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_131\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_131\auto

# Solutions to linear systems

Solve systems of equations of the form $( \underline { { x } } _ { i } , \ 1 \leq i \leq d$ : columns of X )

$$
{ \pmb x } { \pmb w } = { \pmb y } \mathrm { o r } [ { \pmb x } _ { 1 } \ { \pmb x } _ { 2 } \ \ldots \ { \pmb x } _ { d } ] \left[ \begin{array} { l } { m _ { 1 } } \\ { w _ { 2 } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { w _ { d } } \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { y _ { 1 } } \\ { y _ { 2 } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { y _ { d } } \end{array} \right] , 
$$$$
\therefore \cdot \cdot \textstyle \sum _ { d } ] \left[ \begin{array} { l } { w _ { 1 } } \\ { w _ { 2 } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { w _ { d } } \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { y _ { 1 } } \\ { y _ { 2 } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { y _ { d } } \end{array} \right] , \mathrm { ~ w h e r e ~ } \underline { { x } } _ { i } = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { x _ { 1 , i } } \\ { x _ { 2 , i } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { x _ { m , i } } \end{array} \right]
$$

Matrix $\pmb { \chi } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m \times d }$ and vector $\pmb { y } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ are given and $\pmb { w } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ is to be found.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_132\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_132\auto

# Solutions to linear systems

Solve systems of equations of the form $( \underline { { x } } _ { i } , \ 1 \leq i \leq d$ : columns of X )

$$
{ \pmb X } { \pmb w } = { \pmb y } ~ \mathrm { o r } ~ [ { \underline { { x } } } _ { 1 } ~ { \underline { { x } } } _ { 2 } ~ \dots ~ { \underline { { x } } } _ { d } ] \left[ \begin{array} { l } { m _ { 1 } } \\ { w _ { 2 } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { w _ { d } } \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { y _ { 1 } } \\ { y _ { 2 } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { y _ { d } } \end{array} \right] , \ { \mathrm { v } }
$$$$
\therefore \cdot \cdot \textstyle \sum _ { d } ] \left[ \begin{array} { l } { w _ { 1 } } \\ { w _ { 2 } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { w _ { d } } \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { y _ { 1 } } \\ { y _ { 2 } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { y _ { d } } \end{array} \right] , \mathrm { ~ w h e r e ~ } \underline { { x } } _ { i } = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { x _ { 1 , i } } \\ { x _ { 2 , i } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { x _ { m , i } } \end{array} \right]
$$

Matrix $\pmb { \chi } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m \times d }$ and vector $\pmb { y } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ are given and $\pmb { w } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ is to be found.

$m = d$ : if matrix $\pmb { x }$ is square and full rank, $x ^ { - 1 }$ exists $\Longrightarrow$ solve for w by simple matrix inversion and multiplication $\pmb { w } = \pmb { X } ^ { - 1 } \pmb { y }$ .

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_133\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_133\auto

# Solutions to linear systems

Solve systems of equations of the form $( \underline { { x } } _ { i } , \ 1 \leq i \leq d$ : columns of X )

$$
{ \pmb X } { \pmb w } = { \pmb y } ~ \mathrm { o r } ~ [ { \underline { { x } } } _ { 1 } ~ { \underline { { x } } } _ { 2 } ~ \dots ~ { \underline { { x } } } _ { d } ] \left[ \begin{array} { l } { m _ { 1 } } \\ { w _ { 2 } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { w _ { d } } \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { y _ { 1 } } \\ { y _ { 2 } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { y _ { d } } \end{array} \right] , \ { \mathrm { v } }
$$

Matrix $\pmb { \chi } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m \times d }$ and vector $\pmb { y } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ are given and $\pmb { w } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ is to be found.

$m = d$ : if matrix $\pmb { x }$ is square and full rank, $x ^ { - 1 }$ exists $\Longrightarrow$ solve for w by simple matrix inversion and multiplication $\pmb { w } = \pmb { X } ^ { - 1 } \pmb { y }$ .

• $m \neq d$ : existence and uniqueness of solutions to the linear system?

Augmented matrix $\tilde { \pmb { X } } = [ \pmb { X } \pmb { y } ] \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m \times ( d + 1 ) } : \operatorname { r a n k } ( \pmb { X } ) \leq \operatorname { r a n k } ( \tilde { \pmb { X } } ) .$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02\page_134\DSAA2011-L01_intro-L02_page_134\auto

# Solutions to linear systems

$\circledcirc$ Method: apply Guassian-elimination method to the augmented matrix $\tilde { x }$ .

# Theorem 3.8 (Rouch´e-Capelli Theorem)

The system in (3.20) admits a unique solution if and only $i f \operatorname { r a n k } ( { \pmb X } ) = \operatorname { r a n k } ( { \tilde { \pmb X } } ) = d ;$ The system in (3.20) has no solution if and only $i f \operatorname { r a n k } ( { \pmb X } ) < \operatorname { r a n k } ( { \tilde { \pmb X } } ) ,$ The system in (3.20) has infinitely many solutions if and only if $\mathrm { r a n k } ( { \pmb X } ) = \mathrm { r a n k } ( \tilde { \pmb X } ) < d .$ .

Supervised learning - labeled data: e.g., Prediction

Reinforcement learning - environment feedback: e.g., multi-armed bandit

When do we collect data?

Offline learning • Online learning

# DSAA2011 Machine Learning

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_005\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_005\auto

# Taxonomy of Machine Learning (A Simplistic View)

What type of data?

Supervised learning - labeled data: e.g., prediction   
Semi-supervised learning   
Unsupervised learning - unlabeled data: e.g., clustering Reinforcement learning - environment feedback: e.g., multi-armed bandit

When do we collect data?

Offline learning • Online learning

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_010\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_010\auto

# Function of random variable

If $\boldsymbol { g }$ is a function from the domain of $X$ to $\mathbb { R }$ , we can obtain the expectation of $Y = g ( X )$ in the same way.

Proof. I. Discrete case:

$$
\mathbb { E } Y = \mathbb { E } [ g ( X ) ] = \sum _ { y } y p _ { Y } ( y ) = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } g ( x ) p _ { X } ( x ) .
$$

# Function of random variable

If $\boldsymbol { g }$ is a function from the domain of $X$ to $\mathbb { R }$ , we can obtain the expectation of $Y = g ( X )$ in the same way.

$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_016\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_016\auto

# Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)

![](images/80782f81fa73c6d2d1e22ae56bcf3e054489a36efe1ad04c575aa82a66e21fd2.jpg)

Likelihood: probability of observing the dataset $\mathcal { D }$ given a set of parameters $\theta$ Maximum: seeks the set of parameters $\theta$ that maximizes this likelihood function, i.e., makes the observed dataset as “likely” as possible under the model Concept of MLE: linear regression, logistic regression, . . .

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_017\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_017\auto

# Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)

• Consistency. as the sample size increases to infinity, the estimator will converge to the true parameter value: ${ \hat { \theta } } _ { \mathrm { M L } } \ { \xrightarrow { p } } \ \theta$ as $n  \infty$ .

We say $\quad X _ { n } \longrightarrow X$ as $n \to \infty$ if

$$
\operatorname* { l i m } _ { n  \infty } \mathsf { P r } ( | X _ { n } - X | > \varepsilon ) = 0 \forall \varepsilon > 0 .
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_018\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_018\auto

# Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)

• Consistency. as the sample size increases to infinity, the estimator will converge to the true parameter value: ${ \hat { \theta } } _ { \mathrm { M L } } \ { \xrightarrow { p } } \ \theta$ as $n  \infty$ .

We say $\quad X _ { n } \longrightarrow X$ as $n \to \infty$ if

$$
\operatorname* { l i m } _ { n  \infty } \mathsf { P r } ( | X _ { n } - X | > \varepsilon ) = 0 \forall \varepsilon > 0 .
$$

Unbiasedness. MLE is not necessarily unbiased, but in certain cases, it can be unbiased.

▶ We say an estimator of a given parameter is unbiased if its expected value is equal to the true value of the parameter.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_019\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_019\auto

# Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)

Efficiency. MLE is asymptotically efficient in large samples, i.e., it achieves the lowest possible variance among all unbiased estimators.

▶ Cram´er-Rao Lower Bound (CRLB): theoretical lower bound for the variance of any unbiased estimator.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_020\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_020\auto

# Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)

Efficiency. MLE is asymptotically efficient in large samples, i.e., it achieves the lowest possible variance among all unbiased estimators.

▶ Cram´er-Rao Lower Bound (CRLB): theoretical lower bound for the variance of any unbiased estimator.

Asymptotic Normality. MLE is asymptotically normal:

$\sqrt { n } ( \hat { \theta } _ { \mathrm { M L } } - \theta ) \xrightarrow { d } { \mathcal { N } } ( 0 , I ( \theta ) ^ { - 1 } ) .$

$I ( \theta )$ : Fisher information of $\theta$ ( larger information $\Longrightarrow$ smaller variance).

We say $\quad X _ { n } \longrightarrow X$ as $n \to \infty$

$\operatorname* { l i m } _ { n  \infty } F _ { X _ { n } } ( x ) = F _ { X } ( x ) \ \forall x$ at which $F _ { X } ( x )$ is continuous.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_021\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_021\auto

# Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)

Efficiency. MLE is asymptotically efficient in large samples, i.e., it achieves the lowest possible variance among all unbiased estimators.

▶ Cram´er-Rao Lower Bound (CRLB): theoretical lower bound for the variance of any unbiased estimator.

Asymptotic Normality. MLE is asymptotically normal:

$\sqrt { n } ( \hat { \theta } _ { \mathrm { M L } } - \theta ) \xrightarrow { d } { \mathcal { N } } ( 0 , I ( \theta ) ^ { - 1 } ) .$

$I ( \theta )$ : Fisher information of $\theta$ ( larger information $\Longrightarrow$ smaller variance). We say $\quad X _ { n } \longrightarrow X$ as $n \to \infty$ if

$\operatorname* { l i m } _ { n  \infty } F _ { X _ { n } } ( x ) = F _ { X } ( x ) \ \forall x$ at which $F _ { X } ( x )$ is continuous.

Model Sensitivity. MLE is sensitive to model assumptions, and incorrect assumptions can lead to biased or inconsistent estimates.

Consistency. as the sample size increases to infinity, the estimator will converge to the true parameter value: ${ \hat { \theta } } _ { \mathrm { M L } } \ { \xrightarrow { p } } \theta$ as $n  \infty$ .

• Unbiasedness. MLE is not necessarily unbiased, but in certain cases, it can be unbiased.

Efficiency. MLE is asymptotically efficient in large samples, i.e., it achieves the lowest possible variance among all unbiased estimators.

Asymptotic Normality. MLE is asymptotically normal: $\sqrt { n } ( \hat { \theta } _ { \mathrm { M L } } - \theta ) \xrightarrow { d } { \mathcal { N } } ( 0 , I ( \theta ) ^ { - 1 } ) .$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_024\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_024\auto

# Solutions to linear systems

$\circledcirc$ Method: apply Guassian-elimination method to the augmented matrix $\tilde { \pmb { X } } = [ \pmb { X } \pmb { y } ] .$ .

$$
\underline { { x _ { 2 } } } \ \cdot \cdot \cdot \ \underline { { x _ { d } } } ] \left[ \begin{array} { l } { w _ { 1 } } \\ { w _ { 2 } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { w _ { d } } \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { y _ { 1 } } \\ { y _ { 2 } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { y _ { d } } \end{array} \right] , \ \mathsf { w h e r e } \ \underline { { x } } _ { i } = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { x _ { 1 , i } } \\ { x _ { 2 , i } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { x _ { m , i } } \end{array} \right]
$$

# Theorem 0.1 (Rouch´e-Capelli Theorem)

。 The system in (0.1) admits a unique solution if and only if rank(X ) = rank(X˜ ) = d; The system in (0.1) has no solution if and only $i f \operatorname { r a n k } ( { \pmb X } ) < \operatorname { r a n k } ( { \tilde { \pmb X } } )$ ; The system in (0.1) has infinitely many solutions if and only if $\operatorname { r a n k } ( { \pmb X } ) = \operatorname { r a n k } ( { \tilde { \pmb X } } ) < d$ .

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_029\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_029\auto

# Motivation for linear regression

Consider five indicators (data set from Kaggle):

(a) Hours Studied $x _ { 1 }$ : total number of hours of study;   
(b) Previous Scores $x _ { 2 }$ : scores obtained in previous tests;   
(c) Extracurricular Activities $x _ { 3 }$ : participation in extracurricular activities (Yes/No);   
(d) Sleep Hours $x _ { 4 }$ : average number of hours of sleep per day;   
(e) Sample question papers practiced $x _ { 5 }$ : number of sample question papers practiced

Which factor is most important for determining the student’s performance?

where $x _ { i , 1 }$ is the number of study hours of student $i$ (etc.) and $y _ { i }$ is the student’s performance index.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_032\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_032\auto

# Linear regression

• Linear regression is a linear approach for modelling the relationship between a scalar response $y$ and one or more explanatory variables (or attributes, or features) $\pmb { \times }$ .

We have a dataset $\{ ( \pmb { x } _ { i } , y _ { i } ) : i = 1 , \ldots , m \}$ where $\mathbf { x } _ { i } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ and $y _ { i } \in \mathbb { R }$ are the feature vector and target of the $j .$ -th sample respectively.

Without the offset, we can form the design matrix and the target vector

$$
\mathbf { \Sigma } = \left[ \begin{array} { c c c c c } { x _ { 1 , 1 } } & { x _ { 1 , 2 } } & { \ldots } & { x _ { 1 , d } } \\ { x _ { 2 , 1 } } & { x _ { 2 , 2 } } & { \ldots } & { x _ { 2 , d } } \\ { \vdots } & { \vdots } & { \ddots } & { \vdots } \\ { x _ { m , 1 } } & { x _ { m , 2 } } & { \ldots } & { x _ { m , d } } \end{array} \right] \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m \times d } \qquad \mathbf { y } = \left[ \begin{array} { c } { y _ { 1 } } \\ { y _ { 2 } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { y _ { n } } \end{array} \right]
$$

We wish to find $\pmb { w } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ satisfying (or approximately satisfying) the linear system

$$
\mathbf { x } \mathbf { w } = \mathbf { y } .
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_033\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_033\auto

# Linear regression (with offset)

m: size of the dataset $d$ : dimension/length of each feature vector (input) $y _ { i }$ : scalar or real-valued target/output (e.g., height, exam marks)

# Goal:

Design a function/model/regressor $f _ { { \mathbf { w } } , b }$ as a linear combination of the features in $\pmb { \times }$ , i.e.,

$$
f _ { \mathbf { w } , b } ( \mathbf { x } ) = \mathbf { w } ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } + b ,
$$

where $\pmb { w } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , the unknown, is the $d$ -dimensional weight vector and $b$ is the bias or offset.

The notation $f _ { { \mathbf { w } } , b }$ means that the model is parametrized by two quantities w and $b$ .

Note that the model can also be more compactly written as

$$
f _ { \mathbf { w } , b } ( \mathbf { x } ) = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { b } \\ { \mathbf { w } } \end{array} \right] ^ { \top } \left[ \begin{array} { l } { 1 } \\ { \mathbf { x } } \end{array} \right] .
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_034\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_034\auto

# Objective (loss) function in linear regression

We wish to minimize the error $e _ { j }$ between the prediction $f _ { { \mathbf { w } } , b } ( { \mathbf { x } } _ { i } )$ and the target, where

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \pmb { e } _ { i } = f _ { \mathbf { w } , b } ( \pmb { x } _ { i } ) - y _ { i } . } \end{array}
$$

● We average the square of the errors over all training samples. This defines the objective or loss function

$$
\operatorname { L o s s } ( \boldsymbol { \mathsf { w } } , b ) = \frac { 1 } { m } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } { ( f _ { \boldsymbol { \mathsf { w } } , b } ( \boldsymbol { \mathsf { x } } _ { i } ) - y _ { i } ) ^ { 2 } } .
$$

$\mathrm { L o s s } ( { \boldsymbol { \mathsf { w } } } , { \boldsymbol { b } } )$ is known as the (squared or $\ell _ { 2 }$ ) loss or objective function.

$( f _ { { \mathbf { w } } , b } ( { \mathbf { x } } _ { i } ) - y _ { i } ) ^ { 2 }$ is also called the per-sample loss or objective function and is a measure of the difference or penalty between the prediction $f _ { { \mathbf { w } } , b } ( { \\mathbf { x } } _ { i } )$ and the target $y _ { i }$ .

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_036\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_036\auto

# Objective (loss) function in linear regression

• Define $\overline { { \mathbf { w } } } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d + 1 }$ as the $( d + 1 )$ -dimensional vector that concatenates $b$ and w, i.e.,

$$
{ \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } } = \left[ { b \atop \mathbf { w } } \right] = \left[ { b \atop w _ { 2 } } \right] { \overset { } { = } } \left[ { b \atop { \vdots \atop w _ { d } } } \right] .
$$

Similarly, define $\bar { \pmb { x } } _ { i } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d + 1 }$ as the $( d + 1 )$ -dimensional vector that concatenates 1 and xi

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \bar { \mathbf { x } } _ { i } = \left[ \mathbf { 1 } \right] = \left[ \begin{array} { c } { 1 } \\ { x _ { i , 1 } } \\ { x _ { i , 2 } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { x _ { i , d } } \end{array} \right] . } \end{array}
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_037\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_037\auto

# Objective (loss) function in linear regression

• We wish to find $\overline { { \mathbf { w } } } ^ { * } = [ b ^ { * } , \mathbf { w } ^ { * } ] ^ { \top } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d + 1 }$ that minimizes

$$
\overline { { \mathbf { w } } } ^ { * } = \underset { \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } = [ b , \mathbf { w } ] ^ { \top } } { \mathsf { a r g m i n } } \mathrm { L o s s } ( \mathbf { w } , b )
$$

where the $\ell _ { 2 }$ or squared loss is

$$
\operatorname { L o s s } ( \boldsymbol { \mathsf { w } } , b ) = \frac { 1 } { m } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } \left( f _ { \boldsymbol { \mathsf { w } } , b } ( \mathsf { x } _ { i } ) - y _ { i } \right) ^ { 2 }
$$

The $1 / m$ does not affect the solution so we can choose to include or exclude it.

$$

$$
\sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } { \left( { f _ { \boldsymbol { \mathsf { w } } } } , b \left( { \boldsymbol { \mathsf { x } } } _ { i } \right) - y _ { i } \right) ^ { 2 } } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } { \left( { \overline { { \mathsf { x } } } } _ { i } ^ { \top } \overline { { \boldsymbol { \mathsf { w } } } } - y _ { i } \right) ^ { 2 } } .

\sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } \left( f _ { \mathbf { w } , b } ( \mathbf { x } _ { i } ) - y _ { i } \right) ^ { 2 } = ( \mathbf { \pmb { X } } \mathbf { \overline { { w } } } - \mathbf { y } ) ^ { \top } ( \mathbf { \pmb { X } } \mathbf { \overline { { w } } } - \mathbf { y } )
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_039\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_039\auto

# Optimizing the loss function in linear regression

The objective function is now simplified to

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { = ( \mathsf { X } \overline { { \mathsf { w } } } - \mathsf { y } ) ^ { \top } ( \mathsf { X } \overline { { \mathsf { w } } } - \mathsf { y } ) = \overline { { \mathsf { w } } } ^ { \top } \mathsf { X } ^ { \top } \mathsf { X } \overline { { \mathsf { w } } } - \overline { { \mathsf { w } } } ^ { \top } \mathsf { X } ^ { \top } \mathsf { y } - \mathsf { y } } \\ & { = \overline { { \mathsf { w } } } ^ { \top } \mathsf { X } ^ { \top } \mathsf { X } \overline { { \mathsf { w } } } - 2 \overline { { \mathsf { w } } } ^ { \top } ( \mathsf { X } ^ { \top } \mathsf { y } ) + \mathsf { y } ^ { \top } \mathsf { y } } \end{array}
$$

The terms in blue are the same. Why?

Differentiating this w.r.t. $\overline { { \mathbf { w } } }$ ,

$$
\nabla _ { \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } } J ( \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } ) = 2 \mathbf { X } ^ { \top } \mathbf { X } \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } - 2 \mathbf { X } ^ { \top } \mathbf { y } .
$$

● Setting this to zero yields

$$
2 \mathbf { X } ^ { \top } \mathbf { X } \mathbf { \overline { { w } } } ^ { * } = 2 \mathbf { X } ^ { \top } \mathbf { y } .
$$

If X has full column rank, $\mathbf { x } ^ { \top } \mathbf { x }$ is invertible and

$$
\overline { { \mathbf { w } } } ^ { * } = ( \mathbf { x } ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } ) ^ { - 1 } \mathbf { x } ^ { \top } \mathbf { y } .
$$

This is the least squares solution. Is it a global or local minimum?

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_040\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_040\auto

# Least squares: training and prediction

In summary, given a dataset $\left( \mathbf { x } _ { i } , y _ { i } \right)$ for $i = 1 , 2 , \dots , m _ { \mathrm { \scriptsize ~ \cdot ~ } }$ form the design matrix and target vector

$$
\left[ \bar { \bar { \mathbf { x } } } _ { 1 } ^ { \top } \right] = \left[ \begin{array} { c c } { 1 } & { \mathbf { x } _ { 1 } ^ { \top } } \\ { 1 } & { \mathbf { x } _ { 2 } ^ { \top } } \\ { \vdots } & { \vdots } \\ { \bar { \mathbf { x } } _ { m } ^ { \top } } \end{array} \right] \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m \times ( d + 1 ) } \quad \mathsf { a n d } \quad \mathbf { y } = \left[ \begin{array} { c c } { y _ { 1 } } \\ { y _ { 2 } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { y _ { m } } \end{array} \right]
$$

Training/Learning:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } ^ { * } = \left[ \pmb { b } ^ { * } \right] = ( \pmb { \mathsf { X } } ^ { \top } \pmb { \mathsf { X } } ) ^ { - 1 } \pmb { \mathsf { X } } ^ { \top } \pmb { \mathsf { y } } . } \end{array}
$$

• Prediction/Testing: Given a new training sample $\tt { \bf { x } } _ { \mathrm { { n e w } } }$

$$
\hat { y } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } = \biggl [ \mathbf { 1 } _ { \mathrm { x _ { \mathrm { n e w } } } } \biggr ] ^ { \top } \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } ^ { \ast } = b ^ { \ast } + \mathbf { x } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } ^ { \top } \mathbf { w } ^ { \ast } .
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_045\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_045\auto

# Solutions to linear systems

$\circledcirc$ Method: apply Guassian-elimination method to the augmented matrix $\tilde { x }$ .

$$
\underline { { \boldsymbol { x } } } _ { 2 } \mathbin { \mathrm { ~ . ~ . ~ . ~ } } \underline { { \boldsymbol { x } } } _ { d } ] \left[ \begin{array} { l } { \boldsymbol { w } _ { 1 } } \\ { \boldsymbol { w } _ { 2 } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { \boldsymbol { w } _ { d } } \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { \boldsymbol { y } _ { 1 } } \\ { \boldsymbol { y } _ { 2 } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { \boldsymbol { y } _ { d } } \end{array} \right] \mathrm { , ~ w h e r e ~ } \underline { { \boldsymbol { x } } } _ { i } = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { \boldsymbol { x } _ { 1 , i } } \\ { \boldsymbol { x } _ { 2 , i } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { \boldsymbol { x } _ { m , i } } \end{array} \right]

# Learning vector-valued linear functions: training

● Objective:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \overline { { \mathbf { W } } } ^ { * } = \underset { \mathbf { W } , \mathbf { b } } { \arg \operatorname* { m i n } } \operatorname { L o s s } ( \overline { { \mathbf { W } } } ) \quad \mathrm { w h e r e } \quad \overline { { \mathbf { W } } } = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { \mathbf { b } ^ { \top } } \\ { \mathbf { W } } \end{array} \right] . } \end{array}
$$

• By differentiating with respect to each column $\overline { { \mathbf { w } } } _ { k }$ and setting the result to zero, we find that the least squares solution is

$$
\overline { { \pmb { \mathscr { N } } } } ^ { * } = [ \overline { { \pmb { \mathscr { w } } } } _ { 1 } ^ { * } \quad \overline { { \pmb { \mathscr { w } } } } _ { 2 } ^ { * } \quad . . . \quad \overline { { \pmb { \mathscr { w } } } } _ { h } ^ { * } ] = ( \mathbf { \pmb { \times } } ^ { \top } \mathbf { \pmb { \mathscr { x } } } ) ^ { - 1 } \mathbf { \pmb { \times } } ^ { \top } \mathbf { \pmb { \gamma } } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { ( d - }
$$

This may be an exercise in a tutorial.

In this new setting, what condition does $\pmb { \times }$ have to satisfy for $\overline { { \boldsymbol { \mathsf { W } } } } ^ { * }$ to exist? We need $( { \pmb X } ^ { \top } { \pmb X } ) ^ { - 1 }$ to exist, which means that X has to have full column rank.

$$
\overline { { \mathbf { W } } } ^ { * } = \left[ \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } _ { 1 } ^ { * } \quad \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } _ { 2 } ^ { * } \quad \ldots \quad \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } _ { h } ^ { * } \right] = ( \mathsf { X } ^ { \top } \mathsf { \mathbf { X } } ) ^ { - 1 } \mathsf { \mathbf { X } } ^ { \top } \mathsf { \pmb { Y } } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { ( }
$$

• Given a new sample $\mathbf { x } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , the predictions are contained in the row vector

\begin{array} { r } { \hat { { \mathbf { y } } } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } = \left[ \begin{array} { c } { 1 } \\ { { \mathbf { x } } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } } \end{array} \right] ^ { \top } \overline { { { \mathbf { W } } } } ^ { * } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { 1 \times h } . } \end{array}
$$

and targets are

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_066\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_066\auto

# Summary

(Learning/Training) Given a dataset $\{ ( \mathbf { x } _ { i } , y _ { i } ) \} _ { i = 1 } ^ { m }$ where $\mathbf { x } _ { i } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ and $y _ { i } \in \mathbb { R }$ , the least squares solution (with offset) is

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } ^ { * } = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { b ^ { * } } \\ { \mathbf { w } ^ { * } } \end{array} \right] = ( \mathbf { X } ^ { \top } \mathbf { X } ) ^ { - 1 } \mathbf { X } ^ { \top } \mathbf { y } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d + 1 } } \end{array}
$$

where

$$
\left[ \begin{array} { c } { \overline { { \mathbf { x } } } _ { 1 } ^ { \top } } \\ { \overline { { \mathbf { x } } } _ { 2 } ^ { \top } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { \overline { { \mathbf { x } } } _ { m } ^ { \top } } \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array} { c c } { 1 } & { \mathbf { x } _ { 1 } ^ { \top } } \\ { 1 } & { \mathbf { x } _ { 2 } ^ { \top } } \\ { \vdots } & { \vdots } \\ { 1 } & { \mathbf { x } _ { m } ^ { \top } } \end{array} \right] \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m \times ( d + 1 ) } \quad \mathsf { a n d } \quad \mathbf { y } = \left[ \begin{array} { c } { y _ { 1 } } \\ { y _ { 2 } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { y _ { m } } \end{array} \right]
$$

(Prediction/Testing) Given a new feature vector (sample, example) $\mathbf { x } _ { \mathrm { n e w } }$ , the prediction based on the least squares solution is

$$
\hat { y } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } = \biggl [ \mathbf { 1 } _ { \mathrm { x _ { \mathrm { n e w } } } } \biggr ] ^ { \top } \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } ^ { \ast } = b ^ { \ast } + \mathbf { x } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } ^ { \top } \mathbf { w } ^ { \ast } .
$$

# Objective (loss) function in linear regression

$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_076\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_076\auto

# MLE and linear regression

Maximizing the Log-Likelihood: take the derivative of the log-likelihood function with respect to $\overline { { \mathbf { w } } }$ and set it equal to a $( d + 1 )$ -dimensional zero vector:

$$
\operatorname { g } L \left( { \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } } , \sigma ^ { 2 } \mid \left\{ y _ { i } , \mathbf { x } _ { i } \right\} \right) = { \frac { 1 } { \sigma ^ { 2 } } } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } \left( y _ { i } - { \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } } ^ { \top } { \overline { { \mathbf { x } } } } _ { i } \right) { \overline { { \mathbf { x } } } } _ { i } = \mathbf { 0 }
$$

If ${ \pmb X } = \left[ \overline { { \pmb x } } _ { 1 } ^ { \top } \ \overline { { \pmb x } } _ { 2 } ^ { \top } \ \hdots \ \overline { { \pmb x } } _ { n } ^ { \top } \right] ^ { \top }$ has full column rank, X⊤X is invertible and

$$
\begin{array} { l } { \hat { \pmb w } = ( { \pmb x } ^ { \top } { \pmb x } ) ^ { - 1 } { \pmb x } ^ { \top } { \pmb y } , } \\ { \hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 } = \displaystyle \frac { 1 } { m } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } ( y _ { i } - \Big [ 1 ~ x _ { i } ^ { \top } \Big ] \cdot \hat { \pmb w } ) ^ { 2 } = \frac { 1 } { m } ( { \pmb x } \hat { \pmb w } - { \pmb y } ) ^ { \top } ( { \pmb x } } \end{array}
$$

$( \hat { \pmb w } , \hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 } )$ is the maximizer of $L \left( \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } , \sigma ^ { 2 } \mid \{ y _ { i } , \mathbf { x } _ { i } \} \right) .$

# MLE and linear regression

Maximizing the Log-Likelihood: take the derivative of the log-likelihood function with respect to $\overline { { \mathbf { w } } }$ and set it equal to a $( d + 1 )$ -dimensional zero vector:

$$
\operatorname { g } L \left( { \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } } , \sigma ^ { 2 } \mid \left\{ y _ { i } , \mathbf { x } _ { i } \right\} \right) = { \frac { 1 } { \sigma ^ { 2 } } } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } \left( y _ { i } - { \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } } ^ { \top } { \overline { { \mathbf { x } } } } _ { i } \right) { \overline { { \mathbf { x } } } } _ { i } = \mathbf { 0 }
$$

If ${ \pmb X } = \left[ \overline { { \pmb x } } _ { 1 } ^ { \top } \ \overline { { \pmb x } } _ { 2 } ^ { \top } \ \hdots \ \overline { { \pmb x } } _ { n } ^ { \top } \right] ^ { \top }$ has full column rank, X⊤X is invertible and

$$
\begin{array} { l } { \hat { \pmb w } = ( { \pmb x } ^ { \top } { \pmb x } ) ^ { - 1 } { \pmb x } ^ { \top } { \pmb y } , } \\ { \hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 } = \displaystyle \frac { 1 } { m } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } ( y _ { i } - \Big [ 1 ~ x _ { i } ^ { \top } \Big ] \cdot \hat { \pmb w } ) ^ { 2 } = \frac { 1 } { m } ( { \pmb x } \hat { \pmb w } - { \pmb y } ) ^ { \top } ( { \pmb x } } \end{array}
$$

$( \hat { \pmb w } , \hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 } )$ is the maximizer of $L \left( \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } , \sigma ^ { 2 } \mid \{ y _ { i } , \mathbf { x } _ { i } \} \right) .$

# MLE and linear regression

Assume $y _ { i } = \mathbf { w } ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } _ { i } + b + e _ { i }$ for each data point $i$ and error $\boldsymbol { e } _ { i } \sim \mathcal { N } \left( 0 , \sigma ^ { 2 } \right)$ . Likelihood function for the entire dataset $\{ ( \mathsf { x } _ { i } , y _ { i } ) \} _ { i = 1 } ^ { m }$ is

$$
\left( \mathbf { W } , \sigma ^ { 2 } \mid \{ y _ { i } , \mathbf { x } _ { i } \} \right) = \prod _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } { \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 2 \pi \sigma ^ { 2 } } } } \exp \left( - { \frac { \left( y _ { i } - \mathbf { W } ^ { \top } \right) } { 2 \sigma ^ { 2 } } } \right.
$$

• If X has full column rank, $\mathbf { x } ^ { \top } \mathbf { x }$ is invertible and the maximizer $( \hat { \mathbf { w } } , \hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 } )$ is:

wˆ = (X⊤X)−1X⊤y (least squares solution),

$$
\dot { \bar { \mathbf { \rho } } } ^ { 2 } = \frac { 1 } { m } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } ( y _ { i } - \left[ 1 \mathbf { \rho } x _ { i } ^ { \top } \right] \cdot \hat { \mathbf { w } } ) ^ { 2 } = \frac { 1 } { m } ( \mathbf { \nabla } \times \hat { \mathbf { w } } - \mathbf { y } ) ^ { \top } ( \mathbf { \nabla } \times \hat { \mathbf { w } }
$$

$\odot$ MLE of distribution of error: $e _ { i } \sim \mathcal { N } ( 0 , \hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 } ) = \mathcal { N } ( 0 , ( \pmb { \times } \hat { \mathbf { w } } - \mathbf { y } ) ^ { \top } ( \pmb { \times } \hat { \mathbf { w } } - \mathbf { y } ) / m ) .$

# MLE and linear regression: why Gaussian noise?

# Theorem 1.3 (Central limit theorem (CLT))

Suppose $X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } , X _ { 3 } \ldots$ . is a sequence of i.i.d. random variables with $\operatorname { E } \left[ X _ { i } \right] = \mu$ and Var $[ X _ { i } ] = \sigma ^ { 2 } < \infty$ . Then, as $n  \infty$ , the distribution of $\sqrt { n } \left( { \bar { X } } _ { n } - \mu \right)$ converges to ${ \mathcal { N } } \left( 0 , \sigma ^ { 2 } \right)$ :

$$
\sqrt { n } \left( \bar { X } _ { n } - \mu \right) \overset { d } { \to } \mathcal { N } \left( 0 , \sigma ^ { 2 } \right)
$$

# MLE and linear regression: why Gaussian noise?

# Theorem 1.3 (Central limit theorem (CLT))

Suppose $X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } , X _ { 3 } \ldots$ . is a sequence of i.i.d. random variables with $\operatorname { E } \left[ X _ { i } \right] = \mu$ and Var $[ X _ { i } ] = \sigma ^ { 2 } < \infty$ . Then, as $n  \infty$ , the distribution of $\sqrt { n } \left( { \bar { X } } _ { n } - \mu \right)$ converges to ${ \mathcal { N } } \left( 0 , \sigma ^ { 2 } \right)$ :

$$
\sqrt { n } \left( \bar { X } _ { n } - \mu \right) \overset { d } { \to } \mathcal { N } \left( 0 , \sigma ^ { 2 } \right)
$$

We say $\quad X _ { n } \longrightarrow X$ as $n \to \infty$ if

$\operatorname* { l i m } _ { n  \infty } F _ { X _ { n } } ( x ) = F _ { X } ( x ) \ \forall x$ at which $F _ { X } ( x )$ is continuous.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_087\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_087\auto

# MLE and linear regression: why Gaussian noise?

# Theorem 1.3 (Central limit theorem (CLT))

Suppose $X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } , X _ { 3 } \ldots$ . is a sequence of i.i.d. random variables with $\operatorname { E } \left[ X _ { i } \right] = \mu$ and Var $[ X _ { i } ] = \sigma ^ { 2 } < \infty$ . Then, as $n  \infty$ , the distribution of $\sqrt { n } \left( { \bar { X } } _ { n } - \mu \right)$ converges to ${ \mathcal { N } } \left( 0 , \sigma ^ { 2 } \right)$ :

$$
\sqrt { n } \left( \bar { X } _ { n } - \mu \right) \overset { d } { \to } \mathcal { N } \left( 0 , \sigma ^ { 2 } \right)
$$

We say $\quad X _ { n } \longrightarrow X$ as $n \to \infty$ if

$\operatorname* { l i m } _ { n  \infty } F _ { X _ { n } } ( x ) = F _ { X } ( x ) \ \forall x$ at which $F _ { X } ( x )$ is continuous.

In the case $\sigma > 0$ , CLT implies that the cumulative distribution functions (cdf) of $\sqrt { n } \left( { \bar { X } } _ { n } - \mu \right)$ converge pointwise to the cdf of the ${ \mathcal { N } } \left( 0 , \sigma ^ { 2 } \right)$ distribution:

$$
\sqrt { n } ( \bar { X } _ { n } - \mu ) \leq z ] = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } \mathbb { P } [ \frac { \sqrt { n } ( \bar { X } _ { n } - \mu ) } { \sigma } \leq \frac { z } { \sigma } ]
$$

where $\Phi ( z )$ is the standard normal cdf evaluated at $z$ . Zixin Zhong (HKUTS-GZ)

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_095\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_095\auto

# Numerical example for binary classification

Using some numerical software, we can find the least square approximation

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } ^ { * } = ( \mathbf { X } ^ { \top } \mathbf { X } ) ^ { - 1 } \mathbf { X } ^ { \top } \mathbf { y } = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { 0 . 2 9 6 7 } \\ { 0 . 1 9 7 8 } \end{array} \right] . } \end{array}
$$

• If we want to predict what’s the label for ${ \tt x } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } = - 2$ , we plug ${ \tt x } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } = - 2$ into the learned affine model to get

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \hat { y } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } = \mathrm { s i g n } \left( \left[ \begin{array} { l } { 1 } \\ { \mathsf { x } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } } \end{array} \right] ^ { \top } \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } ^ { * } \right) } \\ & { \qquad = \mathrm { s i g n } \left( 1 \times ( 0 . 2 9 6 7 ) + ( - 2 ) \times ( 0 . 1 9 7 8 ) \right) } \\ & { \qquad = \mathrm { s i g n } ( - 0 . 0 9 8 9 ) = - 1 . } \end{array}
$$

So we predict that the label of the new test point ${ \tt x } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } = - 2$ is $\hat { y } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } = - 1$ (negative class).

# Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)

• Consistency. as the sample size increases to infinity, the estimator will converge to the true parameter value: ${ \hat { \theta } } _ { \mathrm { M L } } \ { \xrightarrow { p } } \ \theta$ as $n  \infty$ .

We say $\quad X _ { n } \longrightarrow X$ as $n \to \infty$ if

$$
\operatorname* { l i m } _ { n  \infty } \mathsf { P r } ( | X _ { n } - X | > \varepsilon ) = 0 \forall \varepsilon > 0 .
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_101\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_101\auto

# Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)

• Consistency. as the sample size increases to infinity, the estimator will converge to the true parameter value: ${ \hat { \theta } } _ { \mathrm { M L } } \ { \xrightarrow { p } } \ \theta$ as $n  \infty$ .

We say $\quad X _ { n } \longrightarrow X$ as $n \to \infty$ if

$$
\operatorname* { l i m } _ { n  \infty } \mathsf { P r } ( | X _ { n } - X | > \varepsilon ) = 0 \forall \varepsilon > 0 .
$$

Unbiasedness. MLE is not necessarily unbiased, but in certain cases, it can be unbiased.

▶ We say an estimator of a given parameter is unbiased if its expected value is equal to the true value of the parameter.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_102\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_102\auto

# Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)

Efficiency. MLE is asymptotically efficient in large samples, i.e., it achieves the lowest possible variance among all unbiased estimators.

▶ Cram´er-Rao Lower Bound (CRLB): theoretical lower bound for the variance of any unbiased estimator.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_103\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_103\auto

# Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)

Efficiency. MLE is asymptotically efficient in large samples, i.e., it achieves the lowest possible variance among all unbiased estimators.

▶ Cram´er-Rao Lower Bound (CRLB): theoretical lower bound for the variance of any unbiased estimator.

Asymptotic Normality. MLE is asymptotically normal:

$\sqrt { n } ( \hat { \theta } _ { \mathrm { M L } } - \theta ) \xrightarrow { d } { \mathcal { N } } ( 0 , I ( \theta ) ^ { - 1 } ) .$

$I ( \theta )$ : Fisher information of $\theta$ ( larger information $\Longrightarrow$ smaller variance).

We say $\quad X _ { n } \longrightarrow X$ as $n \to \infty$

$\operatorname* { l i m } _ { n  \infty } F _ { X _ { n } } ( x ) = F _ { X } ( x ) \ \forall x$ at which $F _ { X } ( x )$ is continuous.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_104\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_104\auto

# Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)

Efficiency. MLE is asymptotically efficient in large samples, i.e., it achieves the lowest possible variance among all unbiased estimators.

▶ Cram´er-Rao Lower Bound (CRLB): theoretical lower bound for the variance of any unbiased estimator.

Asymptotic Normality. MLE is asymptotically normal:

$\sqrt { n } ( \hat { \theta } _ { \mathrm { M L } } - \theta ) \xrightarrow { d } { \mathcal { N } } ( 0 , I ( \theta ) ^ { - 1 } ) .$

$I ( \theta )$ : Fisher information of $\theta$ ( larger information $\Longrightarrow$ smaller variance). We say $\quad X _ { n } \longrightarrow X$ as $n \to \infty$ if

$\operatorname* { l i m } _ { n  \infty } F _ { X _ { n } } ( x ) = F _ { X } ( x ) \ \forall x$ at which $F _ { X } ( x )$ is continuous.

Model Sensitivity. MLE is sensitive to model assumptions, and incorrect assumptions can lead to biased or inconsistent estimates.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_105\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_105\auto

# Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)

Consistency. as the sample size increases to infinity, the estimator will converge to the true parameter value: ${ \hat { \theta } } _ { \mathrm { M L } } \ { \xrightarrow { p } } \theta$ as $n  \infty$ .

• Unbiasedness. MLE is not necessarily unbiased, but in certain cases, it can be unbiased.

Efficiency. MLE is asymptotically efficient in large samples, i.e., it achieves the lowest possible variance among all unbiased estimators.

Asymptotic Normality. MLE is asymptotically normal: $\sqrt { n } ( \hat { \theta } _ { \mathrm { M L } } - \theta ) \xrightarrow { d } { \mathcal { N } } ( 0 , I ( \theta ) ^ { - 1 } ) .$

Model Sensitivity. MLE is sensitive to model assumptions, and incorrect assumptions can lead to biased or inconsistent estimates.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_106\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_106\auto

# Linear regression

Learning/Training: Given a dataset $\{ ( \mathbf { x } _ { i } , y _ { i } ) \} _ { i = 1 } ^ { m }$ where $\mathbf { x } _ { i } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ and $y _ { i } \in \mathbb { R }$ , the least squares solution (with offset) is

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } ^ { * } = \left[ \pmb { b } ^ { * } \right] = ( \pmb { \mathsf { X } } ^ { \top } \pmb { \mathsf { X } } ) ^ { - 1 } \pmb { \mathsf { X } } ^ { \top } \pmb { \mathsf { y } } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d + 1 } } \end{array}
$$

where the design matrix and target vector are

$$
\mathbf { X } = \left[ \begin{array} { c c } { - \overline { { \mathbf { x } } } _ { 1 } ^ { \top } - } \\ { - \overline { { \mathbf { x } } } _ { 2 } ^ { \top } - } \\ { \vdots } \\ { - \overline { { \mathbf { x } } } _ { m } ^ { \top } - } \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array} { c c } { 1 } & { - \mathbf { x } _ { 1 } ^ { \top } - } \\ { 1 } & { - \mathbf { x } _ { 2 } ^ { \top } - } \\ { \vdots } & { \vdots } \\ { 1 } & { - \mathbf { x } _ { m } ^ { \top } - } \end{array} \right] \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m \times ( d + 1 ) }
$$

Prediction/Testing: Given a new feature vector (sample, example) $\mathbf { x } _ { \mathrm { n e w } }$ , the prediction based on the least squares solution is

$$
\hat { y } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } = \biggl [ \mathbf { 1 } _ { \mathrm { { n e w } } } \biggr ] ^ { \top } \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } ^ { \ast } = b ^ { \ast } + \mathbf { x } _ { \mathrm { { n e w } } } ^ { \top } \mathbf { w } ^ { \ast } .
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_109\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_109\auto

# Linear regression with multiple outputs

Learning/Training: Least Squares Solution

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \overline { { \mathbf { W } } } ^ { * } = ( \mathbf { X } ^ { \top } \mathbf { X } ) ^ { - 1 } \mathbf { X } ^ { \top } \mathbf { Y } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { ( d + 1 ) \times h } . } \end{array}
$$

Prediction/Testing: Given a new feature vector $\mathbf { x } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , we can predict its $h$ outputs as

$$
\widehat { \mathbf { y } } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } = \left[ \mathbf { 1 } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } \right] ^ { \top } \overline { { \mathbf { W } } } ^ { * } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { 1 \times h }
$$

• The $k$ -th $( 1 \leq k \leq h )$ component of $\hat { \bf y } _ { \mathrm { n e w } }$ is the prediction of the $k$ -th output based the dataset $\{ ( \mathbf { x } _ { i } , \mathbf { y } _ { i } ) \} _ { i = 1 } ^ { m }$ .

$\circledcirc$ Is the matrix X⊤X invertible?

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a\page_110\DSAA2011-L02_supervised_a_page_110\auto

# MLE and linear regression

Assume $y _ { i } = \mathbf { w } ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } _ { i } + b + e _ { i }$ for each data point $i$ and error $\boldsymbol { e } _ { i } \sim \mathcal { N } \left( 0 , \sigma ^ { 2 } \right)$ . Likelihood function for the entire dataset $\{ ( \mathsf { x } _ { i } , y _ { i } ) \} _ { i = 1 } ^ { m }$ is

$$
\left( \mathbf { W } , \sigma ^ { 2 } \mid \{ y _ { i } , \mathbf { x } _ { i } \} \right) = \prod _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } { \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 2 \pi \sigma ^ { 2 } } } } \exp \left( - { \frac { \left( y _ { i } - \mathbf { W } ^ { \top } \right) } { 2 \sigma ^ { 2 } } } \right.
$$

• If X has full column rank, $\mathbf { x } ^ { \top } \mathbf { x }$ is invertible and the maximizer $( \hat { \mathbf { w } } , \hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 } )$ is:

wˆ = (X⊤X)−1X⊤y (least squares solution),

$$
\dot { \bar { \mathbf { \rho } } } ^ { 2 } = \frac { 1 } { m } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } ( y _ { i } - \left[ 1 \mathbf { \rho } x _ { i } ^ { \top } \right] \cdot \hat { \mathbf { w } } ) ^ { 2 } = \frac { 1 } { m } ( \mathbf { \nabla } \times \hat { \mathbf { w } } - \mathbf { y } ) ^ { \top } ( \mathbf { \nabla } \times \hat { \mathbf { w } }
$$

$\odot$ MLE of distribution of error: $e _ { i } \sim \mathcal { N } ( 0 , \hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 } ) = \mathcal { N } ( 0 , ( \pmb { \times } \hat { \mathbf { w } } - \mathbf { y } ) ^ { \top } ( \pmb { \times } \hat { \mathbf { w } } - \mathbf { y } ) / m ) .$

Main idea: to treat binary classification as regression where each label $y _ { i }$ can only take on $^ { - 1 }$ or $+ 1$ .

Learning/Training: given a dataset $\{ ( \mathbf { x } _ { i } , y _ { i } ) \} _ { i = 1 } ^ { m }$ (where each $y _ { i } \in \{ + 1 , - 1 \} )$ , learn the weights using least squares

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } ^ { * } = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { b ^ { * } } \\ { \mathbf { w } ^ { * } } \end{array} \right] = ( \mathbf { X } ^ { \top } \mathbf { X } ) ^ { - 1 } \mathbf { X } ^ { \top } \mathbf { y } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d + 1 } . } \end{array}
$$

Prediction/Testing: given a new data sample $\mathbf { x } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , its predicted label is

$$
\mathbf { \Sigma } _ { \mathbf { \Sigma } ^ { \mathbf { \Sigma } } } = \mathrm { s i g n } \left( \mathbf { \bar { x } } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } ^ { \top } \mathbf { \overline { { w } } } ^ { * } \right) = \mathrm { s i g n } \left( \left[ \mathbf { \Sigma } _ { \mathbf { x } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } } ^ { 1 } \right] ^ { \top } \mathbf { \overline { { w } } } ^ { * } \right) \in \{ + 1 ,
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L03_supervised_b\page_006\DSAA2011-L03_supervised_b_page_006\auto

# Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)

• Consistency. as the sample size increases to infinity, the estimator will converge to the true parameter value: ${ \hat { \theta } } _ { \mathrm { M L } } \ { \xrightarrow { p } } \ \theta$ as $n  \infty$ .

We say $\quad X _ { n } \longrightarrow X$ as $n \to \infty$ if

$$
\operatorname* { l i m } _ { n  \infty } \mathsf { P r } ( | X _ { n } - X | > \varepsilon ) = 0 \forall \varepsilon > 0 .
$$

Unbiasedness. MLE is not necessarily unbiased, but in certain cases, it can be unbiased.

▶ We say an estimator of a given parameter is unbiased if its expected value is equal to the true value of the parameter.

$I ( \theta )$ : Fisher information of $\theta$ ( larger information $\Longrightarrow$ smaller variance). We say $\quad X _ { n } \longrightarrow X$ as $n \to \infty$ if

# MLE and linear regression

Assume $y _ { i } = \mathbf { w } ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } _ { i } + b + e _ { i }$ for each data point $i$ and error $\boldsymbol { e } _ { i } \sim \mathcal { N } \left( 0 , \sigma ^ { 2 } \right)$ . Likelihood function for the entire dataset $\{ ( \mathsf { x } _ { i } , y _ { i } ) \} _ { i = 1 } ^ { m }$ is

$$
\left( \mathbf { W } , \sigma ^ { 2 } \mid \{ y _ { i } , \mathbf { x } _ { i } \} \right) = \prod _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } { \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 2 \pi \sigma ^ { 2 } } } } \exp \left( - { \frac { \left( y _ { i } - \mathbf { W } ^ { \top } \right) } { 2 \sigma ^ { 2 } } } \right.
$$

• If X has full column rank, $\mathbf { x } ^ { \top } \mathbf { x }$ is invertible and the maximizer $( \hat { \mathbf { w } } , \hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 } )$ is:

wˆ = (X⊤X)−1X⊤y (least squares solution),

$$
\dot { \bar { \mathbf { \rho } } } ^ { 2 } = \frac { 1 } { m } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } ( y _ { i } - \left[ 1 \mathbf { \rho } x _ { i } ^ { \top } \right] \cdot \hat { \mathbf { w } } ) ^ { 2 } = \frac { 1 } { m } ( \mathbf { \nabla } \times \hat { \mathbf { w } } - \mathbf { y } ) ^ { \top } ( \mathbf { \nabla } \times \hat { \mathbf { w } }
$$

$\odot$ MLE of distribution of error: $e _ { i } \sim \mathcal { N } ( 0 , \hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 } ) = \mathcal { N } ( 0 , ( \pmb { \times } \hat { \mathbf { w } } - \mathbf { y } ) ^ { \top } ( \pmb { \times } \hat { \mathbf { w } } - \mathbf { y } ) / m ) .$

# MLE and linear regression: why Gaussian noise?

# Theorem 0.1 (Central limit theorem (CLT))

Suppose $X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } , X _ { 3 } \ldots$ . is a sequence of i.i.d. random variables with $\operatorname { E } \left[ X _ { i } \right] = \mu$ and Var $[ X _ { i } ] = \sigma ^ { 2 } < \infty$ . Then, as $n  \infty$ , the distribution of $\sqrt { n } \left( { \bar { X } } _ { n } - \mu \right)$ converges to ${ \mathcal { N } } \left( 0 , \sigma ^ { 2 } \right)$ :

$$
\sqrt { n } \left( \bar { X } _ { n } - \mu \right) \overset { d } { \to } \mathcal { N } \left( 0 , \sigma ^ { 2 } \right)
$$

# MLE and linear regression: why Gaussian noise?

# Theorem 0.1 (Central limit theorem (CLT))

Suppose $X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } , X _ { 3 } \ldots$ . is a sequence of i.i.d. random variables with $\operatorname { E } \left[ X _ { i } \right] = \mu$ and Var $[ X _ { i } ] = \sigma ^ { 2 } < \infty$ . Then, as $n  \infty$ , the distribution of $\sqrt { n } \left( { \bar { X } } _ { n } - \mu \right)$ converges to ${ \mathcal { N } } \left( 0 , \sigma ^ { 2 } \right)$ :

$$
\sqrt { n } \left( \bar { X } _ { n } - \mu \right) \overset { d } { \to } \mathcal { N } \left( 0 , \sigma ^ { 2 } \right)
$$

We say $\quad X _ { n } \longrightarrow X$ as $n \to \infty$ if

$\operatorname* { l i m } _ { n  \infty } F _ { X _ { n } } ( x ) = F _ { X } ( x ) \ \forall x$ at which $F _ { X } ( x )$ is continuous.
