## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_024\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_024\auto

# Variation/convergence of gradient descent (GD)

Standard GD: $\mathbf { w } _ { k + 1 }  \mathbf { w } _ { k } - \eta \nabla _ { \mathbf { w } } C ( \mathbf { w } _ { k } )$

◦ Changing learning rate:

Decreasing learning rate, Adagrad (Adaptive Gradient Algorithm) with adaptive learning rate

◦ Different ‘gradient’:

Momentum-based GD, Nesterov Accelerated Gradient (NAG)

◦ Design of cost function:

Batched GD, Stochastic GD, Mini-Batch GD

Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation), Newton

$\odot$ Book: ‘Convex Optimization’ by Stephen Boyd and Lieven Vandenberghe Available at https://stanford.edu/\~boyd/cvxbook/

function/sigmoid

Logistic regression: given a sample $\pmb { \times }$ and the parameters $( \theta , \theta _ { 0 } )$ , we set the probability of label $y = 1$ as

$$
| \textbf { x } , \theta , \theta _ { 0 } ) = g ( \langle \theta , \mathbf { x } \rangle + \theta _ { 0 } ) = \frac { 1 }  1 + \exp ( - ( \langle \theta , \mathbf { x } \rangle + 
$$

This is known as the class conditional probability.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_039\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_039\auto

# Logistic regression: Why?

One way to derive the form of the logistic function: $\odot$ The log-odds of the predicted class probabilities should be a linear function of the inputs

$$
\log \frac { \mathsf { P r } \left( y = 1 \mid \mathbf { x } , \pmb { \theta } , \theta _ { 0 } \right) } { \mathsf { P r } \left( y = - 1 \mid \mathbf { x } , \pmb { \theta } , \theta _ { 0 } \right) } = \langle \pmb { \theta } , \mathbf { x } \rangle + \theta _ { 0 } .
$$

### Images:
- data\1. Machine_Learning\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_039\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_039\auto\images\d1a0d7cded8d92fad4cc836f42273cb29d4c0487fff83e51e44ad18b6f52cab4.jpg

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_040\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_040\auto

# Logistic regression: Why?

One way to derive the form of the logistic function: $\odot$ The log-odds of the predicted class probabilities should be a linear function of the inputs

$$
\log \frac { \mathsf { P r } \left( y = 1 \mid \mathbf { x } , \pmb { \theta } , \theta _ { 0 } \right) } { \mathsf { P r } \left( y = - 1 \mid \mathbf { x } , \pmb { \theta } , \theta _ { 0 } \right) } = \langle \pmb { \theta } , \mathbf { x } \rangle + \theta _ { 0 } .
$$

Since $\mathsf { P r } ( y = 1 \mid E ) = 1 - \mathsf { P r } ( y = - 1 \mid E )$ (probabilities add to 1), we have

$$
\log \frac { \mathsf { P r } \left( y = 1 \mid \mathbf { x } , \pmb { \theta } , \theta _ { 0 } \right) } { 1 - \mathsf { P r } \left( y = 1 \mid \mathbf { x } , \pmb { \theta } , \theta _ { 0 } \right) } = \langle \pmb { \theta } , \mathbf { x } \rangle + \theta _ { 0 } .
$$

C Solving this for $\mathsf { P r } \left( y = 1 \mid \mathsf { x } , \pmb { \theta } , \theta _ { 0 } \right)$ yields the logistic regression model in (1.2) with logistic function in (1.1).

$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_042\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_042\auto

# Samples on the boundary

Sample x sits on the decision boundary:

$$
\left. \pmb { \theta } , \mathbf { x } \right. + \theta _ { 0 } = 0 .
$$

$\Rightarrow$ We are maximally uncertain about its label:

$$
\mathsf { P r } \left( y = 1 \mid \mathbf { x } , \pmb { \theta } , \theta _ { 0 } \right) = \mathsf { P r } \left( y = - 1 \mid \mathbf { x } , \pmb { \theta } , \theta _ { 0 } \right) = 1 / 2
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_043\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_043\auto

# Samples on the boundary

Sample x sits on the decision boundary:

$$
\left. \pmb { \theta } , \mathbf { x } \right. + \theta _ { 0 } = 0 .
$$

$\Rightarrow$ We are maximally uncertain about its label:

$$
\mathsf { P r } \left( y = 1 \mid \mathbf { x } , \pmb { \theta } , \theta _ { 0 } \right) = \mathsf { P r } \left( y = - 1 \mid \mathbf { x } , \pmb { \theta } , \theta _ { 0 } \right) = 1 / 2
$$

• Logistic regression is known as a generalized linear model because the class conditional probabilities are a function (namely $\boldsymbol { g }$ ) of a linear function of the sample $\pmb { \times }$

$$
\mathsf { P r } \left( y = 1 \mid \mathbf { x } , \pmb { \theta } , \theta _ { 0 } \right) = \frac { 1 } { 1 + \mathsf { e x p } \left( - \left( \langle \pmb { \theta } , \mathbf { x } \rangle + \theta _ { 0 } \right) \right) } .
$$

, \theta , \theta _ { 0 } \mathbf { \Psi } , \theta _ { } \mathbf { \Psi } , \theta _ { } \mathbf { \Psi } , \theta _ { } \mathbf { \Psi } , \theta _ { } \mathbf { \Psi } , \theta _ { } \mathbf { \Psi } , \theta _ { } \mathbf { \Psi } , \theta _ { } \mathbf { \Psi } , \theta _ { } \mathbf { \Psi } , \theta _ { } \mathbf { \Psi } , \theta _ { } \mathbf { \Psi } , \theta _ { } \mathbf { \Psi } .

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_046\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_046\auto

# Logistic regression: How?

Estimate parameters $( \theta , \theta _ { 0 } )$ with MLE.

Given the logistic regression probabilistic model

$$
, \theta , \theta _ { 0 } \mathbf { \Psi } , \theta _ { } \mathbf { \Psi } , \theta _ { } \mathbf { \Psi } , \theta _ { } \mathbf { \Psi } , \theta _ { } \mathbf { \Psi } , \theta _ { } \mathbf { \Psi } , \theta _ { } \mathbf { \Psi } , \theta _ { } \mathbf { \Psi } , \theta _ { } \mathbf { \Psi } , \theta _ { } \mathbf { \Psi } , \theta _ { } \mathbf { \Psi } , \theta _ { } \mathbf { \Psi } .
$$

we want to learn the parameters given the dataset $\mathcal { D } = \{ ( \mathbf { x } _ { t } , y _ { t } ) _ { t } \}$

Maximize the probability of seeing the dataset $\mathcal { D }$ over all the parameters $( \theta , \theta _ { 0 } )$ . Likelihood of $\left( \mathbf { x } _ { t } , y _ { t } \right)$ given $( \theta , \theta _ { 0 } )$ : probability of seeing one sample $\left( \mathbf { x } _ { t } , y _ { t } \right)$ given that the current parameters are $( \theta , \theta _ { 0 } )$ is

$$
\mid \mathbf { x } _ { t } , y _ { t } \rangle : = \mathsf { P r } \big ( y _ { t } \mid \mathbf { x } _ { t } , \boldsymbol { \theta } , \boldsymbol { \theta } _ { 0 } \big ) = g \big ( y _ { t } ( \langle \mathbf { x } _ { t } , \boldsymbol { \theta } \rangle + \boldsymbol { \theta } _ { 0 } ) \big )
$$

Is this a good formulation?

Assumption: samples are independent.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_050\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_050\auto

# Why MLE

J Obtain maximum likelihood estimates (MLE) of the parameters by maximizing this conditional likelihood with respect to $\pmb \theta$ and $\theta _ { 0 }$ .

Assumptions:

Right model class is selected: e.g., logistic regression model. Certain regularity conditions hold: e.g., l 2-norm. ‘Likelihood’: $L ( \pmb { \theta } , \theta _ { 0 } \mid \mathcal { D } ) + \lambda | | \pmb { \theta } | | _ { 2 }$

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_051\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_051\auto

# Why MLE

J Obtain maximum likelihood estimates (MLE) of the parameters by maximizing this conditional likelihood with respect to $\pmb \theta$ and $\theta _ { 0 }$ .

Assumptions:

Right model class is selected: e.g., logistic regression model.

Certain regularity conditions hold: e.g., l2-norm. ‘Likelihood’: $L ( \pmb { \theta } , \theta _ { 0 } \mid \mathcal { D } ) + \lambda | | \pmb { \theta } | | _ { 2 }$

J MLE has many nice properties (considering $| \hat { \pmb { \theta } } _ { n } - \pmb { \theta } | )$ : θˆn → θ as n → ∞.

Consistent/unbiased with l 2-norm (we will get the right parameter values in the limit of a large number of training examples);

Asymptotically normal;

Efficient (no other estimator will converge to the correct parameter values faster in the mean squared sense).

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_057\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_057\auto

# Find MLE of parameters: stochastic gradient descent (SGD)

• Take the gradients with respect to $\theta$ and $\theta _ { 0 }$ separately

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \displaystyle \frac { \mathrm { d } } { \mathrm { d } \theta _ { 0 } } \log \left[ 1 + \exp ( - y _ { t } ( \langle x _ { t } , \pmb \theta \rangle + \theta _ { 0 } ) ) \right] = - y _ { t } \frac { \exp \big ( } { 1 + \exp ( - y _ { t } ( \pmb x _ { t } , \pmb \theta ) + \theta _ { 0 } ) \big ) } { 1 + \exp ( - y _ { t } ( \pmb x _ { t } , \pmb \theta ) + \theta _ { 0 } ) } } \\ { = - y _ { t } \big [ 1 - \mathsf { P r } ( } \\ { \displaystyle \frac { \mathrm { d } } { \mathrm { d } \pmb \theta } \log \big [ 1 + \exp ( - y _ { t } ( \langle x _ { t } , \pmb \theta \rangle + \theta _ { 0 } ) ) \big ] = - y _ { t } \pmb x _ { t } \big [ 1 - \mathsf { P r } ( } \end{array}
$$

Parameter update: by selecting training examples at random and moving the parameters in the opposite direction of the derivatives ( $\eta > 0$ : small learning rate)

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \pmb { \theta } \longleftarrow \pmb { \theta } + \eta \cdot y _ { t } \pmb { \times } _ { t } \big [ 1 - \mathsf { P r } ( y _ { t } \mid \mathbf { x } _ { t } , \pmb { \theta } , \theta _ { 0 } ) \big ] } \\ { \theta _ { 0 } \longleftarrow \theta _ { 0 } + \eta \cdot y _ { t } \big [ 1 - \mathsf { P r } ( y _ { t } \mid \mathbf { x } _ { t } , \pmb { \theta } , \theta _ { 0 } ) \big ] . } \end{array}
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_066\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_066\auto

# Understand $\pmb { \theta } ^ { * }$ and $\theta _ { 0 } ^ { * }$ (optional)

$\odot$ Vector of optimal prediction errors $\mathfrak { s } : = ( \tilde { y } _ { t } - \mathsf { P r } ( y = 1 \mid \mathsf { x } _ { t } , \pmb { \theta } ^ { \ast } , \pmb { \theta } _ { 0 } ^ { \ast } ) ) _ { t = 1 } ^ { n }$ is orthogonal to any linear function of the inputs (data) d $\mathbf { \nabla } : = ( \langle \tilde { \pmb { \theta } } , \mathbf { x } _ { t } \rangle + \tilde { \theta } _ { 0 } ) _ { t = 1 } ^ { n }$ .

$\Rightarrow$ There is no further linearly available information in the training samples $\{ \mathbf { x } _ { t } \} _ { t = 1 } ^ { n }$ to improve the prediction probabilities (or mistake probabilities).

# Theorem 1.1

At the optimal solution for the parameter and offset vector $\theta ^ { \ast } , \theta _ { 0 } ^ { \ast }$ , the prediction error vector e $\therefore = ( \tilde { y } _ { t } - \mathsf { P r } ( y = 1 | \mathsf { x } _ { t } , \theta ^ { * } , \theta _ { 0 } ^ { * } ) ) _ { t = 1 } ^ { n }$ is orthogonal to any linear function of the data, i.e., for any $\bar { \theta } , \bar { \theta } _ { 0 }$ ,

$$
\langle \mathbf { z } , \mathbf { e } \rangle = 0 , \quad w h e r e \quad \mathbf { z } : = ( \langle \bar { \theta } , \mathbf { x } _ { t } \rangle + \bar { \theta } _ { 0 } ) _ { t = 1 } ^ { n } .
$$

Furthermore if a prediction vector e satisfies (1.17), it has the minimal $\ell _ { 2 }$ norm of $( \widetilde { y } _ { t } - \mathsf { P r } ( y = 1 | \mathbf { x } _ { t } , \pmb { \theta } , \theta _ { 0 } ) ) _ { t = 1 } ^ { n }$ over all $\theta , \theta _ { 0 }$ .

$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_076\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_076\auto

# Multi-class logistic regression

$\odot$ When we have $M \geq 2$ classes, replace

$$
\mathsf { P r } \left( y = 1 \mid \mathbf { x } , \pmb { \theta } , \theta _ { 0 } \right) = \frac { 1 } { 1 + \mathsf { e x p } \left( - \left( \langle \pmb { \theta } , \mathbf { x } \rangle + \theta _ { 0 } \right) \right) }
$$

by the soft-max function

$$
\boldsymbol { y } = c \mid \mathbf { x } , \{ \theta _ { c } , \theta _ { 0 , c } \} _ { c = 1 } ^ { M } ) = \frac { \exp ( \langle \theta _ { c } , \mathbf { x } \rangle + \theta _ { 0 , c } ) } { \sum _ { c ^ { \prime } = 1 } ^ { M } \exp ( \langle \theta _ { c ^ { \prime } } , \mathbf { x } \rangle + \theta _ { 0 } }
$$

where we now have a different pair $( \theta _ { c } , \theta _ { 0 , c } )$ for each class.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_077\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_077\auto

# Multi-class logistic regression

$\odot$ When we have $M \geq 2$ classes, replace

$$
\mathsf { P r } \left( y = 1 \mid \mathbf { x } , \pmb \theta , \theta _ { 0 } \right) = \frac { 1 } { 1 + \mathsf { e x p } \left( - \left( \langle \pmb \theta , \mathbf { x } \rangle + \theta _ { 0 } \right) \right) }
$$

by the soft-max function

$$
\boldsymbol { y } = c \mid \mathbf { x } , \{ \theta _ { c } , \theta _ { 0 , c } \} _ { c = 1 } ^ { M } ) = \frac { \exp ( \langle \theta _ { c } , \mathbf { x } \rangle + \theta _ { 0 , c } ) } { \sum _ { c ^ { \prime } = 1 } ^ { M } \exp ( \langle \theta _ { c ^ { \prime } } , \mathbf { x } \rangle + \theta _ { 0 } }
$$

where we now have a different pair $( \theta _ { c } , \theta _ { 0 , c } )$ for each class.

• Without loss of generality, we can assume that one of the classes (say the first one) has $( \theta _ { 1 } , \theta _ { 0 , 1 } ) = ( \mathbf { 0 } , 0 )$ , which is useful for showing that (1.2) is a special case of (1.27). ◦ Why?

$$

by the soft-max function

$$
\mathsf { P r } ( y = c \mid \mathbf { x } , \{ \pmb { \theta } _ { c } , \pmb { \theta } _ { 0 , c } \} _ { c = 1 } ^ { M } ) = \frac { \mathsf { e x p } ( \langle \pmb { \theta } _ { c } , \mathbf { x } \rangle + \pmb { \theta } _ { 0 } } { \sum _ { c ^ { \prime } = 1 } ^ { M } \mathsf { e x p } ( \langle \pmb { \theta } _ { c ^ { \prime } } , \mathbf { x } \rangle \pmb { \theta } _ { c } }

where we now have a different pair $( \theta _ { c } , \theta _ { 0 , c } )$ for each class.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_080\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_080\auto

# Summary of logistic regression

• Given the logistic regression probabilistic model

$$
\mathbf { \nabla } \theta , \theta _ { 0 } ) = g ( y _ { t } ( \langle \theta , \mathbf { x } _ { t } \rangle + \theta _ { 0 } ) ) =  \frac { 1 }  1 + \exp ( - y _ { t } ( \langle \theta , \mathbf { \cdot }
$$

• Take the gradients of

$$
\log \left[ 1 + \exp ( - y _ { t } ( \langle \mathbf { x } _ { t } , \pmb { \theta } \rangle + \theta _ { 0 } ) ) \right]
$$

with respect to $\theta$ and $\theta _ { 0 }$ separately and update parameters $\pmb \theta$ and $\theta _ { 0 }$ ( $\rvert \eta > 0$ : small learning rate)

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \pmb { \theta } \longleftarrow \pmb { \theta } + \eta \cdot y _ { t } \pmb { \times } _ { t } \big [ 1 - \mathsf { P r } ( y _ { t } \mid \mathbf { x } _ { t } , \pmb { \theta } , \theta _ { 0 } ) \big ] } \\ { \theta _ { 0 } \longleftarrow \theta _ { 0 } + \eta \cdot y _ { t } \big [ 1 - \mathsf { P r } ( y _ { t } \mid \mathbf { x } _ { t } , \pmb { \theta } , \theta _ { 0 } ) \big ] . } \end{array}
$$

• Stochastic gradient descent: update $\pmb \theta$ and $\theta _ { 0 }$ until the termination condition is met.

# Summary of logistic regression: regularization

$\odot$ The likelihood is strictly increasing as a function of $y _ { t } ( \langle \theta ^ { * } , \mathbf { x } _ { t } \rangle + \theta _ { 0 } ^ { * } )$ .

$$
{ \textrm { 0 } } | \mathcal { D } ) = \prod _ { t = 1 } ^ { n } \operatorname* { P r } ( y _ { t } \mid \mathbf { x } _ { t } , \theta , \theta _ { 0 } ) = \prod _ { t = 1 } ^ { n }  \frac { 1 }  1 + \exp ( - y _ { t } (  \frac { }  \langle
$$

Infinite scaling of any parameters corresponding to a perfect linear classifier would attain the highest likelihood.

▶ If the training data are linearly- or affinely-separable, we can find parameters $( \theta ^ { * } , \theta _ { 0 } ^ { * } )$ such that $y _ { t } \big ( \langle { \pmb { \theta } } ^ { * } , { \pmb { x } } _ { t } \rangle + { \pmb { \theta } } _ { 0 } ^ { * } \big ) \geq 0$ for all $t$ . By scaling up the parameters, we make these values larger and larger.

Regularization: e.g., $\ell _ { 2 }$ -norm

$$
\operatorname* { m i n } _ { \substack { \jmath _ { 0 } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } } } \frac { \lambda } { 2 } \| \pmb { \theta } \| ^ { 2 } + \sum _ { t = 1 } ^ { n } \log \big [ 1 + \exp \big ( - y _ { t } \big ( \langle \mathbf { x } _ { t } , \pmb { \theta } \rangle + \theta _ { 0 }
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_089\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_089\auto

# Margin of classifier

• Given a set of data $\mathcal { D } = \{ ( \mathbf { x } _ { t } , y _ { t } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \{ - 1 , + 1 \} \}$ , we can find some classifier. • For any $\mathbf { x } , y$ , correct classification by classifier $f _ { \pmb \theta } = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \pmb \theta ^ { \top } \pmb x )$ means

$$
\left\{ \begin{array} { l } { \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } > 0 , y = + 1 } \\ { \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } < 0 , y = - 1 } \end{array} \right. \Leftrightarrow \ y = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } ) \ \Leftrightarrow \ y \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x }
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_090\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_090\auto

# Margin of classifier

• Given a set of data $\mathcal { D } = \{ ( \mathbf { x } _ { t } , y _ { t } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \{ - 1 , + 1 \} \}$ , we can find some classifier. • For any $\mathbf { x } , y$ , correct classification by classifier $f _ { \pmb \theta } = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \pmb \theta ^ { \top } \pmb x )$ means

$$
\left\{ \begin{array} { l } { \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } > 0 , y = + 1 } \\ { \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } < 0 , y = - 1 } \end{array} \right. \Leftrightarrow \ y = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } ) \ \Leftrightarrow \ y \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x }
$$

# Definition 2.1 (Margin of classifier)

The margin of classifier $f _ { \pmb \theta } = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \pmb \theta ^ { \top } \pmb x )$ on sample $( \mathbf { x } , y )$ is

$$
y { \pmb \theta } ^ { \top } { \pmb x } \ \circ \ r \ y \langle { \pmb \theta } , { \pmb x } \rangle
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_091\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_091\auto

# Margin of classifier

• Given a set of data $\mathcal { D } = \{ ( \mathbf { x } _ { t } , y _ { t } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \{ - 1 , + 1 \} \}$ , we can find some classifier. • For any $\mathbf { x } , y$ , correct classification by classifier $f _ { \pmb \theta } = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \pmb \theta ^ { \top } \pmb x )$ means

$$
\left\{ \begin{array} { l } { \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } > 0 , y = + 1 } \\ { \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } < 0 , y = - 1 } \end{array} \right. \Leftrightarrow \ y = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } ) \ \Leftrightarrow \ y \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x }
$$

# Definition 2.1 (Margin of classifier)

The margin of classifier $f _ { \pmb \theta } = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \pmb \theta ^ { \top } \pmb x )$ on sample $( \mathbf { x } , y )$ is

$$
y { \pmb \theta } ^ { \top } { \pmb x } \ \circ \ r \ y \langle { \pmb \theta } , { \pmb x } \rangle
$$

Positive margin: $( \mathsf { x } , y )$ is correctly classified by $\pmb \theta$ .   
Negative margin: $( \mathbf { x } , y )$ is not correctly classified by $\pmb \theta$ .

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_092\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_092\auto

# Margin of classifier

• Given a set of data $\mathcal { D } = \{ ( \mathbf { x } _ { t } , y _ { t } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \{ - 1 , + 1 \} \}$ , we can find some classifier. • For any $\mathbf { x } , y$ , correct classification by classifier $f _ { \pmb \theta } = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \pmb \theta ^ { \top } \pmb x )$ means

$$
\left\{ \begin{array} { l } { \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } > 0 , y = + 1 } \\ { \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } < 0 , y = - 1 } \end{array} \right. \Leftrightarrow \ y = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } ) \ \Leftrightarrow \ y \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x }
$$

# Definition 2.1 (Margin of classifier)

The margin of classifier $f _ { \pmb \theta } = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \pmb \theta ^ { \top } \pmb x )$ on sample $( \mathbf { x } , y )$ is

$$
y { \pmb \theta } ^ { \top } { \pmb x } \ \circ \ r \ y \langle { \pmb \theta } , { \pmb x } \rangle
$$

Positive margin: $( \mathsf { x } , y )$ is correctly classified by $\pmb \theta$ .   
Negative margin: $( \mathbf { x } , y )$ is not correctly classified by $\pmb \theta$ .   
Bigger margin: $( \mathsf { x } , y )$ is more correctly classified by $\pmb \theta$ .

# Linearly separable

# Definition 2.2 (Linearly separable)

The dataset $\mathcal { D } = \{ ( \boldsymbol { \mathsf { x } } _ { t } , y _ { t } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \{ - 1 , + 1 \} : t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n \}$ is linearly separable if there exists some $\pmb { \theta }$ such that

$$
\begin{array} { r } { y _ { t } = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \pmb { \theta } ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } _ { t } ) \ \mathrm { o r } \ y _ { t } \pmb { \theta } ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } _ { t } > 0 \qquad \forall t = 1 , 2 , . . . } \end{array}
$$

# Linearly separable

# Definition 2.2 (Linearly separable)

The dataset $\mathcal D = \{ ( \boldsymbol x _ { t } , y _ { t } ) \in \mathbb R ^ { d } \times \{ - 1 , + 1 \} : t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n \}$ is linearly separable if there exists some $\pmb \theta$ such that

$$
\begin{array} { r } { y _ { t } = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \pmb { \theta } ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } _ { t } ) \ \mathrm { o r } \ y _ { t } \pmb { \theta } ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } _ { t } > 0 \qquad \forall t = 1 , 2 , . . . } \end{array}
$$

There is some hyperplane that (strictly) separates the data into positive and negative samples

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_095\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_095\auto

# Linearly separable

# Definition 2.2 (Linearly separable)

The dataset $\mathcal D = \{ ( \boldsymbol x _ { t } , y _ { t } ) \in \mathbb R ^ { d } \times \{ - 1 , + 1 \} : t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n \}$ is linearly separable if there exists some $\pmb { \theta }$ such that

$$
\begin{array} { r } { y _ { t } = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \pmb { \theta } ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } _ { t } ) \ \mathrm { o r } \ y _ { t } \pmb { \theta } ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } _ { t } > 0 \qquad \forall t = 1 , 2 , . . . } \end{array}
$$

There is some hyperplane that (strictly) separates the data into positive and negative samples

$\pmb \theta$ has positive margin $y _ { t } \langle \pmb { \theta } , \mathbf { x } _ { t } \rangle > 0$ for all $t$ Minimum margin $\gamma = \underset { 1 \leq t \leq n } { \min } y _ { t } \langle \pmb \theta , \mathbf x _ { t } \rangle > 0$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_098\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_098\auto

# γ-linearly separable

# Definition 2.3 (γ-linearly separable)

The dataset $\mathcal { D } = \{ ( \boldsymbol { \mathsf { x } } _ { t } , y _ { t } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \{ - 1 , + 1 \} : t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n \}$ is $\gamma \cdot$ -linearly separable for some $\gamma > 0$ if there exists some $\pmb \theta$ such that

$$
y _ { t } \langle \pmb { \theta } , \mathbf { x } _ { t } \rangle \geq \gamma \qquad \forall t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n .
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_099\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_099\auto

# γ-linearly separable

The dataset $\mathcal D = \{ ( \boldsymbol x _ { t } , y _ { t } ) \in \mathbb R ^ { d } \times \{ - 1 , + 1 \} : t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n \}$ is $\gamma \cdot$ -linearly separable for some $\gamma > 0$ if there exists some $\pmb \theta$ such that

$$
y _ { t } \langle \pmb { \theta } , \mathbf { x } _ { t } \rangle \geq \gamma \qquad \forall t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n .
$$

There is some hyperplane that (strictly) separates the data into positive and negative samples

$\pmb \theta$ has positive margin $y _ { t } \langle \pmb { \theta } , \mathbf { x } _ { t } \rangle > 0$ for all $t$ • Minimum margin $\gamma = \mathsf { m i n } _ { 1 \leq t \leq n } y _ { t } \langle \pmb \theta , \mathbf { x } _ { t } \rangle > 0$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_100\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_100\auto

# Geometric margin

$\odot$ Geometric margin:

$$
\gamma _ { \mathrm { g e o m } } : = \frac { \gamma } { \| \pmb { \theta } \| } = \frac { \displaystyle \operatorname* { m i n } _ { 1 \leq t \leq n } y _ { t } \pmb { \times } _ { t } ^ { \top } \pmb { \theta } } { \| \pmb { \theta } \| } .
$$

Smallest distance over all samples to the decision boundary $L = \{ x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } : \langle { \bf x } , \pmb \theta \rangle = 0 \} .$ $\gamma _ { \mathrm { g e o m } } ^ { - 1 }$ : fair measure of the difficulty of the classification problem

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_107\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_107\auto

# Maximum margin linear classifier

• We can prove that the solution is unique.

• For $\gamma$ -linearly separable dataset Optimization problem:

$$
\operatorname* { m a x } _ { \pmb { \theta } ^ { \prime } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } } \frac { \gamma } { \lVert \pmb { \theta } ^ { \prime } \rVert } \mathbb { s } . \operatorname { t } . \ y _ { t } \pmb { \times } _ { t } ^ { \top } \pmb { \theta } ^ { \prime } \geq \gamma , \quad \forall t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n
$$

Minimization −→ minimization:

$$
\operatorname* { m i n } _ { \pmb { \theta } ^ { \prime } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } } \frac { \| \pmb { \theta } ^ { \prime } \| } { \gamma } \mathbb { s . t . } \ y _ { t } \pmb { \times } _ { t } ^ { \top } \pmb { \theta } ^ { \prime } \geq \gamma , \quad \forall t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n
$$

# Maixmum margin linear classifier

Since $\gamma > 0$ , this can be rewritten as:

$$
\operatorname* { m i n } _ { \theta ^ { \prime } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } } \left\| \frac { \theta ^ { \prime } } { \gamma } \right\| \textrm { s . t . } y _ { t } \pm \frac { \theta ^ { \prime } } { \gamma } \geq 1 , \quad \forall t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n
$$

• The classification problem is dependent on the rati o θ ′ , not $\pmb { \theta } ^ { \prime }$ or $\gamma$ separately. e.g. Geometric margin $\begin{array} { r } { \gamma _ { \mathrm { g e o m } } = \frac { \gamma } { \| \pmb { \theta } ^ { \prime } \| } } \end{array}$ .   
• ≈ Optimize $\pmb { \theta } ^ { \prime }$ and $\gamma$ together by optimizing $\frac { \theta ^ { \prime } } { \gamma }$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_118\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_118\auto

# Primal-SVM: unique solution

# Claim 2.4

The solution to Primal-SVM is unique.

# Proof:

C Suppose to the contrary, $\exists 2$ distinct min length solution vectors $\theta _ { 1 } , \theta _ { 2 }$ $\ b \theta _ { 1 } \neq \pmb \theta _ { 2 } )$ ) Then $\lVert \pmb { \theta } _ { 1 } \rVert = \lVert \pmb { \theta } _ { 2 } \rVert$ (otherwise they cannot both be the min length solutions) Let $\bar { \pmb { \theta } } = ( \pmb { \theta } _ { 1 } + \pmb { \theta } _ { 2 } ) / 2$   
Check feasibility: Since $\forall t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n , y _ { t } \mathbf { x } _ { t } ^ { \top } \pmb { \theta } _ { 1 } \geq 1$ and $y _ { t } \mathbf { x } _ { t } ^ { \top } \pmb { \theta } _ { 2 } \geq 1$ , by linearity of inner product, we have

$$
y _ { t } { \mathbf { x } _ { t } ^ { \top } } \bar { \pmb { \theta } } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } y _ { t } { \mathbf { x } _ { t } ^ { \top } } \pmb { \theta } _ { 1 } + \frac { 1 } { 2 } y _ { t } { \mathbf { x } _ { t } ^ { \top } } \pmb { \theta } _ { 2 } \geq 1
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_119\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_119\auto

# Primal-SVM: unique solution

# Claim 2.4

The solution to Primal-SVM is unique.

# Proof:

C Suppose to the contrary, $\exists 2$ distinct min length solution vectors $\theta _ { 1 } , \theta _ { 2 }$ $\ b \theta _ { 1 } \neq \pmb \theta _ { 2 } )$ )   
Then $\lVert \pmb { \theta } _ { 1 } \rVert = \lVert \pmb { \theta } _ { 2 } \rVert$ (otherwise they cannot both be the min length solutions)   
Let $\bar { \pmb { \theta } } = ( \pmb { \theta } _ { 1 } + \pmb { \theta } _ { 2 } ) / 2$   
Check feasibility: Since $\forall t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n , y _ { t } \mathbf { x } _ { t } ^ { \top } \pmb { \theta } _ { 1 } \geq 1$ and $y _ { t } \mathbf { x } _ { t } ^ { \top } \pmb { \theta } _ { 2 } \geq 1$ , by linearity of inner product, we have

$$
y _ { t } { \mathbf { x } _ { t } ^ { \top } } \bar { \pmb { \theta } } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } y _ { t } { \mathbf { x } _ { t } ^ { \top } } \pmb { \theta } _ { 1 } + \frac { 1 } { 2 } y _ { t } { \mathbf { x } _ { t } ^ { \top } } \pmb { \theta } _ { 2 } \geq 1
$$

$\Rightarrow \bar { \theta }$ is feasible

Proof (continued):

$$
= \left\| \frac { 1 } { 2 } \left( \pmb { \theta } _ { 1 } + \pmb { \theta } _ { 2 } \right) \right\| \qquad \pmb { \operatorname { T r i a n g l e \ i n e q u a l i t y } } \quad \frac { 1 } { 2 } \left\| \pmb { \theta } _ { 1 } \right\| + \frac { 1 } { 2 } \left\| \pmb { \theta } _ { 2 } \right\|
$$

# Two case:

1. $\lVert \bar { \pmb { \theta } } \rVert < \lVert \pmb { \theta _ { 1 } } \rVert = \lVert \pmb { \theta _ { 2 } } \rVert \Rightarrow \mathrm { C o n t r a d i c t i o n } \rVert$   
2. $\| \bar { \pmb { w } } \| = \| \pmb { \theta } _ { 1 } \| = \| \pmb { \theta } _ { 2 } \| \ \Rightarrow$ Triangle inequality holds with equality. This can only happen if $\pmb { \theta } _ { 1 }$ is in the same direction as $\pmb { \theta } _ { 2 }$ .

lusion: there DO NOT exist 2 distinct min length solution vectors to Primal-SVM.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d\page_125\DSAA2011-L05_supervised_d_page_125\auto

# Incorporating an offset

Till now, we only considered the linear classifier without offset: $f _ { \pmb \theta } ( \mathbf x ) = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \pmb \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf x )$ • If data are not “centered” at zero, we need to incorporate an offset $\theta _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { R }$ :

$$
{ \displaystyle \ f _ { \theta , b } ( \mathbf { x } ) = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } + \theta ) = \mathrm { s i g n } \left( \left[ \theta \right] ^ { \top } \left[ \mathbf { x } \right] \right) }
$$

• Then the decision boundary is

$$
L = \{ x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } : { \pmb { \theta } } ^ { \top } { \pmb { x } } + { \theta } _ { 0 } = 0 \}
$$

If $\theta = 0$ , the line $L$ passes through the origin.

To assess the robustness of the SVM

$$
\mathrm { L O O C V } = \frac { 1 } { n } \sum _ { t = 1 } ^ { n } \mathrm { L o s s } \bigl ( y _ { t } , f \bigl ( \mathbf { x } _ { t } , \bigl ( \theta ^ { - t } , \theta _ { 0 } ^ { - t } \bigr ) \bigr ) \bigr ) ,
$$

$( \theta ^ { - t } , \theta _ { 0 } ^ { - t } )$ is learnt from the dataset with $i ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ sample left out, i.e., $\mathcal { D } ^ { - t } = \mathcal { D } \setminus \left\{ { \bf x } _ { t } , y _ { t } \right\}$ Loss function: $\operatorname { L o s s } = \mathbb { 1 } \{ y \neq y ^ { \prime } \}$ is zero-one loss

If $\mathbf { \boldsymbol { x } } _ { t }$ is not a support vector, then it cannot influence the solution of the primal SVM. Hence,

$$
\begin{array} { r } { f ( \mathbf { x } _ { t } , ( \pmb { \theta } ^ { - t } , \pmb { b } ^ { - t } ) ) = y _ { t } , \quad \forall \mathbf { x } _ { t } \notin \mathrm { S u p p o r t } \mathrm { V e c t o r s } \ ( } \end{array}
$$

and

$$
\operatorname { L o s s } ( y _ { t } , f ( \mathbf { x } _ { t } , ( \pmb { \theta } ^ { - t } , \pmb { \theta } _ { 0 } ^ { - t } ) ) ) = 0 , \quad \forall \mathbf { x } _ { t } \notin \mathsf { S u p p o r t } \lor
$$

For any other $\mathbf { x } _ { t } \in \mathsf { S V }$ ,

$$
\mathrm { L o s s } ( y _ { t } , f ( \mathbf { x } _ { t } , ( \theta ^ { - t } , \theta _ { 0 } ^ { - t } ) ) ) \leq 1 , \quad \forall \mathbf { x } _ { t } \in \mathsf { S u p p o r t V }
$$

(Primal-SVM with offset and slack) $\operatorname* { m i n } _ { \theta , \theta _ { 0 } , \xi \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } \times \mathbb { R } _ { + } ^ { n } } \frac { 1 } { 2 } \left. \theta ^ { \prime } \right. ^ { 2 } + C \sum _ { t = 1 } ^ { n } \xi _ { t }$ s. t. $y _ { t } ( \mathsf { x } _ { t } ^ { } \theta + \theta _ { 0 } ) \geq 1 - \xi _ { t } , \xi _ { t } \geq 0 \quad \forall t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n$

$\Rightarrow$ the original max margin classifier without slack

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng\page_008\DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng_page_008\auto

# Summary of logistic regression

• Given the logistic regression probabilistic model

$$
\mathbf { \theta } , \theta , \theta _ { 0 } \mathbf { \eta } ) = g ( y _ { t } ( \langle \theta , \mathbf { x } _ { t } \rangle + \theta _ { 0 } ) ) = \frac { 1 } { 1 + \exp ( - y _ { t } ( \langle \theta , \mathbf { \eta } } _ { \mathrm { ~ } }
$$

• Take the gradients of

$$
\log \left[ 1 + \exp ( - y _ { t } ( \langle \mathbf { x } _ { t } , \pmb { \theta } \rangle + \theta _ { 0 } ) ) \right]
$$

with respect to $\theta$ and $\theta _ { 0 }$ separately and update parameters $\pmb \theta$ and $\theta _ { 0 }$ ( $\rvert \eta > 0$ : small learning rate)

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \pmb { \theta } \longleftarrow \pmb { \theta } + \eta \cdot y _ { t } \pmb { \times } _ { t } \big [ 1 - \mathsf { P r } ( y _ { t } \mid \mathbf { x } _ { t } , \pmb { \theta } , \theta _ { 0 } ) \big ] } \\ { \theta _ { 0 } \longleftarrow \theta _ { 0 } + \eta \cdot y _ { t } \big [ 1 - \mathsf { P r } ( y _ { t } \mid \mathbf { x } _ { t } , \pmb { \theta } , \theta _ { 0 } ) \big ] . } \end{array}
$$

• Stochastic gradient descent: update $\pmb \theta$ and $\theta _ { 0 }$ until the termination condition is met.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng\page_009\DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng_page_009\auto

# Summary of logistic regression: regularization

$\odot$ The likelihood is strictly increasing as a function of $y _ { t } \big ( \langle { \theta ^ { * } } , \mathbf { x } _ { t } \rangle + \theta _ { 0 } ^ { * } \big )$ .

$$
{ \textrm { 0 } } | \mathcal { D } ) = \prod _ { t = 1 } ^ { n } \operatorname* { P r } ( y _ { t } \mid \mathbf { x } _ { t } , \theta , \theta _ { 0 } ) = \prod _ { t = 1 } ^ { n }  \frac { 1 }  1 + \exp ( - y _ { t } (  \frac { }  \langle
$$

Infinite scaling of any parameters corresponding to a perfect linear classifier would attain the highest likelihood.

▶ If the training data are linearly- or affinely-separable, we can find parameters $( \theta ^ { * } , \theta _ { 0 } ^ { * } )$ such that $y _ { t } \big ( \langle { \pmb { \theta } } ^ { * } , { \pmb { x } } _ { t } \rangle + { \pmb { \theta } } _ { 0 } ^ { * } \big ) \geq 0$ for all $t$ . By scaling up the parameters, we make these values larger and larger.

Regularization: e.g., $\ell _ { 2 }$ -norm

$$
\operatorname* { m i n } _ { \substack { \jmath _ { 0 } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } } } \frac { \lambda } { 2 } \| \pmb { \theta } \| ^ { 2 } + \sum _ { t = 1 } ^ { n } \log \big [ 1 + \exp \big ( - y _ { t } \big ( \langle \mathbf { x } _ { t } , \pmb { \theta } \rangle + \theta _ { 0 }
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng\page_010\DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng_page_010\auto

# Summary of logistic regression: multi-class classification

$\odot$ When we have $M \geq 2$ classes, replace

$$
\mathsf { P r } \left( y = 1 \mid \mathbf { x } , \pmb { \theta } , \theta _ { 0 } \right) = \frac { 1 } { 1 + \mathsf { e x p } \left( - \left( \langle \pmb { \theta } , \mathbf { x } \rangle + \theta _ { 0 } \right) \right) }
$$

by the soft-max function

$$
\mathsf { P r } ( y = c \mid \mathbf { x } , \{ \pmb { \theta } _ { c } , \pmb { \theta } _ { 0 , c } \} _ { c = 1 } ^ { M } ) = \frac { \mathsf { e x p } ( \langle \pmb { \theta } _ { c } , \mathbf { x } \rangle + \pmb { \theta } _ { 0 } } { \sum _ { c ^ { \prime } = 1 } ^ { M } \mathsf { e x p } ( \langle \pmb { \theta } _ { c ^ { \prime } } , \mathbf { x } \rangle \pmb { \theta } _ { c } }
$$

where we now have a different pair $( \theta _ { c } , \theta _ { 0 , c } )$ for each class.

• Without loss of generality, we can assume that one of the classes (say the first one) has $( \theta _ { 1 } , \theta _ { 0 , 1 } ) = ( \mathbf { 0 } , 0 )$ , which is useful for showing that (0.4) is a special case of (0.5). ◦ Why?

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng\page_015\DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng_page_015\auto

# Margin of classifier

• Given a set of data $\mathcal { D } = \{ ( \mathbf { x } _ { t } , y _ { t } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \{ - 1 , + 1 \} \}$ , we can find some classifier. • For any $\mathbf { x } , y$ , correct classification by classifier $f _ { \pmb \theta } = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \pmb \theta ^ { \top } \pmb x )$ means

$$
\left\{ \begin{array} { l } { \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } > 0 , y = + 1 } \\ { \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } < 0 , y = - 1 } \end{array} \right. \Leftrightarrow \ y = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } ) \ \Leftrightarrow \ y \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x }
$$

# Definition 1.1 (Margin of classifier)

The margin of classifier $f _ { \pmb \theta } = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \pmb \theta ^ { \top } \pmb x )$ on sample $( \mathbf { x } , y )$ is

$$
y { \pmb \theta } ^ { \top } { \pmb x } \ \circ \ r \ y \langle { \pmb \theta } , { \pmb x } \rangle
$$

Positive margin: $( \mathsf { x } , y )$ is correctly classified by $\pmb \theta$ .   
Negative margin: $( \mathbf { x } , y )$ is not correctly classified by $\pmb \theta$ .   
Bigger margin: $( \mathsf { x } , y )$ is more correctly classified by $\pmb \theta$ .

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng\page_016\DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng_page_016\auto

# Linearly separable

# Definition 1.2 (Linearly separable)

The dataset $\mathcal D = \{ ( \boldsymbol x _ { t } , y _ { t } ) \in \mathbb R ^ { d } \times \{ - 1 , + 1 \} : t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n \}$ is linearly separable if there exists some $\pmb { \theta }$ such that

$$
\begin{array} { r } { y _ { t } = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \pmb { \theta } ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } _ { t } ) \ \mathrm { o r } \ y _ { t } \pmb { \theta } ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } _ { t } > 0 \qquad \forall t = 1 , 2 , . . . } \end{array}
$$

There is some hyperplane that (strictly) separates the data into positive and negative samples

$\pmb \theta$ has positive margin $y _ { t } \langle \pmb { \theta } , \mathbf { x } _ { t } \rangle > 0$ for all $t$ Minimum margin $\gamma = \underset { 1 \leq t \leq n } { \min } y _ { t } \langle \pmb \theta , \mathbf x _ { t } \rangle > 0$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng\page_017\DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng_page_017\auto

# γ-linearly separable

The dataset $\mathcal { D } = \{ ( \boldsymbol { \mathsf { x } } _ { t } , y _ { t } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \{ - 1 , + 1 \} : t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n \}$ is $\gamma \cdot$ -linearly separable for some $\gamma > 0$ if there exists some $\pmb \theta$ such that

$$
y _ { t } \langle \pmb { \theta } , \mathbf { x } _ { t } \rangle \geq \gamma \qquad \forall t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n .
$$

There is some hyperplane that (strictly) separates the data into positive and negative samples

$\pmb \theta$ has positive margin $y _ { t } \langle \pmb { \theta } , \mathbf { x } _ { t } \rangle > 0$ for all $t$ • Minimum margin $\gamma = \mathsf { m i n } _ { 1 \leq t \leq n } y _ { t } \langle \pmb \theta , \mathbf { x } _ { t } \rangle > 0$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng\page_018\DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng_page_018\auto

# Geometric margin

$\odot$ Geometric margin:

$$
\gamma _ { \mathrm { g e o m } } : = \frac { \gamma } { \| \pmb { \theta } \| } = \frac { \displaystyle \operatorname* { m i n } _ { 1 \leq t \leq n } y _ { t } \pmb { \times } _ { t } ^ { \top } \pmb { \theta } } { \| \pmb { \theta } \| } .
$$

Smallest distance over all samples to the decision boundary $L = \{ x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } : \langle { \bf x } , \pmb \theta \rangle = 0 \} .$ $\gamma _ { \mathrm { g e o m } } ^ { - 1 }$ : fair measure of the difficulty of the classification problem

![](images/99f8d7d17634d6cbfb537553f89454661959e4c7093f45109a7b66fbfb3309d2.jpg)

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng\page_025\DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng_page_025\auto

# Maximum margin linear classifier

• We can prove that the solution is unique.

• For $\gamma$ -linearly separable dataset Optimization problem:

$$
\operatorname* { m a x } _ { \pmb { \theta } ^ { \prime } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } } \frac { \gamma } { \lVert \pmb { \theta } ^ { \prime } \rVert } \mathbb { s } . \operatorname { t } . \ y _ { t } \pmb { \times } _ { t } ^ { \top } \pmb { \theta } ^ { \prime } \geq \gamma , \quad \forall t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n
$$

Minimization −→ minimization:

$$
\operatorname* { m i n } _ { \pmb { \theta } ^ { \prime } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } } \frac { \| \pmb { \theta } ^ { \prime } \| } { \gamma } \mathbb { s . t . } \ y _ { t } \pmb { \times } _ { t } ^ { \top } \pmb { \theta } ^ { \prime } \geq \gamma , \quad \forall t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng\page_026\DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng_page_026\auto

# Maixmum margin linear classifier

Since $\gamma > 0$ , this can be rewritten as:

$$
\operatorname* { m i n } _ { \theta ^ { \prime } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } } \left\| \frac { \theta ^ { \prime } } { \gamma } \right\| \textrm { s . t . } y _ { t } \pm \frac { \theta ^ { \prime } } { \gamma } \geq 1 , \quad \forall t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n
$$

• The classification problem is dependent on the rati o θ ′ , not $\pmb { \theta } ^ { \prime }$ or $\gamma$ separately. e.g. Geometric margin $\begin{array} { r } { \gamma _ { \mathrm { g e o m } } = \frac { \gamma } { \| \pmb { \theta } ^ { \prime } \| } } \end{array}$ .   
• ≈ Optimize $\pmb { \theta } ^ { \prime }$ and $\gamma$ together by optimizing $\frac { \theta ^ { \prime } } { \gamma }$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng\page_036\DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng_page_036\auto

# Primal-SVM: unique solution

# Claim 1.4

The solution to Primal-SVM is unique.

# Proof:

C Suppose to the contrary, $\exists 2$ distinct min length solution vectors $\theta _ { 1 } , \theta _ { 2 }$ $\ b \theta _ { 1 } \neq \pmb \theta _ { 2 } )$ ) Then $\lVert \pmb { \theta } _ { 1 } \rVert = \lVert \pmb { \theta } _ { 2 } \rVert$ (otherwise they cannot both be the min length solutions) Let $\bar { \pmb { \theta } } = ( \pmb { \theta } _ { 1 } + \pmb { \theta } _ { 2 } ) / 2$   
Check feasibility: Since $\forall t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n , y _ { t } \mathbf { x } _ { t } ^ { \top } \pmb { \theta } _ { 1 } \geq 1$ and $y _ { t } \mathbf { x } _ { t } ^ { \top } \pmb { \theta } _ { 2 } \geq 1$ , by linearity of inner product, we have

$$
y _ { t } { \mathbf { x } _ { t } ^ { \top } } \bar { \pmb { \theta } } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } y _ { t } { \mathbf { x } _ { t } ^ { \top } } \pmb { \theta } _ { 1 } + \frac { 1 } { 2 } y _ { t } { \mathbf { x } _ { t } ^ { \top } } \pmb { \theta } _ { 2 } \geq 1
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng\page_037\DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng_page_037\auto

# Primal-SVM: unique solution

# Claim 1.4

The solution to Primal-SVM is unique.

# Proof:

C Suppose to the contrary, $\exists 2$ distinct min length solution vectors $\theta _ { 1 } , \theta _ { 2 }$ $\ b \theta _ { 1 } \neq \pmb \theta _ { 2 } )$ )   
Then $\lVert \pmb { \theta } _ { 1 } \rVert = \lVert \pmb { \theta } _ { 2 } \rVert$ (otherwise they cannot both be the min length solutions)   
Let $\bar { \pmb { \theta } } = ( \pmb { \theta } _ { 1 } + \pmb { \theta } _ { 2 } ) / 2$   
Check feasibility: Since $\forall t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n , y _ { t } \mathbf { x } _ { t } ^ { \top } \pmb { \theta } _ { 1 } \geq 1$ and $y _ { t } \mathbf { x } _ { t } ^ { \top } \pmb { \theta } _ { 2 } \geq 1$ , by linearity of inner product, we have

$$
y _ { t } { \mathbf { x } _ { t } ^ { \top } } \bar { \pmb { \theta } } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } y _ { t } { \mathbf { x } _ { t } ^ { \top } } \pmb { \theta } _ { 1 } + \frac { 1 } { 2 } y _ { t } { \mathbf { x } _ { t } ^ { \top } } \pmb { \theta } _ { 2 } \geq 1
$$

$\Rightarrow \bar { \theta }$ is feasible

$$

# Two case:

1. $\lVert \bar { \pmb { \theta } } \rVert < \lVert \pmb { \theta _ { 1 } } \rVert = \lVert \pmb { \theta _ { 2 } } \rVert \Rightarrow \mathrm { C o n t r a d i c t i o n } \rVert$

lusion: there DO NOT exist 2 distinct min length solution vectors to Primal-SVM.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng\page_043\DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng_page_043\auto

# Incorporating an offset

Till now, we only considered the linear classifier without offset: $f _ { \pmb \theta } ( \mathbf x ) = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \pmb \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf x )$ • If data are not “centered” at zero, we need to incorporate an offset $\theta _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { R }$ :

$$
{ \displaystyle \ f _ { \theta , b } ( \mathbf { x } ) = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } + \theta ) = \mathrm { s i g n } \left( \left[ \theta \right] ^ { \top } \left[ \mathbf { x } \right] \right) }
$$

• Then the decision boundary is

$$
L = \{ x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } : { \pmb { \theta } } ^ { \top } { \pmb { x } } + { \theta } _ { 0 } = 0 \}
$$

If $\theta = 0$ , the line $L$ passes through the origin.

$\operatorname* { m i n } _ { \theta ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } } \frac { 1 } { 2 } \left\| \theta \right\| ^ { 2 } \mathrm { ~ s . ~ t . ~ } y _ { t } ( \mathbf { x } _ { t } ^ { \top } \theta + \theta _ { 0 } ) \geq 1 , \quad \forall t = 1 , 2$ 2, . . . , n

# Remarks:

1. The offset $b$ only appears in constraints

2. Different from $\tilde { \mathbf { x } } = [ \mathbf { x } ; 1 ] \colon$

$ \mathsf { W e }$ do not bias in any way where the separating hyperplane should appear, only that it should maximize the geometric margin.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng\page_049\DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng_page_049\auto

# Leave-one-out cross-validation error

To assess the robustness of the SVM

$$
\mathrm { L O O C V } = \frac { 1 } { n } \sum _ { t = 1 } ^ { n } \mathrm { L o s s } \bigl ( y _ { t } , f \bigl ( \mathbf { x } _ { t } , \bigl ( \theta ^ { - t } , \theta _ { 0 } ^ { - t } \bigr ) \bigr ) \bigr ) ,
$$

$( \theta ^ { - t } , \theta _ { 0 } ^ { - t } )$ is learnt from the dataset with $i ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ sample left out, i.e., $\mathcal { D } ^ { - t } = \mathcal { D } \setminus \left\{ { \bf x } _ { t } , y _ { t } \right\}$ Loss function: $\operatorname { L o s s } = \mathbb { 1 } \{ y \neq y ^ { \prime } \}$ is zero-one loss

# Leave-one-out cross-validation error

To assess the robustness of the SVM

$$
\mathrm { L O O C V } = \frac { 1 } { n } \sum _ { t = 1 } ^ { n } \mathrm { L o s s } \bigl ( y _ { t } , f \bigl ( \mathbf { x } _ { t } , \bigl ( \theta ^ { - t } , \theta _ { 0 } ^ { - t } \bigr ) \bigr ) \bigr ) ,
$$

$( \theta ^ { - t } , \theta _ { 0 } ^ { - t } )$ is learnt from the dataset with $i ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ sample left out, i.e., $\mathcal { D } ^ { - t } = \mathcal { D } \setminus \left\{ { \bf x } _ { t } , y _ { t } \right\}$ Loss function: $\operatorname { L o s s } = \mathbb { 1 } \{ y \neq y ^ { \prime } \}$ is zero-one loss

In other words,

$$
\in \underset { ( \theta , \theta ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } } { \mathrm { a r g } \operatorname* { m i n } } \left\{ \frac { 1 } { 2 } \left\| \pmb { \theta } \right\| ^ { 2 } : y _ { t } ( \mathbf { x } _ { t } ^ { \top } \pmb { \theta } + \theta _ { 0 } ) \geq 1 , \quad \forall t \in [ \begin{array} { r } { \ } \\ { \ } \end{array} \right.
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng\page_054\DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng_page_054\auto

# Leave-one-out cross-validation error

# Proof:

If $\mathbf { x } _ { t }$ is not a support vector, then it cannot influence the solution of the primal SVM. Hence,

$$
\begin{array} { r } { f ( \mathbf { x } _ { t } , ( \pmb { \theta } ^ { - t } , \pmb { b } ^ { - t } ) ) = y _ { t } , \quad \forall \mathbf { x } _ { t } \notin \mathrm { S u p p o r t } \mathrm { V e c t o r s } \ ( } \end{array}
$$

and

$$
\operatorname { L o s s } ( y _ { t } , f ( \mathbf { x } _ { t } , ( \pmb { \theta } ^ { - t } , \pmb { \theta } _ { 0 } ^ { - t } ) ) ) = 0 , \quad \forall \mathbf { x } _ { t } \notin \mathsf { S u p p o r t } \lor
$$

For any other $\mathbf { x } _ { t } \in \mathsf { S V }$ ,

$$
\mathrm { L o s s } ( y _ { t } , f ( \mathbf { x } _ { t } , ( \theta ^ { - t } , \theta _ { 0 } ^ { - t } ) ) ) \leq 1 , \quad \forall \mathbf { x } _ { t } \in \mathsf { S u p p o r t V }
$$

\begin{array} { c l l } { { \displaystyle \mathrm { L O O C V } = \frac { 1 } { n } \left( \sum _ { t \notin \mathrm { S V } } + \sum _ { t \in \mathrm { S V } } \right) \mathrm { L o s s } ( y _ { t } , f ( \mathsf { x } _ { t } , ( \theta ^ { - t } , ( } } & { { } } \\ { { } } & { { \leq 0 + \displaystyle \frac { 1 } { n } \sum _ { i \in \mathrm { S V } } } 1 = \displaystyle \frac { N } { n } . } \end{array}

# Polynomial tranformation

Generalized Linear Discriminant Function

$$
) = w _ { 0 } + \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } w _ { i } x _ { i } + \sum _ { 1 \leq i \leq j \leq d } w _ { i , j } x _ { i } x _ { j } + \sum _ { 1 \leq i \leq j \leq k \leq d } w
$$

Noting that $x _ { I , i }$ is the $j .$ -th $( 1 \leq i \leq d )$ ) component of the l-th $( 1 \leq I \leq m )$ ) sample, we can stack this into

$$
f _ { \mathbf { w } } ( \mathbf { x } ) = \mathbf { P } \mathbf { w } = \left[ \begin{array} { c } { \mathbf { p } _ { 1 } ^ { \top } \mathbf { w } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { \mathbf { p } _ { m } ^ { \top } \mathbf { w } } \end{array} \right]
$$

and

$$
\begin{array}{c} \begin{array} { r } { \mathfrak { p } _ { I } ^ { \top } \mathbf { w } = \left[ \mathbf { 1 } \quad x _ { I , 1 } \quad \ldots \quad x _ { I , d } \quad \ldots \quad x _ { I , i } x _ { I , j } \quad \ldots \quad x _ { I , i } x _ { I , j } x _ { I , k } \quad \ldots \quad x _ { I , i } x _ { I , j } x _ { I , k } \quad \ldots \quad x _ { I , i } x _ { I , j } x _ { I , k } \quad \ldots \quad x _ { I , i } x _ { I , j } x _ { I , k } \quad \ldots \quad x _ { I , i } x _ { I , j } x _ { I , k } \right]} \end{array}   \end{array}
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng\page_072\DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng_page_072\auto

# Polynomial transformation

Note that the polynomial matrix

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \mathbf { P } = \mathbf { P } ( \mathbf { x } _ { 1 } , \mathbf { x } _ { 2 } , \ldots , \mathbf { x } _ { m } ) = [ { \bf \Xi } _ { \mathbf { \Lambda } ; \mathbf { \Lambda } } ^ { - \mathbf { p } _ { 1 } ^ { \top } } - ] \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m \times ( \mathbf { \Lambda } _ { p } ^ { d + p } ) } } \\ { - \mathbf { p } _ { m } ^ { \top } - ] } \end{array}
$$

is a function of the data samples $\{ \pmb { x } _ { 1 } , \pmb { x } _ { 2 } , \ldots , \pmb { x } _ { m } \}$

For an $d$ -variable, order- $p$ polynomial, the matrix $\mathbf { P }$ is of size $m \times \left( { { d + p } \atop { p } } \right)$ . • $d ^ { \prime } = { \binom { d + p } { p } }$ can be far larger than $d$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng\page_086\DSAA2011-L06_supervised_e_feature_eng_page_086\auto

# Missing values

Remove rows/columns with missing entries   
(For time series) back-fill with most recent observed value   
Impute with mean, median, or mode   
Fancier imputation methods (unfortunately NOT covered in this class): matrix completion, deep learning, . . .   
Add new feature: Boolean indicator 1(data is missing)   
◦ Can detect if missingness is informative   
◦ Can complement imputation method   
◦ Can use different indicators for different kinds of missingness (refused, missing, illegible response, . . . )

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L07_model_sel\page_006\DSAA2011-L07_model_sel_page_006\auto

# Margin of classifier

• Given a set of data $\mathcal { D } = \{ ( \mathbf { x } _ { t } , y _ { t } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \{ - 1 , + 1 \} \}$ , we can find some classifier. • For any $\mathbf { x } , y$ , correct classification by classifier $f _ { \pmb \theta } = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \pmb \theta ^ { \top } \pmb x )$ means

$$
\left\{ \begin{array} { l } { \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } > 0 , y = + 1 } \\ { \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } < 0 , y = - 1 } \end{array} \right. \Leftrightarrow \ y = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } ) \ \Leftrightarrow \ y \theta ^ { \top } \mathbf { x }
$$

# Definition 0.1 (Margin of classifier)

The margin of classifier $f _ { \pmb \theta } = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \pmb \theta ^ { \top } \pmb x )$ on sample $( \mathbf { x } , y )$ is

$$
y { \pmb \theta } ^ { \top } { \pmb x } \ \circ \ r \ y \langle { \pmb \theta } , { \pmb x } \rangle
$$

Positive margin: $( \mathsf { x } , y )$ is correctly classified by $\pmb \theta$ .   
Negative margin: $( \mathbf { x } , y )$ is not correctly classified by $\pmb \theta$ .   
Bigger margin: $( \mathsf { x } , y )$ is more correctly classified by $\pmb \theta$ .

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L07_model_sel\page_007\DSAA2011-L07_model_sel_page_007\auto

# Linearly separable

# Definition 0.2 (Linearly separable)

The dataset $\mathcal { D } = \{ ( \boldsymbol { \mathsf { x } } _ { t } , y _ { t } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \{ - 1 , + 1 \} : t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n \}$ is linearly separable if there exists some $\pmb \theta$ such that

$$
\begin{array} { r } { y _ { t } = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \pmb { \theta } ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } _ { t } ) \ \mathrm { o r } \ y _ { t } \pmb { \theta } ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } _ { t } > 0 \qquad \forall t = 1 , 2 , . . . } \end{array}
$$

There is some hyperplane that (strictly) separates the data into positive and negative samples

$\pmb \theta$ has positive margin $y _ { t } \langle \pmb { \theta } , \mathbf { x } _ { t } \rangle > 0$ for all $t$ Minimum margin $\gamma = \underset { 1 \leq t \leq n } { \min } y _ { t } \langle \pmb \theta , \mathbf x _ { t } \rangle > 0$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L07_model_sel\page_008\DSAA2011-L07_model_sel_page_008\auto

# γ-linearly separable

The dataset $\mathcal { D } = \{ ( \boldsymbol { \mathsf { x } } _ { t } , y _ { t } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \{ - 1 , + 1 \} : t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n \}$ is $\gamma \cdot$ -linearly separable for some $\gamma > 0$ if there exists some $\pmb \theta$ such that

$$
y _ { t } \langle \pmb { \theta } , \mathbf { x } _ { t } \rangle \geq \gamma \qquad \forall t = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n .
$$

There is some hyperplane that (strictly) separates the data into positive and negative samples

$\pmb \theta$ has positive margin $y _ { t } \langle \pmb { \theta } , \mathbf { x } _ { t } \rangle > 0$ for all $t$ • Minimum margin $\gamma = \mathsf { m i n } _ { 1 \leq t \leq n } y _ { t } \langle \pmb \theta , \mathbf { x } _ { t } \rangle > 0$

$$

Smallest distance over all samples to the decision boundary $L = \{ x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } : \langle { \bf x } , \pmb \theta \rangle = 0 \} .$ $\gamma _ { \mathrm { g e o m } } ^ { - 1 }$ : fair measure of the difficulty of the classification problem

To assess the robustness of the SVM

$$
\mathrm { L O O C V } = \frac { 1 } { n } \sum _ { t = 1 } ^ { n } \mathrm { L o s s } \bigl ( y _ { t } , f \bigl ( \mathbf { x } _ { t } , \bigl ( \theta ^ { - t } , \theta _ { 0 } ^ { - t } \bigr ) \bigr ) \bigr ) ,
$$

$( \theta ^ { - t } , \theta _ { 0 } ^ { - t } )$ is learnt from the dataset with $i ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ sample left out, i.e., $\mathcal { D } ^ { - t } = \mathcal { D } \setminus \left\{ { \bf x } _ { t } , y _ { t } \right\}$ Loss function: $\operatorname { L o s s } = \mathbb { 1 } \{ y \neq y ^ { \prime } \}$ is zero-one loss

In other words,

$$
\in \underset { ( \theta , \theta ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } } { \mathrm { a r g } \operatorname* { m i n } } \{ \frac { 1 } { 2 } \| \pmb { \theta } \| ^ { 2 } : y _ { t } ( \mathbf { x } _ { t } ^ { \top } \pmb { \theta } + \theta _ { 0 } ) \geq 1 , \quad \forall t \in [
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L07_model_sel\page_013\DSAA2011-L07_model_sel_page_013\auto

# Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) error

If LOOCV is small, the model generalizes well (fits well on new samples)

# Proposition 0.4

Let the number of support vectors be $N \in \{ 0 , 1 , \ldots , n \}$ . Then

$$
\mathrm { L O O C V } \leq { \frac { N } { n } } .
$$

• If the number of support vectors is small, then LOOCV is also small and the SVM works well on new samples

# Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) error

# Hint for proof:

If $\mathbf { x } _ { t }$ is not a support vector, then it cannot influence the solution of the primal SVM. Hence,

$$
\begin{array} { r } { f ( \mathbf { x } _ { t } , ( \pmb { \theta } ^ { - t } , \pmb { b } ^ { - t } ) ) = y _ { t } , \quad \forall \mathbf { x } _ { t } \notin \mathrm { S u p p o r t } \mathrm { V e c t o r s } \ ( } \end{array}
$$

and

$$
\operatorname { L o s s } ( y _ { t } , f ( \mathbf { x } _ { t } , ( \pmb { \theta } ^ { - t } , \pmb { \theta } _ { 0 } ^ { - t } ) ) ) = 0 , \quad \forall \mathbf { x } _ { t } \notin \mathsf { S u p p o r t } \lor
$$

For any other $\mathbf { x } _ { t } \in \mathsf { S V }$ ,

$$
\mathrm { L o s s } ( y _ { t } , f ( \mathbf { x } _ { t } , ( \theta ^ { - t } , \theta _ { 0 } ^ { - t } ) ) ) \leq 1 , \quad \forall \mathbf { x } _ { t } \in \mathsf { S u p p o r t V }
$$

# Missing values

Remove rows/columns with missing entries   
(For time series) back-fill with most recent observed value   
Impute with mean, median, or mode   
Fancier imputation methods (unfortunately NOT covered in this class): matrix completion, deep learning, . . .   
Add new feature: Boolean indicator 1(data is missing)   
◦ Can detect if missingness is informative   
◦ Can complement imputation method   
◦ Can use different indicators for different kinds of missingness (refused, missing, illegible response, . . . )

$\mathsf { l o g } ( y ) =  { \mathbf { w } } ^ { \top }  { \mathbf { x } }$ equivalent to $y = \exp ( \mathbf { w } ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } )$

can transform $x$ or (even more important) y ◦ Familiar?

• Nonlinear transforms:

log, exp, quantile, median, . . . More systematic ways to handle nonlinearities (unfortunately NOT covered here): ◦ Deep learning, . . .

# A cautionary tale: predict who will be approved for credit card

Dataset $\mathcal { D } =$ all previous applicants + decisions {zxi {zyi

Hypothesis set $\mathcal { H } =$ rules of the form:

pick a subset of names from $\mathcal { D }$ , and predicts 1 if applicant is on the subset, i.e.,

$$
h ( \mathsf { a p p l i c a n t } ) = \left\{ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & { \mathsf { a p p l i c a n t ~ n a m e = A l p h a ~ } \beta } \\ { 1 } & { \mathsf { a p p l i c a n t ~ n a m e = B e t a ~ B e } } \\ { 1 } & { \cdot \cdot } \\ { - 1 } & { \mathsf { o t h e r w i s e } } \end{array} \right.
$$

Learning algorithm $\mathcal { A }$ : pick $h$ that performs best on $\mathcal { D }$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L07_model_sel\page_045\DSAA2011-L07_model_sel_page_045\auto

# Linear regression: key elements

$\odot$ Learning/Training: Given a dataset $\{ ( \mathbf { x } _ { i } , y _ { i } ) \} _ { i = 1 } ^ { m }$ where $\mathbf { x } _ { i } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ and $y _ { i } \in \mathbb { R }$ . Design an affine model such that $f _ { \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } } ( \mathbf { x } ) = \mathbf { w } ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } + b = y$ where $\overline { { \mathbf { w } } } = [ \mathbf { w } ^ { \top } \mathbf { \Sigma } b ] ^ { \top }$ . Find the minimizer of loss function

$$
J ( \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } ) = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } \left( f _ { \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } } ( \mathbf { x } _ { i } ) - y _ { i } \right) ^ { 2 } = ( \mathbf { X } \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } - \mathbf { y } ) ^ { \top } ( \mathbf { X } \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } - \mathbf { y } )
$$

Least squares solution (with offset)

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } ^ { * } = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { b ^ { * } } \\ { \mathbf { w } ^ { * } } \end{array} \right] = ( \mathbf { X } ^ { \top } \mathbf { X } ) ^ { - 1 } \mathbf { X } ^ { \top } \mathbf { y } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d + 1 } . } \end{array}
$$

$\odot$ Prediction/Testing: Given a new feature vector (sample, example) $\mathbf { x } _ { \mathrm { n e w } }$ , the prediction based on the least squares solution is

$$
\hat { y } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } = \biggl [ \mathbf { 1 } _ { \mathrm { x _ { \mathrm { n e w } } } } \biggr ] ^ { \top } \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } ^ { \ast } = b ^ { \ast } + \mathbf { x } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } ^ { \top } \mathbf { w } ^ { \ast } .
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L07_model_sel\page_046\DSAA2011-L07_model_sel_page_046\auto

# Linear regression: key elements

$\odot$ Learning/Training: Given a dataset $\{ ( \mathbf { x } _ { i } , y _ { i } ) \} _ { i = 1 } ^ { m }$ where $\mathbf { x } _ { i } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ and $y _ { i } \in \mathbb { R }$ .   
(Hypothesis class) Design an affine model such that $\begin{array} { r } { f _ { \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } } ( \mathbf { x } ) = \mathbf { w } ^ { \top } \mathbf { x } + b = y } \end{array}$ where $\dot { \mathbf { w } } = [ \mathbf { w } ^ { \top } \mathbf { \Sigma } b ] ^ { \top }$ .   
(Learning algorithm) Find the minimizer of loss function

$$
J ( \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } ) = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } \left( f _ { \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } } ( \mathbf { x } _ { i } ) - y _ { i } \right) ^ { 2 } = \left( \mathbf { \mathbf { X } } \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } - \mathbf { y } \right) ^ { \top } ( \mathbf { \mathbf { X } } \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } - \mathbf { y } )
$$

(Final hypothesis) Least squares solution (with offset)

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } ^ { * } = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { b ^ { * } } \\ { \mathbf { w } ^ { * } } \end{array} \right] = ( \mathbf { X } ^ { \top } \mathbf { X } ) ^ { - 1 } \mathbf { X } ^ { \top } \mathbf { y } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d + 1 } . } \end{array}
$$

$\odot$ Prediction/Testing: Given a new feature vector (sample, example) $\pmb { \mathrm { x } } _ { \mathrm { n e w } }$ , the prediction based on the least squares solution is

$$
\hat { y } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } = \biggl [ \mathbf { 1 } _ { \mathrm { x _ { \mathrm { n e w } } } } \biggr ] ^ { \top } \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } ^ { \ast } = b ^ { \ast } + \mathbf { x } _ { \mathrm { n e w } } ^ { \top } \mathbf { w } ^ { \ast } .
$$

error $\left( y , y ^ { \prime } \right) =$ penalty for predicting $y ^ { \prime }$ when true label is y Choose an error metric that makes sense for your application!

$\odot$ Regression

Square error: $\mathbf { e r r o r { _ { \mathrm { s q } } } } ( y , y ^ { \prime } ) = ( y - y ^ { \prime } ) ^ { 2 }$ Absolute error: $\mathbf { e r r o r a b s } ( y , y ^ { \prime } ) = | y - y ^ { \prime } |$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L07_model_sel\page_053\DSAA2011-L07_model_sel_page_053\auto

# Error metric: some candidates

$\odot$ Regression

Square error: $\mathbf { e r r o r { _ { \mathrm { s q } } } } ( y , y ^ { \prime } ) = ( y - y ^ { \prime } ) ^ { 2 }$ Absolute error: $\mathbf { e r r o r a b s } ( y , y ^ { \prime } ) = | y - y ^ { \prime } |$

# $\odot$ Classification

Misclassification error: $\mathbf { e r r o r } _ { \mathrm { m i s } } ( y , y ^ { \prime } ) = \mathbb { 1 } \{ y \neq y ^ { \prime } \}$ Weighted misclassification error: If false positives are $\beta$ times worse than false negatives

$$
\mathrm { { a } } ( y , y ^ { \prime } ) = \beta \mathbb { 1 } \{ y ^ { \prime } = 1 , y = - 1 \} + ( 1 - \beta ) \mathbb { 1 } \{ y ^ { \prime } = -
$$

Balanced error rate: If dataset contains $n _ { + }$ examples with positive labels and $n _ { - }$ negative

$$
\mathsf { e r r o r } _ { \mathrm { b a l } } ( y , y ^ { \prime } ) = \frac { \mathbb { 1 } \left\{ y \ne y ^ { \prime } \right\} } { n _ { + } \mathbb { 1 } \left\{ y \right\} + n _ { - } \mathbb { 1 } \left\{ 1 - \mathbb { 1 } \left\{ y \right\} \right\} }
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L07_model_sel\page_057\DSAA2011-L07_model_sel_page_057\auto

# Some ways to further evaluate classification model

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L07_model_sel\page_065\DSAA2011-L07_model_sel_page_065\auto

# Train and test error: evaluate the selected error metric on dataset

• Partition data $\mathcal { D }$ into training set $\mathcal { D } _ { \mathrm { t r a i n } }$ and test set Dtest $\mathcal { D } _ { \sf t r a i n } \cap \mathcal { D } _ { \sf t e s t } = \emptyset , \mathcal { D } _ { \sf t r a i n } \cup \mathcal { D } _ { \sf t e s t } = \mathcal { D }$

Algorithm $\mathcal { A }$ is only allowed to see the training set $\mathcal { D } _ { \mathrm { t r a i n } }$

Training error

$$
E _ { \mathrm { t r a i n } } \left( g \right) = \frac { 1 } { \left| \mathcal { D } _ { \mathrm { t r a i n } } \right| } \sum _ { i \in \mathcal { D } _ { \mathrm { t r a i n } } } \mathrm { e r r o r } \left( y _ { i } , g \left( x _ { i } \right) \right)
$$

# Test error

$$
E _ { \mathrm { t e s t } } \left( \boldsymbol { g } \right) = \frac { 1 } { | \mathcal { D } _ { \mathrm { t e s t } } | } \sum _ { i \in \mathcal { D } _ { \mathrm { t e s t } } } \mathrm { e r r o r } \left( y _ { i } , \boldsymbol { g } \left( \boldsymbol { x } _ { i } \right) \right)
$$

◦ Mean Error: “Mean Square Error” (MSE), “Mean Absolute Error” (MAE), etc.

Ridge regression: For a fixed $\lambda \geq 0$ , consider

$$
= \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } \left( f _ { \mathbf { w } , b } ( \mathbf { x } _ { i } ) - y _ { i } \right) ^ { 2 } + \lambda \sum _ { i = 0 } ^ { d } w _ { j } ^ { 2 } = ( \mathbf { X } \overline { { \mathbf { w } } } - \mathbf { y } ) ^ { \top } ( \mathbf { X } \overline { { \mathbf { \Gamma } } }

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L07_model_sel\page_076\DSAA2011-L07_model_sel_page_076\auto

# No free lunch!

Decompose the expected error:

expected prediction error = bias2 + variance + noise

• bias2: average prediction error over all data sets (squared) variance: how much solutions for different data sets vary (stability) noise: deviation of measurements from the true value (unavoidable error)

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L07_model_sel\page_077\DSAA2011-L07_model_sel_page_077\auto

# No free lunch!

Decompose the expected error:

expected prediction error = bias2 + variance + noise

bias2: average prediction error over all data sets (squared) variance: how much solutions for different data sets vary (stability) noise: deviation of measurements from the true value (unavoidable error)

# Theorem 1.1 (No free lunch!)

roblem: Low bias comes with high variance and low variances comes with high bias! Too high bias: we cannot fit the data well, because our solutions are too restricted. Too low bias: we have too high variance, sensitive to data changes (overfitting). → We need to find the sweet spot inbetween!

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L07_model_sel\page_084\DSAA2011-L07_model_sel_page_084\auto

# ℓp-norm of vector

Definition 1.2 (ℓp-norm of vector)

Let $p \in ( 0 , \infty )$ , $\ell _ { p } .$ -norm of $\boldsymbol { \mathsf { w } } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ is defined as $| | \mathbf { w } | | _ { p } = \left( \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } | w _ { i } | ^ { p } \right) ^ { 1 / p } .$

• $0 < \ell < \infty$ :

$\ell _ { 1 }$ -norm is $| | { \mathbf { w } } | | _ { 1 } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } | w _ { i } | . \qquad \ell _ { 2 } \mathsf { \mathrm { - n o r m ~ i s ~ } } | | { \mathbf { w } } | | _ { 2 } = \sqrt { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } | w _ { i } | ^ { 2 } } .$

$p = 0$ or $\infty$ , $\ell _ { p } .$ -norm is defined by taking limit:

$$
\begin{array} { l } { \displaystyle \mathsf { \Pi } _ { \mathsf { - n o r m ~ i s ~ } } | | \mathbf { w } | | _ { \infty } = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { p \to \infty } \left( \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } | w _ { i } | ^ { p } \right) ^ { 1 / p } = \mathsf { m a x } | w _ { i } | . } \\ { \displaystyle \mathsf { \Pi } _ { \mathsf { 1 o r m ~ i s ~ } } | | \mathbf { w } | | _ { 0 } = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { p \to 0 } \left( \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } | w _ { i } | ^ { p } \right) ^ { 1 / p } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } \mathbb { 1 } ( w _ { i } \neq 0 ) . } \end{array}
$$

# Definition 1.2 (ℓp-norm of vector)

Let $p \in ( 0 , \infty )$ , $\ell _ { p } .$ -norm of $\boldsymbol { \mathsf { w } } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ is defined as $| | \mathbf { w } | | _ { p } = \left( \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } | w _ { i } | ^ { p } \right) ^ { 1 / p } .$

• $0 < \ell < \infty$ :

$$
| | { \mathbf { w } } | | _ { 1 } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } | w _ { i } | . \qquad \ell _ { 2 } \mathsf { \mathrm { - n o r m ~ i s ~ } } | | { \mathbf { w } } | | _ { 2 } = \sqrt { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } | w _ { i } | ^ { 2 } } .
$$

$p = 0$ or $\infty$ , $\ell _ { p } .$ -norm is defined by taking limit:

$$
\begin{array} { l } { \displaystyle \mathsf { \Pi } _ { \mathsf { - n o r m ~ i s ~ } } | | \mathbf { w } | | _ { \infty } = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { p \to \infty } \left( \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } | w _ { i } | ^ { p } \right) ^ { 1 / p } = \mathsf { m a x } | w _ { i } | . } \\ { \displaystyle \mathsf { \Pi } _ { \mathsf { 1 o r m ~ i s ~ } } | | \mathbf { w } | | _ { 0 } = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { p \to 0 } \left( \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } | w _ { i } | ^ { p } \right) ^ { 1 / p } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } \mathbb { 1 } ( w _ { i } \neq 0 ) . } \end{array}
$$

◦ Technical note: $\ell _ { 0 }$ is not actually a norm

(not absolutely homogeneous since $| | \alpha \mathbf { w } | | _ { 0 } = | | \mathbf { w } | | _ { 0 }$ for $\alpha \neq 0$ )

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L07_model_sel\page_086\DSAA2011-L07_model_sel_page_086\auto

# ℓ1 regularization

$\ell _ { 1 }$ regularizer ( $\lambda \geq 0$ : regularization parameter)

$$
r ( \boldsymbol { \mathsf { w } } ) = \lambda \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } | w _ { i } |
$$

Lasso problem: linear least squares $+ ~ \ell _ { 1 }$ regularizer

$$
\operatorname* { m i n } _ { \mathbf { \overline { { w } } } } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } ( y _ { i } - \mathbf { \overline { { w } } } ^ { \top } x _ { i } ) ^ { 2 } + \lambda \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } | \bar { w } _ { i } |
$$

with variable $\overline { { \mathbf { w } } } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d + 1 }$ .

$$
r ( \boldsymbol { \mathsf { w } } ) = \lambda \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } | w _ { i } |
$$

Lasso problem: linear least squares $+ ~ \ell _ { 1 }$ regularizer

$$
\operatorname* { m i n } _ { \mathbf { \overline { { w } } } } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } ( y _ { i } - \mathbf { \overline { { w } } } ^ { \top } x _ { i } ) ^ { 2 } + \lambda \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } | \bar { w } _ { i } |
$$

with variable $\overline { { \mathbf { w } } } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d + 1 }$ .

Penalize large $\overline { { \mathbf { w } } }$ less than quadrat $\mathsf { i c } \left( \ell _ { 2 } \right) \mathsf { r e g u l a r i z a t i o n : } r ( \mathsf { w } ) = \lambda | | \mathsf { w } | | _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } = \lambda \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } w _ { i } ^ { 2 }$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L07_model_sel\page_098\DSAA2011-L07_model_sel_page_098\auto

# $\odot$ A simple and effective validation procedure:

1. Split data into training set $\mathcal { D } _ { \mathrm { t r a i n } }$ and validation set $\mathcal { D } _ { \mathsf { v a l i d } }$ 2. Pick $m$ different interesting model classes e.g., different model class $\phi$ : $\phi _ { 1 } , \phi _ { 2 } , \ldots , \phi _ { m }$ 3. Fit (“train”) models on training set $\mathcal { D } _ { \mathrm { t r a i n } }$ Get one hypothesis $h : \mathcal { X } \to \mathcal { Y }$ for each $\phi \mathsf { s }$ , and set

$$
\mathcal { H } = \left\{ h _ { 1 } , h _ { 2 } , \ldots , h _ { m } \right\}
$$

4. Compute error of each hypothesis on validation set $\mathcal { D } _ { \mathsf { v a l i d } }$ and choose the lowest:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { h ^ { * } = \underset { h \in \mathcal { H } } { \mathsf { a r g m i n } } E _ { \mathcal { D } _ { \mathrm { v a l i d } } } ( h ) } \end{array}
$$

◦ OR: select the model class according to $h ^ { * }$ and retrain $h ^ { * }$ on the entire training set.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L07_model_sel\page_100\DSAA2011-L07_model_sel_page_100\auto

# Cross-validation

1. Pick a bunch of interesting model classes (e.g., different $\phi \mathsf { s }$ $\therefore \phi _ { 1 } , \phi _ { 2 } , . . . , \phi _ { m } )$

2. For each possible split of data into training set $\mathcal { D }$ and validation set $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime }$ : $( \mathcal { D } _ { 1 } , \mathcal { D } _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } ) , ( \mathcal { D } _ { 2 } , \mathcal { D } _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } ) , \ldots , ( \mathcal { D } _ { K } , \mathcal { D } _ { K } ^ { \prime } )$ Fit (‘train’) each model (class) $\phi$ on training set $\mathcal { D }$ and obtain hypothesis $h _ { \phi , \mathcal { D } }$ Compute error of each hypothesis on validation set $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime }$ : $E _ { \mathcal { D ^ { \prime } } } ( h _ { \phi , \mathcal { D } } )$   
◦ Now, the validation set $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime }$ is not a single set $\Rightarrow$ multiple validation sets $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime } \mathsf { s }$   
3. Estimate error of model as average of error on each $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime }$ $\phi ^ { * } = \underset { \phi _ { i } } { \arg \operatorname* { m i n } } \frac { 1 } { K } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { K } E _ { \mathcal { D } _ { j } ^ { \prime } } ( h _ { \phi _ { i } , \mathcal { D } _ { j } } )$

4. Fit the model $\phi ^ { * }$ using the entire dataset.

# How to pick splits

Leave-one-out cross-validation

$\circ \mathcal { D } ^ { \prime }$ has one example, $\mathcal { D }$ has all the rest

▶ Advantage: accurate Disadvantage: slow Recall: measure the robustness of SVM

# $n$ -fold cross-validation

◦ $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime }$ has $1 / n$ of the entire training dataset, $\mathcal { D }$ has all the rest (usually, $n = 5$ or 10)

▶ Decently accurate, not too slow

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L07_model_sel\page_104\DSAA2011-L07_model_sel_page_104\auto

# Summary: train, test, validation

We care how well model performs on both old and new data   
“To simulate new data”, split $\mathcal { D }$ into train, validation and test sets   
Evaluate error on each validation set via error metric   
If training set error is high, we say model fits poorly ▶ Solution: use more complex model, or add new features, or add data   
If test set error is much higher than training set error, we say model overfits ▶ Solution: make less complex model, or remove features, or add data

● Reading material: Section 9 in https://cs229.stanford.edu/lectures-spring2022/main_notes.pdf

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_005\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_005\auto

# Generalization of supervised learning algorithms

$\odot$ We need the new ML system generalizes well on unseen data, e.g., data from my hospital or other hospitals

$\circledcirc$ Elements in supervised learning:

Unknown target function $f : \mathcal { X }  \mathcal { Y }$   
Training examples $\mathcal { D } = \{ ( x _ { 1 } , y _ { 1 } ) , \dots , ( x _ { n } , y _ { n } ) \}$   
Hypothesis set $\mathcal { H }$ (set of functions) Learning algorithm $\mathcal { A }$   
Final hypothesis $g : \mathcal { X }  \mathcal { Y }$

$\odot$ How well will our classifier/regressor do on new data? $\Leftarrow$ how well can $\boldsymbol { g }$ approximate $f ?$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_007\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_007\auto

# Error metric: some candidates

# $\odot$ Regression

Square error: $\mathbf { e r r o r { _ { \mathrm { s q } } } } ( y , y ^ { \prime } ) = ( y - y ^ { \prime } ) ^ { 2 }$ Absolute error: $\mathbf { e r r o r } _ { \mathrm { a b s } } ( y , y ^ { \prime } ) = | y - y ^ { \prime } |$

# $\odot$ Classification

Misclassification error: $\mathbf { e r r o r } _ { \mathrm { m i s } } ( y , y ^ { \prime } ) = \mathbb { 1 } \{ y \neq y ^ { \prime } \}$ Weighted misclassification error: If false positives are $\beta$ times worse than false negatives

$$
\mathrm { { a } } ( y , y ^ { \prime } ) = \beta \mathbb { 1 } \{ y ^ { \prime } = 1 , y = - 1 \} + ( 1 - \beta ) \mathbb { 1 } \{ y ^ { \prime } = -
$$

Balanced error rate: If dataset contains $n _ { + }$ examples with positive labels and $n _ { - }$ negative

$$
\mathbf { e r r o r } _ { \mathrm { b a l } } ( y , y ^ { \prime } ) = \frac { ( n _ { + } + n _ { - } ) / 2 \cdot \mathbb { 1 } \{ y \neq y ^ { \prime } \} } { n _ { + } \mathbb { 1 } \{ y \} + n _ { - } \mathbb { 1 } \{ 1 - \mathbb { 1 } \{ y \} \} }
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_009\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_009\auto

# Some ways to further evaluate classification model

Precision $= \#$ true pos / ( $\#$ true pos + # false pos) ◦ Measure the accuracy of positive predictions

Recall (sensitivity) = # true pos / ( $\#$ true pos + # false neg) ◦ Measures the model’s ability to find all the positive instances

$\bullet \mathsf { F 1 } \mathsf { s c o r e } = 2 / ( \mathsf { R e c a l l } ^ { - 1 } + \mathsf { P r e c i s i o n } ^ { - 1 } )$ ◦ Harmonic mean of precision and recall: balance the two metrics into a single number, making it especially useful when precision and recall are in trade-off

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_010\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_010\auto

# Some ways to further evaluate classification model

True Positive Rate $= \#$ true pos / ( $\#$ true pos + # false neg) ◦ Measure the accuracy of prediction for positive samples

False Positive Rate $= \#$ false pos / ( $\#$ false pos + # true neg) ◦ Measure the accuracy of prediction for negative samples

ROC, AUC (AUROC)   
◦ ROC: Receiver Operating Characteristic AUC (AUROC): Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic   
◦ Remove dependence on thresholds

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_011\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_011\auto

Given trhe following classification result:   
Ground truth label: T,T,T,T,T,F,F,F,F,F   
Predictions: T,T,T,T,F,F,F,T,T,T Calculate the precision and recall

A 4/7, 4/5   
B 4/5, 4/7   
C 4/6, 6/10   
D 6/10, 4/7
