## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_013\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_013\auto

# Train and test error: evaluate the selected error metric on dataset

• Partition data $\mathcal { D }$ into training set $\mathcal { D } _ { \mathrm { t r a i n } }$ and test set Dtest $\mathcal { D } _ { \sf t r a i n } \cap \mathcal { D } _ { \sf t e s t } = \emptyset , \mathcal { D } _ { \sf t r a i n } \cup \mathcal { D } _ { \sf t e s t } = \mathcal { D }$

Algorithm $\mathcal { A }$ is only allowed to see the training set $\mathcal { D } _ { \mathrm { t r a i n } }$

Training error

$$
E _ { \mathrm { t r a i n } } \left( g \right) = \frac { 1 } { \left| \mathcal { D } _ { \mathrm { t r a i n } } \right| } \sum _ { i \in \mathcal { D } _ { \mathrm { t r a i n } } } \mathrm { e r r o r } \left( y _ { i } , g \left( x _ { i } \right) \right)
$$

# Test error

$$
E _ { \mathrm { t e s t } } \left( \boldsymbol { g } \right) = \frac { 1 } { | \mathcal { D } _ { \mathrm { t e s t } } | } \sum _ { i \in \mathcal { D } _ { \mathrm { t e s t } } } \mathrm { e r r o r } \left( y _ { i } , \boldsymbol { g } \left( \boldsymbol { x } _ { i } \right) \right)
$$

◦ Mean Error: “Mean Square Error” (MSE), “Mean Absolute Error” (MAE), etc.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_015\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_015\auto

# $\circledcirc$ Why regularize?

Reduce variance of the model (more stable)   
Prevent overfitting   
Impose prior structural knowledge   
Improve interpretability: simpler model, automatic feature selection

# $\textcircled{9}$ Why NOT regularize?

Gauss-Markov theorem:   
◦ Least squares is the best linear unbiased estimator Regularization increases bias

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_016\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_016\auto

# No free lunch! Trade-off between bias and variance!

Decompose the expected error:

expected prediction error = bias2 + variance + noise

• bias2: average prediction error over all data sets (squared) variance: how much solutions for different data sets vary (stability) noise: deviation of measurements from the true value (unavoidable error)

# Theorem 1 (No free lunch!)

roblem: Low bias comes with high variance and low variances comes with high bias! Too high bias: we cannot fit the data well, because our solutions are too restricted. Too low bias: we have too high variance, sensitive to data changes (overfitting). → We need to find the sweet spot inbetween!

---

small

nonnegative   
smooth

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_018\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_018\auto

Definition 2 (ℓp-norm of vector)

Let $p \in ( 0 , \infty )$ , $\ell _ { p } .$ -norm of $\boldsymbol { \mathsf { w } } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ is defined as $| | \mathbf { w } | | _ { p } = \left( \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } | w _ { i } | ^ { p } \right) ^ { 1 / p } .$

• $0 < \ell < \infty$ :

$\ell _ { 1 }$ -norm is $| | { \mathbf { w } } | | _ { 1 } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } | w _ { i } | . \qquad \ell _ { 2 } \mathsf { \mathrm { - n o r m ~ i s ~ } } | | { \mathbf { w } } | | _ { 2 } = \sqrt { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } | w _ { i } | ^ { 2 } } .$

$p = 0$ or $\infty$ , $\ell _ { p } .$ -norm is defined by taking limit:

$$
\begin{array} { l } { \displaystyle \mathsf { \Pi } _ { \mathsf { - n o r m ~ i s ~ } } | | \mathbf { w } | | _ { \infty } = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { p \to \infty } \left( \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } | w _ { i } | ^ { p } \right) ^ { 1 / p } = \mathsf { m a x } | w _ { i } | . } \\ { \displaystyle \mathsf { \Pi } _ { \mathsf { 1 o r m ~ i s ~ } } | | \mathbf { w } | | _ { 0 } = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { p \to 0 } \left( \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } | w _ { i } | ^ { p } \right) ^ { 1 / p } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } \mathbb { 1 } ( w _ { i } \neq 0 ) . } \end{array}
$$

◦ Technical note: $\ell _ { 0 }$ is not actually a norm

(not absolutely homogeneous since $| | \alpha \mathbf { w } | | _ { 0 } = | | \mathbf { w } | | _ { 0 }$ for $\alpha \neq 0$ )

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_021\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_021\auto

# Validation

# $\odot$ A simple and effective validation procedure:

1. Split data into training set $\mathcal { D } _ { \mathrm { t r a i n } }$ and validation set $\mathcal { D } _ { \mathsf { v a l i d } }$ 2. Pick $m$ different interesting model classes e.g., different model class $\phi$ : $\phi _ { 1 } , \phi _ { 2 } , \ldots , \phi _ { m }$ 3. Fit (“train”) models on training set $\mathcal { D } _ { \mathrm { t r a i n } }$ Get one hypothesis $h : \mathcal { X } \to \mathcal { Y }$ for each $\phi \mathsf { s }$ , and set

$$
\mathcal { H } = \left\{ h _ { 1 } , h _ { 2 } , \ldots , h _ { m } \right\}
$$

4. Compute error of each hypothesis on validation set $\mathcal { D } _ { \mathsf { v a l i d } }$ and choose the lowest:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { h ^ { * } = \underset { h \in \mathcal { H } } { \mathsf { a r g m i n } } E _ { \mathcal { D } _ { \mathrm { v a l i d } } } ( h ) } \end{array}
$$

◦ OR: select the model class according to $h ^ { * }$ and retrain $h ^ { * }$ on the entire training set.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_022\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_022\auto

# Cross-validation

1. Pick a bunch of interesting model classes (e.g., different $\phi \mathsf { s }$ $\therefore \phi _ { 1 } , \phi _ { 2 } , . . . , \phi _ { m } )$   
2. For each possible split of data into training set $\mathcal { D }$ and validation set $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime }$ : $( \mathcal { D } _ { 1 } , \mathcal { D } _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } ) , ( \mathcal { D } _ { 2 } , \mathcal { D } _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } ) , \ldots , ( \mathcal { D } _ { K } , \mathcal { D } _ { K } ^ { \prime } )$ Fit (‘train’) each model (class) $\phi$ on training set $\mathcal { D }$ and obtain hypothesis $h _ { \phi , \mathcal { D } }$ Compute error of each hypothesis on validation set $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime }$ : $E _ { \mathcal { D ^ { \prime } } } ( h _ { \phi , \mathcal { D } } )$ ◦ Now, the validation set $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime }$ is not a single set $\Rightarrow$ multiple validation sets $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime } \mathsf { s }$   
3. Estimate error of model as average of error on each $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime }$ $\phi ^ { * } = \underset { \phi _ { i } } { \arg \operatorname* { m i n } } \frac { 1 } { K } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { K } E _ { \mathcal { D } _ { j } ^ { \prime } } ( h _ { \phi _ { i } , \mathcal { D } _ { j } } )$

4. Fit the model $\phi ^ { * }$ using the entire dataset.

# Cross-validation: how to pick splits

Leave-one-out cross-validation

$\circ \mathcal { D } ^ { \prime }$ has one example, $\mathcal { D }$ has all the rest

▶ Advantage: accurate Disadvantage: slow Recall: measure the robustness of SVM

# $n$ -fold cross-validation

$\circ \mathcal { D } ^ { \prime }$ has $1 / n$ of the entire training dataset, $\mathcal { D }$ has all the rest (usually, $n = 5$ or 10)

▶ Decently accurate, not too slow

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_025\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_025\auto

# What is a Decision Tree?

A decision tree is a simple, tree-like model used in machine learning.   
It makes decisions by asking a series of questions (usually yes/no).   
Used for both classification (e.g., spam or not spam) and regression (e.g., predicting house prices).   
• Think of it like a flowchart for decision-making!

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_026\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_026\auto

1 Start with a dataset (e.g., features like age, income).   
2 Pick a feature to split on (e.g., “Is age > 30?”).   
3 Keep splitting based on features until you reach a decision.   
4 Goal: Minimize uncertainty at each step (using metrics like entropy or Gini impurity).

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_027\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_027\auto

# How to Build a Decision Tree

Given a subset of data $M$ (a node in a tree)

For each feature $h _ { i } ( x )$ : ▶ Split data of M according to feature $h _ { i } ( x )$ : ▶ Compute classification error of split:

Chose feature $h ^ { * } ( x )$ with lowest classification error (or other criteria) Stop condition

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_028\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_028\auto

# How to Build a Decision Tree

# Given a subset of data $M$ (a node in a tree)

For each feature $h _ { i } ( x )$ : ▶ Split data of M according to feature $h _ { i } ( x )$ : ▶ Compute classification error of split:

Chose feature $h ^ { * } ( x )$ with lowest classification error (or other criteria)

# Stop condition

The tree doesn’t grow forever—stopping conditions decide when to halt: Purity: All data in a node belongs to one class (e.g., all ”spam”). Max Depth: Limit how many levels the tree can have (e.g., stop at 5 splits). Min Samples: Stop if too few data points remain (e.g., ¡ 10 samples). Prevents overfitting and keeps the tree manageable!

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_029\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_029\auto

# Pros & Cons of Decision Tree

# Pros

Can handle large datasets Can handle mixed predictors (continuous, discrete, qualitative) Can ignore redundant variables Can easily handle missing data Easy to interpret if small

# Cons

Prediction performance is poor Does not generalize well Large trees are hard to interpret

# Error Rate of A Majority Voting Ensemble

Consider a binary classification task. Assume that we have $N$ independent base learners, and the error rate of each base classifier is $\epsilon$ , the error rate of the ensemble model is:

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_039\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_039\auto

# Error Rate of A Majority Voting Ensemble

Consider a binary classification task. Assume that we have $N$ independent base learners, and the error rate of each base classifier is $\epsilon$ , the error rate of the ensemble model is:

$$
\sum _ { k = 0 } ^ { \lfloor N / 2 \rfloor } { \binom { N } { k } } ( 1 - \epsilon ) ^ { k } \epsilon ^ { N - k } \le \exp \left( - { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } N ( 1 - 2 \epsilon ) ^ { 2 } \right)
$$

When $\epsilon < 0 . 5$ , the error rates drop exponentially and eventually approach zero as $N$ increases

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_040\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_040\auto

# Theorem 3 (Hoeffding’s Inequality)

Let $X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n }$ be independent bounded random variables with $X _ { i } \in [ a , b ]$ for all i , where $- \infty < a \le b < \infty$ . Then

$$
\left( { \frac { 1 } { n } } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } X _ { i } - { \frac { 1 } { n } } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \mathbb { E } [ X _ { i } ] \leq - \delta \right) \leq \exp \left( - { \frac { 2 N \delta ^ { 2 } } { ( b - a ) ^ { 2 } } } \right.
$$

In our case, $X = X _ { 1 } + X _ { 2 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + X _ { N }$ is the number of base learners that make the correct predictions.   
$X _ { i } \sim B ( 1 , 1 - \epsilon ) , \mathbb { E } [ X _ { i } ] = 1 - \epsilon , a = 0 , b = 1 .$   
The error rate of the ensemble model is $P ( X \leq N / 2 )$ ;   
Apply Hoeffding’s Inequality to obtain the bound.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_048\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_048\auto

# How Bagging Works: Step 1 - Sampling

Take your original dataset (e.g., 1000 data points).   
Generate $N$ bootstrap samples (e.g., $N = 1 0$ ).   
Each set is the same size as the original but slightly different (by sampling with replacement) ▶ Why not split data into $\boldsymbol { \kappa }$ partitions? $6 3 . 2 \%$ samples will be sampled (why?) ▶ $| \mathfrak { i } \mathfrak { m } _ { n  \infty } ( 1 - 1 / n ) ^ { n } = 1 / e = 0 . 3 6 8$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_049\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_049\auto

# How Bagging Works: Step 2 - Training

Train one model (e.g., decision tree) on each bootstrap sample.   
Each model learns slightly different patterns due to sample variation.   
Result: $N$ weak learners (e.g., 10 decision trees).

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_050\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_050\auto

# How Bagging Works: Step 3 - Aggregation

For classification: Use majority voting (e.g., 6 trees say ”yes,” 4 say ”no” → ”yes”).   
For regression: Average the predictions.   
Combines strengths, reduces individual errors.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_057\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_057\auto

# Issues with Bagging of Decision Trees

Bagging reduces the variance while retaining the bias!

$$
\dot { \bar { f } } ) ^ { 2 } ] = \mathbb { E } [ ( f - \mathbb { E } \hat { f } + \mathbb { E } \hat { f } - \hat { f } ) ^ { 2 } ] = \underbrace { ( f - \mathbb { E } \hat { f } ) ^ { 2 } } _ { \mathrm { b i a s } } + \underbrace { \mathbb { E } [ ( } _ { } \mathrm { d } _ { } \mathrm { d } _ { } \mathrm { d } _ { } \mathrm { d } _ { } \mathrm { } ]
$$

Expectation of bagged trees is equal to the expectation of individual trees

$$
\mathbb { E } [ \hat { f } ( x ) ] = \mathbb { E } [ f _ { b } ( x ) ]
$$

Bias of bagged trees is the same as that of individual trees

● Each tree is identically distributed (i.d. but not i.i.d). Bagged trees are still correlated!

# Correlated Learners Cannot Effectively Reduce Variance

Averaging i.i.d. variables scales their variance $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ to $\sigma ^ { 2 } / B$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_059\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_059\auto

# Correlated Learners Cannot Effectively Reduce Variance

Averaging i.i.d. variables scales their variance $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ to $\sigma ^ { 2 } / B$

$$
\mathsf { V a r } ( \bar { X } ) = \mathsf { V a r } \left( \frac { 1 } { B } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { B } X _ { i } \right) = \frac { 1 } { B ^ { 2 } } \mathsf { V a r } \left( \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { B } X _ { i } \right) =
$$

Averaging i.d. variables with pairwise correlations $\rho$ and variance $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ gives their final variance to be $( \rho + ( 1 - \rho ) / B ) \sigma ^ { 2 }$

# Correlated Learners Cannot Effectively Reduce Variance

Averaging i.i.d. variables scales their variance $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ to $\sigma ^ { 2 } / B$

$$
\mathsf { V a r } ( \bar { X } ) = \mathsf { V a r } \left( \frac { 1 } { B } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { B } X _ { i } \right) = \frac { 1 } { B ^ { 2 } } \mathsf { V a r } \left( \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { B } X _ { i } \right) =
$$

Averaging i.d. variables with pairwise correlations $\rho$ and variance $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ gives their final variance to be $( \rho + ( 1 - \rho ) / B ) \sigma ^ { 2 }$

$$
\sum _ { = 1 } ^ { 3 } X _ { i } ) = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { B } \mathsf { V a r } ( X _ { i } ) + \sum _ { i \ne j } \mathsf { C o v } ( X _ { i } , X _ { j } ) = B \sigma ^ { 2 } + B
$$

▶ When $\rho = 0$ , the variance is $\sigma ^ { 2 } / B$ When $\rho  1$ , the variance $\to \sigma ^ { 2 }$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_061\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_061\auto

# Decision Trees in Bagging

Pruning trees in a bagging model is usually not needed. Why

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_062\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_062\auto

# Decision Trees in Bagging

Pruning trees in a bagging model is usually not needed. Why   
● Decision trees are unstable classifiers, different subsets might yield significantly different trees   
We want them to be low-bias but high-variance   
• Unpruned trees tend to be more different from one another than if they were pru   
“Decorrelate” the trees!

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_063\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_063\auto

# Random Forests

How to further decorrelate the trees generated for bagging?   
• Ideas ▶ We can restrict how many times a feature can be used We only allow a certain number of features ▶ etc..

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_064\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_064\auto

# Random Forests

Introduced by Leo Breiman in 2001.   
As in bagging, choose $B$ bootstrapped splits   
For each split in the $B$ trees, consider only $k$ features from the full feature set m ▶ $k = m$ : same as Bagging ▶ $k < m$ : Random Forests   
• Like a “forest” of diverse trees working together!   
• OOB error rate can be used to fit RF in one sequence with cross validation done along the way

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_065\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_065\auto

# Tuning Random Forests

Random forest models have multiple hyper-parameters to tune

the number of predictors to randomly select at each split • the total number of trees in the ensemble the minimum leaf node size These parameters should be tuned through OOB

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_066\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_066\auto

# Random Forests

• Works great in practice. $k$ to be treated as a hyperparameter

Introduce diversity through 1) randomness in boostrapping; 2) randomness in feature selection

Faster training than bagging (why?)

● Issues:

When you have a large number of features, yet a very small number of relevant features Prob(selecting the relevant feature in $k$ ) could be very small!

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_067\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_067\auto

# Motivation for Boosting

Question: Could we address the shortcomings of single decision tree models in some other way?   
• Learners are trained sequentially: each learner is grown using information from previously grown trees   
• Just like how students learn from their mistakes in multiple exams

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_068\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_068\auto

# Boosting Model

• Key intuition: take an ensemble of simple models $\{ T _ { h } \} _ { h \in H }$ and additively combine them into a single, more complex model

• Each model $T _ { h }$ might be a poor fit for the data, but a linear combination of the ensemble can be expressive

$$
T = \sum _ { h } \lambda _ { h } T _ { h }
$$

Questions: which model should be included in the ensemble model, and how to decide the weights $\lambda _ { h }$

Two representative methods

▶ Gradient Boosting

▶ AdaBoost (Adaptive Boosting)

- data\1. Machine_Learning\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_068\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_068\auto\images\4926da8bef1a50023de9179eccf0e544351c8aac9918c9bd63bdfa13f6cb111a.jpg

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_069\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_069\auto

# Build new models to compensate the error of the current ensemble

# Key features:

A more general boosting method using gradient descent Works with any differentiable loss function • Each new model fits the “residual errors” of the previous ones. ● Powers tools like XGBoost, LightGBM: top performers in ML competitions!

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_070\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_070\auto

# Gradient Boosting Steps

1 Fit a simple model ${ \cal T } = { \cal T } ^ { ( 0 ) }$ on the training data $\{ ( x _ { 1 } , y _ { 1 } ) , \dotsc , ( x _ { N } , y _ { N } ) \}$   
2 Compute the residuals $\left\{ \boldsymbol { r } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \boldsymbol { r } _ { N } \right\}$ for model $\tau$   
3 Fit a simple model $T ^ { ( 1 ) }$ to the current residuals, i.e., train using $\{ ( x _ { 1 } , r _ { 1 } ) , \dotsc , ( x _ { N } , r _ { N } ) \}$   
4 Build a new model $T \gets T + \lambda T ^ { ( 1 ) }$   
5 Compute the updated residuals $r _ { n } \gets r _ { n } - \lambda T ^ { ( 1 ) } ( x _ { n } )$   
6 Repeated steps 2-5 until the stopping condition met

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_071\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_071\auto

# Gradient Boosting Steps

1 Fit a simple model ${ \cal T } = { \cal T } ^ { ( 0 ) }$ on the training data $\{ ( x _ { 1 } , y _ { 1 } ) , \dotsc , ( x _ { N } , y _ { N } ) \}$ 2 Compute the residuals $\left\{ \boldsymbol { r } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \boldsymbol { r } _ { N } \right\}$ for model $\tau$ 3 Fit a simple model $T ^ { ( 1 ) }$ to the current residuals, i.e., train using $\{ ( x _ { 1 } , r _ { 1 } ) , \dotsc , ( x _ { N } , r _ { N } ) \}$   
4 Build a new model $T \gets T + \lambda T ^ { ( 1 ) }$   
5 Compute the updated residuals $r _ { n } \gets r _ { n } - \lambda T ^ { ( 1 ) } ( x _ { n } )$   
6 Repeated steps 2-5 until the stopping condition met   
Question: why does this algorithm work?

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_072\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_072\auto

We aim to minimize a objective function $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { n } \to R$   
If the partial derivatives are simple, we can analytically find a stationary point where all the partial derivatives vanish.   
If the objective function is convex, then the stationary point is precisely the min

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_073\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_073\auto

● In practice, the objective functions are complicated, and analytically finding the stationary point is intractable

• Instead, we use an iterative method called gradient descent

Initialize the variables at any value $x = [ x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n } ]$ 2 Calculate the gradient at current value $\bar { \nabla } f ( x ) = \left[ \frac { \partial f ( x ) } { \partial x _ { 1 } } , \ldots , \frac { \partial f ( x ) } { \partial x _ { n } } \right]$

3 Adjust the variable values by some negative multiple of the gradient $\bar { { \boldsymbol { x } } } \gets { \boldsymbol { x } } - \lambda \nabla { f } ( { \boldsymbol { x } } )$

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_074\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_074\auto

# Gradient Boosting as Gradient Descent

Take a regression task as an example

Our objective function is the MSE:

$$
\mathcal { L } _ { \mathsf { M S E } } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { N } ( y _ { i } - \hat { y } _ { i } ) ^ { 2 }
$$

• Take gradient with respect to the predictions $\hat { y }$ : ∇ $\mathcal { L } _ { \sf M S E } = - 2 [ y _ { 1 } - \hat { y } _ { 1 } , \ldots , y _ { n } - \hat { y } _ { n } ] = - 2 [ r _ { 1 } , \ldots , r _ { n } ]$

Update the variable $\hat { y } _ { i } \gets \hat { y } _ { i } + \lambda r _ { i }$

However, this is trivial because

We know that when $\hat { y } _ { i } = y _ { i } , \mathcal { L } _ { \mathsf { M S E } } = 0$

We should learn a model instead of learn a sequence of $\hat { y } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \hat { y } _ { n }$

- data\1. Machine_Learning\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_074\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_074\auto\images\f0e421d0d4fdd8044fe6e63ab36415d4f023c6135ff9569ea4608853ca715e7f.jpg

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_075\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_075\auto

# Gradient Boosting as Gradient Descent

The solution is to change the update step in gradient descent.

● Instead of using the gradient, we use an approximation of the gradient that depends on the predictors: $\hat { y } _ { i } \gets \hat { y } _ { i } + \lambda r ( x _ { i } )$ we use a simple model to approximate the residuals $r \big ( x _ { i } \big )$ in each iteration.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_077\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_077\auto

# How to choose the learning rate λ

If $\lambda$ is a constant, then it should be tuned through cross validation   
It is better to use a variable $\lambda$   
C Usually, $\lambda$ should be related to the magnitude of the gradient ▶ around the optimum, when the gradient is small, $\lambda$ should be small ▶ far from the optimum, when the gradient is large, $\lambda$ should be large

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_078\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_078\auto

# Tuning Gradient Boosting

# Tunable Parameters:

Number of trees (B): Boosting can overfit unlike Bagging / RFs. Use cross-validation!   
Shrinkage parameter (λ): small positive number that sets the learning rate   
Number of splits in each tree (d): Usually just choose $d = 1$ , i.e., tree stumps work well

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_079\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_079\auto

# Gradient Boosting

# Variants:

Varying the tree constraints   
Weighting each tree to the additive sum using a learning rate (shrinkage)   
d Sampling strategies: stochastic gradient boosting   
Regularization: L1 / L2   
• Successful: XGBoost

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_080\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_080\auto

# Motivation for AdaBoost

Can we still use the Gradient Boosting in classification tasks? Typically, we want to minimize the classification error

$$
\mathcal { L } = \frac { 1 } { N } \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { N } \mathbb { 1 } \left( y _ { n } \neq \hat { y } _ { n } \right)
$$

# Motivation for AdaBoost

Can we still use the Gradient Boosting in classification tasks? Typically, we want to minimize the classification error

$$
\mathcal { L } = \frac { 1 } { N } \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { N } \mathbb { 1 } \left( y _ { n } \neq \hat { y } _ { n } \right)
$$

Unfortunately, it is not differentiable with respect to the predictions ˆy

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_082\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_082\auto

# Motivation for AdaBoost

Solution: replace the loss function with a differentiable function that is a good indicator of classification error   
Here, we use exponential loss

$$
\mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { e x p } } = \frac { 1 } { N } \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { N } \mathrm { e x p } \bigl ( - y _ { n } \hat { y } _ { n } \bigr ) , y _ { n } \in \{ - 1 , 1 \}
$$

Why do we choose this function? ▶ A differentiable function

# Motivation for AdaBoost

• What is the gradient for exponential loss

$$
\nabla \mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { e x p } } = [ - y _ { 1 } \exp ( - y _ { 1 } \hat { y } _ { 1 } ) , \dots , - y _ { n } \exp ( - y _ { n } \hat { y } _ { n } ) ]
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_086\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_086\auto

# Motivation for AdaBoost

• What is the gradient for exponential loss

$$
\nabla \mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { e x p } } = [ - y _ { 1 } \exp ( - y _ { 1 } \hat { y } _ { 1 } ) , \dots , - y _ { n } \exp ( - y _ { n } \hat { y } _ { n } ) ]
$$

Each component $y _ { n } \exp ( - y _ { n } \hat { y } _ { n } ) : = w _ { n } y _ { n }$

The gradient is just a re-weighting applied to the target values!

# Motivation for AdaBoost

• What is the gradient for exponential loss

$$
\nabla \mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { e x p } } = [ - y _ { 1 } \exp ( - y _ { 1 } \hat { y } _ { 1 } ) , \dots , - y _ { n } \exp ( - y _ { n } \hat { y } _ { n } ) ]
$$

Each component $y _ { n } \exp ( - y _ { n } \hat { y } _ { n } ) : = w _ { n } y _ { n }$

The gradient is just a re-weighting applied to the target values!

When ${ \hat { y } } = y$ , the weight is small When $\hat { y } \neq y$ , the weight is large

# Adaptively reweights samples

# Key Features:

Put more weight on difficult to classify instances and less on those already handled well New weak learners are added sequentially that focus their training on the more difficult patterns

rate $\boldsymbol { \epsilon } ^ { ( t ) }$

Compute the classifier weight $\begin{array} { l } { { \displaystyle \lambda ^ { ( t ) } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } \mathsf { I n } \left( \frac { 1 - \epsilon ^ { ( t ) } } { \epsilon ^ { ( t ) } } \right) } } \end{array}$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_096\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_096\auto

# Update the sample weight

$T ^ { ( t + 1 ) }$ should correct the errors in $\begin{array} { r } { T = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { t } \lambda ^ { ( i ) } T ^ { ( i ) } } \end{array}$

Why does this simple update formula achieve this?

$$
w _ { i } ^ { ( t + 1 ) } \gets w _ { i } ^ { ( t ) } \exp ( - \lambda ^ { ( t ) } y _ { i } T ^ { ( t ) } ( x _ { i } ) ) / Z
$$

• Obtain $T ^ { ( t + 1 ) }$ that minimize exponential loss for $T + T ^ { ( t + 1 ) }$

$$
\begin{array} { r l } {  { \mathbb { E } _ { ( x , y ) \in D } [ \exp ( - y ( T ( x ) + T ^ { ( t + 1 ) } ( x ) ) ] } } \\ & { = \mathbb { E } _ { ( x , y ) \in D } [ \exp ( - y T ( x ) ) \exp ( - y T ^ { ( t + 1 ) } ( x ) ) ] } \\ & { \approx \mathbb { E } _ { ( x , y ) \in D } [ \exp ( - y T ( x ) ) ( 1 - y T ^ { ( t + 1 ) } ( x ) + \frac { 1 } { 2 } y ^ { 2 } \hat { T } } \\ & { = \mathbb { E } _ { ( x , y ) \in D } [ \exp ( - y T ( x ) ) ( \frac { 3 } { 2 } - y T ^ { ( t + 1 ) } ( x ) ) ] } \end{array}
$$

• Thats why we trained $T ^ { ( t + 1 ) }$ using the weighted distribution $D _ { t }$ . Note that $D ^ { ( t + 1 ) } ( x ) \propto D ( x ) \exp ( - y ( \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { t } \lambda ^ { ( t ) } T ^ { ( t ) } ( x ) ) ) ,$ $\begin{array} { r } { D ^ { ( t ) } ( x ) \propto D ( x ) \exp ( - y ( \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { t - 1 } \lambda ^ { ( t ) } T ^ { ( t ) } ( x ) ) ) , } \end{array}$ we have

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_098\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_098\auto

# Advantages of Boosting Methods

# High Accuracy:

AdaBoost: Turns weak learners into strong classifiers (e.g., great for spam detection). ▶ Gradient Boosting: Often beats other methods (e.g., powers XGBoost wins in competitions).

# ● Flexibility:

▶ AdaBoost: Simple and fast for binary tasks. Gradient Boosting: Handles any loss function—regression, classification, ranking.

Bonus: Both can rank feature importance (Gradient Boosting especially).

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_099\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_099\auto

# Limitations of Boosting Methods

# Overfitting Risk:

▶ AdaBoost: Sensitive to noisy data and outliers (overemphasizes them).   
▶ Gradient Boosting: Too many trees or poor tuning can overfit.

# Computational Cost:

Both: Sequential training—slower than parallel methods like bagging.   
Gradient Boosting: Especially resource-heavy with many iterations.

Tuning needed (e.g., learning rate, rounds) for best results.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_100\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_100\auto

Use simple weak learners (e.g., stumps) for best results.   
Limit rounds (e.g., 50-100) to avoid overfitting. Preprocess data to reduce noise and outliers.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_101\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_101\auto

# What is Feature Selection?

• Choosing a subset of relevant features from your dataset. Why? Improve accuracy, reduce overfitting, speed up training. Very important in ensemble methods like bagging and boosting!

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_102\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_102\auto

# Why Feature Selection Matters

• Too many features: Noise, redundancy, slow models. Too few: Miss important patterns. Goal: Find the “sweet spot” for better performance. Ensembles handle many features, but selection makes them

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_103\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_103\auto

# Types of Feature Selection

Filter: Rank features (e.g., correlation) before modeling. Wrapper: Test feature subsets with a model (e.g., recursive elimination). Embedded: Selection during training (e.g., feature importance). ▶ Bagging and boosting often use embedded methods!

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_104\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_104\auto

Rank features before modeling using stats.

How:

Correlation (numeric), chi-squared (categorical), mutual information. Or using some prior knowledge

Pros: Fast, simple, scalable.

Cons: Misses feature interactions.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_105\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_105\auto

# Wrapper Methods

Test feature subsets by training a model.   
How: Forward selection (add feature), backward elimination (remove feature), recursive feature elimination.   
C Example: Try “size,” then “size $^ +$ location,” pick best accuracy.   
Pros: Model-specific, considers interactions.   
Cons: Slow, can overfit to training data.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_106\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_106\auto

# Embedded Methods

Selection during model training.   
How: Lasso (shrinks weak features), trees (split on key features).   
• Example: Gradient Boosting prioritizes “size” reducing loss.   
Pros: Efficient, tailored to model.   
Cons: Depends on model choice.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_107\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_107\auto

# Feature Importance in Tree Ensembles

Two main ways:

Impurity/Gain: How much a feature improves splits or reduces error.   
Usage: How often a feature is picked.

In different models:

Bagging: Averages impurity reduction across bootstrapped trees. XGBoost: Boosting-based; uses gain (loss reduction), weight (split count), or cover (sample count). ▶ LightGBM: Fast boosting; uses split count or gain, optimized for big data.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_108\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_108\auto

# Gradient Boosting Feature Importance

Mechanism: Trees fit residuals, reduce loss (e.g., MSE).   
How: Sum loss reduction per feature across trees.   
Example: ”Size” drops error from 100Kto20K High rank.   
Details: Weighted by depth or samples; refined in XGBoost.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_109\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_109\auto

# AdaBoost Feature Importance

Mechanism: Weak learners (e.g., stumps) weighted by error $( \alpha )$ How: Features in high- $\alpha$ learners matter more.   
Example: ”Has spam word” in top stumps Important.   
Details: Indirect—sum $\alpha$ or count feature use.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L08_ensemble\page_110\DSAA2011-L08_ensemble_page_110\auto

# Comparing Importance in Bagging vs. Boosting

Bagging (RF): Impurity-based, parallel, broad ranking. AdaBoost: Learner-weight-based, sequential, less direct. Gradient Boosting: Loss-based, sequential, precise. All help select features for better models!

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_008\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_008\auto

# Ensemble Learning

• Aggregate multiple learners to obtain a better model   
The base learners should be accurate and diverse   
For a binary classification, if we have $N$ independent base learners with error rate $\epsilon < 0 . 5$ , the error rate of their majority voting can be significantly decreased

$$
\sum _ { k = 0 } ^ { \lfloor N / 2 \rfloor } { \binom { N } { k } } ( 1 - \epsilon ) ^ { k } \epsilon ^ { N - k } \le \exp \left( - \frac { 1 } { 2 } N ( 1 - 2 \epsilon ) ^ { 2 } \right)
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_009\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_009\auto

# Proof (Optional)

# Theorem 1 (Hoeffding’s Inequality)

Let $X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n }$ be independent bounded random variables with $X _ { i } \in [ a , b ]$ for all i , where $- \infty < a \le b < \infty$ . Then for $\delta > 0$ we have

$$
\geqslant \left( { \frac { 1 } { n } } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } X _ { i } - { \frac { 1 } { n } } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \mathbb { E } [ X _ { i } ] \leq - \delta \right) \leq \exp \left( - { \frac { 2 N \delta } { \left( b - a \right) } } \right)
$$

In our case, $X _ { i } \sim B ( 1 , 1 - \epsilon ) , \mathbb { E } [ X _ { i } ] = 1 - \epsilon , a = 0 , b = 1 .$

$$
= P ( { \frac { 1 } { n } } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } X _ { i } < { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } ) = P ( { \frac { 1 } { n } } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } X _ { i } - ( 1 - \epsilon ) \leq
$$

When $\epsilon > 1 / 2 , \delta = 1 / 2 - \epsilon < 0 !$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_011\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_011\auto

# Probability Inequalities (Optional)

Markov’s Inequality: For a non-negative random variable $X$ and $a > 0$

$$
P ( X \geq a ) \leq { \frac { E [ X ] } { a } }
$$

• Chebyshev’s Inequality: For any random variable $X$ with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ , and $k > 0$ :

$$
P ( | X - \mu | \geq k \sigma ) \leq { \frac { 1 } { k ^ { 2 } } }
$$

Hoeffding’s Inequality: For independent bounded random variables $X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n }$ where $a _ { i } \leq X _ { i } \leq b _ { i } , S _ { n } = X _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + X _ { n }$ , and $t > 0$ :

$$
P ( S _ { n } - E [ S _ { n } ] \geq t ) \leq \exp \left( - { \frac { 2 t ^ { 2 } } { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } ( b _ { i } - a _ { i } ) ^ { 2 } } } \right)
$$

● You don’t need to master all of them; the goal is to gain a basic understanding of how they allow you to compute an upper bound on the probability that a random variable deviates from its expected value.

\begin{array} { r l } & { [ ( X - a ) ^ { 2 } ] = \operatorname { \mathbb { E } } [ ( X - \operatorname { \mathbb { E } } X + \operatorname { \mathbb { E } } X - a ) ^ { 2 } ] } \\ & { \qquad = \operatorname { \mathbb { E } } [ ( X - \operatorname { \mathbb { E } } X ) ^ { 2 } ] + \operatorname { \mathbb { E } } [ ( \operatorname { \mathbb { E } } X - a ) ^ { 2 } ] + \operatorname { \mathbb { E } } [ 2 } \\ & { \qquad = \operatorname { \mathbb { E } } [ ( X - \operatorname { \mathbb { E } } X ) ^ { 2 } ] + ( \operatorname { \mathbb { E } } X - a ) ^ { 2 } + 2 ( \operatorname { \mathbb { E } } X - } \\ & { \qquad = \operatorname { V a r i a n c e } + \operatorname { \mathrm { B i a s } } ^ { 2 } + 0 } \end{array}

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_013\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_013\auto

● Sequentially builds learners that approximate the gradient at each step.

Fit a simple model $T ^ { ( 0 ) }$ on training data $\{ ( X , y ) \}$ Compute the residuals $r$   
Fit a new model $T ^ { ( 1 ) }$ to the current residuals $\{ ( X , r ) \}$   
Compute the updated residuals $r - T ^ { ( 1 ) } ( x )$ (cid:) Repeated steps 3-4

Example: XGBoost, LightGBM enhance efficiency and scalability.

Usually use stumps as learners C High predictive power, though requires careful tuning to avoid overfitting.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_014\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_014\auto

# Adaptive Boosting

Sequentially builds learners on weighted samples.

Initialize equal weights $1 / N$ for all training samples 2 For each iteration:

$\star$ Train a weak learner $T ^ { ( t ) }$ on weighted data $\{ ( x _ { 1 } , w _ { 1 } y _ { 1 } ) , \dotsc , ( x _ { N } , w _ { N } y _ { N } ) \}$ and get the error rate ϵ(t)   
$\star$ If $\epsilon ^ { ( t ) } > 0 . 5$ then break   
$\star$ Compute the classifier weight $\lambda ^ { ( t ) } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } \ln \left( \frac { 1 - \epsilon ^ { ( t ) } } { \epsilon ^ { ( t ) } } \right)$   
$\star$ Update sample weights $w _ { i } ^ { ( t + 1 ) } \gets w _ { i } ^ { ( t ) } \exp ( - \lambda ^ { ( t ) } y _ { i } T ^ { ( t ) } ( x _ { i } ) ) / Z$

3 Combine all weak classifiers $\begin{array} { r } { T = \sum _ { t } \lambda ^ { ( t ) } T ^ { ( t ) } } \end{array}$

C Simple and effective, though sensitive to noisy data.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_015\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_015\auto

# Feature Selection

Filter Methods: Select features based on statistical correleation, independent of the model.   
Wrapper Methods: Evaluate feature subsets using model performance, computationally intensive.   
● Embedded Methods: Integrate feature selection into the model training process (e.g., LASSO, tree-based importance), balancing efficiency and accuracy.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_021\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_021\auto

# What is a good clustering result

We need some numerical measures!

● External

▶ Use external information, e.g., the category of images ▶ Measure how well the clustering results match the groundtruth labels ⋆ What is the difference with classification?

Internal

Do not use any external information

Assess the goodness of clusters based only on the intrinsic structure of the data. Focus on:

$^ { \star }$ Compactness of clusters (how close points are within a cluster).   
$\star$ Separation between clusters (how distinct clusters are from each other).

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_022\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_022\auto

# External Clustering Metric

Purity: Measures the extent to which clusters contain a single class.   
• (Adjusted) Rand index: Compares cluster assignments to true labels, adjusted for chance.   
• Fowlkes-Mallows index: Geometric mean of precision and recall for pairs of points.   
• (Adjusted) Mutual Information: Measures the mutual information between cluster assignments and true labels.   
V-measure

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_023\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_023\auto

Measures the fraction of correctly classified points.

Formula:

$$
\mathsf { P u r i t y } = \frac { 1 } { N } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } \mathsf { m a x } | C _ { i } \cap L _ { j } |
$$

where:

N: Total number of points.   
$k$ : Number of clusters.   
$C _ { j }$ : Points in cluster $j$ .   
$L _ { j }$ : Points in true class $j$ .

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_029\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_029\auto

# Rand Index (RI)

For a sample pair $x _ { i } , x _ { j }$ , consider their clustering labels $c _ { i } , c _ { j }$ and groundtruth labels $I _ { i } , I _ { j }$ If $c _ { i } = c _ { j }$ but $I _ { i } \neq I _ { j }$ it it TP/TN/FP/FN ?

• Rand index: examine all the sample pairs

True Negative (TN) True Positive (TP): $\begin{array} { l } { c _ { i } = c _ { j } , I _ { i } = I _ { j } } \\ { \mathrm { ! } \ c _ { i } \neq c _ { j } , I _ { i } \neq I _ { j } } \\ { c _ { i } = c _ { j } , I _ { i } \neq I _ { j } } \\ { \mathrm { ! } \ c _ { i } \neq c _ { j } , I _ { i } = I _ { j } } \\ { R I = \cfrac { T P + T N } { T P + T N + F P + F N } = \cfrac { T P + T N } { \binom { n } { 2 } } } \end{array}$   
False Positive (FP):   
False Negative (FN)

Range: 0 to 1 $1 =$ perfect match).

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_032\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_032\auto

# Adjusted Rand Index (ARI)

Adjusted for chance to handle random clustering.   
Using the expected similarity of all pair-wise comparisons between clusterings specified by a random model

$$
\mathsf { A R I } = \frac { \mathsf { R I } - \mathsf { E x p e c t e d \ R I } } { \mathsf { m a x } ( \mathsf { R I } ) - \mathsf { E x p e c t e d \ R I } }
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_035\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_035\auto

# Fowlkes-Mallows Index (FMI)

Measures the geometric mean of precision and recall for pairs of points.

Formula:

$$
\mathsf { F M I } = \sqrt { \mathsf { P r e c i s i o n } \cdot \mathsf { R e c a l l } }
$$

where:

TP ▶ Precision: Fraction of pairs correctly clustered together. TP + FP TP ▶ Recall: Fraction of true pairs correctly identified. TP + FN Range: 0 to 1 $\mathbf { \nabla } ^ { 1 } =$ perfect match).

# Conditional Entropy

• Quantifies the amount of information needed to describe $Y$ given that the value of X

$$
\begin{array} { r } { | X ) = \mathbb { E } [ - \ln P ( Y | X ) ] = \displaystyle \sum _ { x \in X , y \in Y } - P ( x , y ) \ln P ( x | . } \\ { = \displaystyle \sum _ { x \in X , y \in Y } - P ( x , y ) \ln \frac { P ( x , y ) } { P ( y } } \end{array}

Or you can view it like this

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \ell = x \displaystyle M ( Y | X = x ) = \sum _ { x \in X } P ( x ) \sum _ { y \in Y } - P ( y | x ) \ln P ( y | } \\ { = \sum _ { x \in X , y \in Y } P ( x ) P ( y | x ) \ln P ( y | } \end{array}

$0 \leq H ( Y | X ) \leq H ( Y )$ $H ( Y | X ) = 0$ if $Y$ is determined by $X$ $H ( Y | X ) = H ( Y )$ if $X$ and $Y$ are independent $H ( Y | X ) = H ( X , Y ) - H ( X )$

# Mutual Information

● Quantifies the amount of information obtained about $Y$ after observing $X$ (and vice versa)

$$
\begin{array} { r l } { I ( X , Y ) = I ( Y , X ) = H ( X ) - H ( X \vert Y ) } \\ { \ } & { = H ( Y ) - H ( Y \vert X ) } \\ { \ } & { = H ( X ) + H ( Y ) - H ( X , Y ) } \\ { \ } & { = H ( X , Y ) - H ( X \vert Y ) - H ( Y } \end{array}
$$

Let $X$ be the clustering results and $Y$ be the groundtruth labels, MI reflets the alignment between them

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_042\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_042\auto

# Normalized Mutual Information (NMI)

Normalized to account for different numbers of clusters.

● Formula:

$$
\mathsf { N M I } = \frac { 2 \cdot I ( C , L ) } { H ( C ) + H ( L ) }
$$

where:

$I ( C ; L )$ : Mutual information between clusters $C$ and labels $L$ .   
$H ( C ) , H ( L )$ : Entropy of clusters and labels.

Range: 0 to 1 $1 =$ perfect match).

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_047\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_047\auto

# V-measure

A harmonic mean of two complementary components:

Homogeneity: Measures how pure each cluster is (all points in a cluster belong to a single class).

Completeness: Measures how well all points of a class are assigned to the same cluster.

$$
{ \mathsf { H o m o g e n e i t y } } = 1 - { \frac { H ( C | L ) } { H ( C ) } } ,
$$

$$
\dot { \mathbf { \tau } } = 1 - \frac { H ( C | L ) } { H ( C ) } , \quad \mathsf { C o m p l e t e n e s s } = 1 - \frac { H ( L | C ) } { H ( L ) }
$$

where:

$H ( C | L )$ : Conditional entropy of clusters given labels.   
$H ( L | C )$ : Conditional entropy of labels given clusters.   
$H ( C ) , H ( L )$ : Entropy of clusters and labels.

● Formula:

• Range: 0 to 1 $1 =$ perfect match).

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_048\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_048\auto

# Summary of External Metrics

• External metrics evaluate clustering performance using ground truth labels.

Key metrics:

Purity: Measures the fraction of correctly classified points. Adjusted Rand Index (ARI): Compares cluster assignments to true labels, adjusted for chance.   
▶ Fowlkes-Mallows Index (FMI): Geometric mean of precision and recall for pairs of points.   
▶ Normalized Mutual Information (NMI): Measures mutual information between cluster assignments and true labels.   
V-measure: Harmonic mean of homogeneity and completeness.

Choose the metric based on the specific use case and requirements.

---

# Internal Clustering Metric

• Silhouette Coefficient   
Calinski-Harabaz Index (Variance Ratio Criterion)   
Davies-Bouldin Index   
o Dunn index

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_050\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_050\auto

# Silhouette Score

Measures how similar a point is to its own cluster compared to other clusters.

• Formula for a single point:

$$
\frac { b ( i ) - a ( i ) } { \mathfrak { m a x } \{ a ( i ) , b ( i ) \} } = \left\{ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 - a ( i ) / b ( i ) } & { a ( i ) < b ( i ) } \\ { a ( i ) / b ( i ) - 1 } & { a ( i ) \ge b ( i ) } \end{array} \right. ,
$$

where:

$a ( i )$ : Average distance of point $i$ to other points in the same cluster.   
$b ( i )$ : Average distance of point $i$ to points in the nearest neighboring cluster.

Overall score is the average of $s ( i )$ for all points.

C Range: $^ { - 1 }$ to 1 ( $1 =$ well-clustered, $- 1 =$ poorly clustered).

### Images:
- data\1. Machine_Learning\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_050\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_050\auto\images\b36ee179698ab71cdf0c9805a1e1b33b74c342f14690c75ce9f98818b91992ac.jpg

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_051\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_051\auto

# Calinski-Harabasz Index

• Measures the ratio of between-cluster dispersion to within-cluster dispersion.

Formula:

$$
{ \mathsf { C H } } = { \frac { { \mathsf { B e t w e e n } } - { \mathsf { C l u s t e r } } { \mathsf { D i s p e r s i o n } } / { \left( k - 1 \right) } } { \mathsf { W i t h i n } } }
$$

where:

N: Total number of points. k: Number of clusters.   
▶ Between-Cluster Dispersion: Sum of squared distances between cluster centers and global center, i.e., $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } n _ { i } \bigcap _ { i } c _ { i } - c \Vert ^ { 2 }$   
▶ Within-Cluster Dispersion: Sum of squared distances between points and their cluster center. $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } \sum _ { x \in C _ { k } } \lVert c _ { i } - x \rVert ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$

Higher values indicate better clustering.

Similar to one-way ANOVA F-test statistic

### Images:
- data\1. Machine_Learning\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_051\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_051\auto\images\280772cd6a1e260b1b76e4c001f79d0915475a83fd82a6db43121f7862ba53f3.jpg

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_052\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_052\auto

# Davies-Bouldin Index

• Measures the average similarity ratio of within-cluster scatter to between-cluster separation.

● Formula:

$$
{ \mathsf { D B } } = { \frac { 1 } { k } } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } \operatorname* { m a x } _ { j \neq i } \left( { \frac { S _ { i } + S _ { j } } { d ( c _ { i } , c _ { j } ) } } \right)
$$

where:

$\nu \ k$ : Number of clusters. $S _ { j }$ : Average distance of points in cluster $j$ to its center. $d \big ( c _ { i } , c _ { j } \big )$ : Distance between centers of clusters $i$ and $j$ .

Lower values indicate better clustering.

### Images:
- data\1. Machine_Learning\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_052\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_052\auto\images\fa90061f7db595598a9c1bbb67d5545fa47de137b9dfaaa98adcd0a834799572.jpg

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_053\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_053\auto

# Dunn Index

Measures the ratio of the smallest inter-cluster distance to the largest intra-cluster distance.

● Formula:

$$
\mathsf { D u n n \ l n d e x } = \frac { \mathsf { m i n } _ { 1 \leq i < j \leq k } d \big ( C _ { i } , C _ { j } \big ) } { \mathsf { m a x } _ { 1 \leq I \leq k } \mathsf { d i a m } \big ( C _ { I } \big ) }
$$

where:

▶ $d ( C _ { i } , C _ { j } )$ : Distance between clusters $C _ { j }$ and $C _ { j }$ (e.g., minimum or average distance).   
▶ diam $\left( C _ { I } \right)$ : Diameter of cluster $C _ { I }$ (e.g., maximum distance between points in the cluster).   
▶ $k$ : Number of clusters.

• Higher values indicate better clustering: ▶ Large inter-cluster distances (well-separated clusters). ▶ Small intra-cluster distances (compact clusters).

Sensitive to noise and outliers.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_054\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_054\auto

# Summary of Internal Metrics

● Internal metrics evaluate clustering quality without ground truth.

● Key metrics:

Silhouette Score: Measures cohesion and separation. Calinski-Harabasz Index: Measures dispersion ratio. Davies-Bouldin Index: Measures average cluster similarity. ▶ Dunn Index: Measures the ratio of inter-cluster distance to intra-cluster diameter.

Each metric has its strengths and is suited for different scenarios:

Silhouette Score: General-purpose, easy to interpret. Calinski-Harabasz Index: Emphasizes dispersion and separation. Davies-Bouldin Index: Focuses on cluster similarity. ▶ Dunn Index: Highlights compactness and separation explicitly.

0 Choose the metric based on the clustering goals and data characteristics.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_056\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_056\auto

# Clustering Methods

C Can we find a good clustering results by directly optimizing the above metrics?   
Non-Differentiable: Most metrics are discrete or non-smooth, making gradient-based optimization infeasible.   
• Combinatorial Complexity: Many require evaluating all possible cluster assignments, which is computationally intractable.   
o Clustering Goal: Find natural groupings in data without predefined labels, unlike supervised learning.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_057\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_057\auto

# Clustering Methods

Can we find a good clustering results by directly optimizing the above metrics?   
• Non-Differentiable: Most metrics are discrete or non-smooth, making gradient-based optimization infeasible.   
• Combinatorial Complexity: Many require evaluating all possible cluster assignments, which is computationally intractable.   
o Clustering Goal: Find natural groupings in data without predefined labels, unlike supervised learning.   
o We use heuristic algorithms that optimize proxy objectives instead.   
• Metrics serve as evaluator and assess quality after clustering, not during optimization.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_062\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_062\auto

# Prototype-Based Clustering Methods

Definition: Clustering methods that represent each cluster by a prototype (e.g., centroid, medoid) summarizing the group.   
• Key Idea: Assign data points to the nearest prototype, optimizing a distance-based objective (e.g., sum of squares).

# Examples:

▶ K-Means: Uses centroids (mean of points) to minimize within-cluster variance. K-Medoids: Uses actual data points (medoids) for robustness to outliers.

• Advantages: Simple, scalable, and effective for spherical clusters; sensitive to initialization and cluster shape.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_064\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_064\auto

# Algorithm k-means Clustering

Require: Dataset $X = \{ x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } \}$ , number of clusters K   
Ensure: Cluster assignments for each $x _ { j }$   
1: Initialize centers $\left\{ \mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } , \ldots , \mu _ { K } \right\}$ (e.g., random points from X )   
2: repeat   
3: Assign step: Assign each point $x _ { j }$ to the closest center

$$
r _ { i } = \mathsf { a r g } \operatorname* { m i n } _ { k \in \{ 1 , \ldots , K \} } \| x _ { i } - \mu _ { k } \|
$$

4: Update step: Recompute each center as the mean of all points assigned to it

$$
\mu _ { k } = \frac { \sum _ { i : r _ { i } = k } x _ { i } } { \sum _ { i : r _ { i } = k } 1 }
$$

5: until Stop conditions are met

convergence to local optimum of cost $\mathcal { L }$ (defined next)

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_066\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_066\auto

# The k-means cost

$$
\mathcal { L } ( \Delta ) = \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } \sum _ { i \in C _ { k } } \| x _ { i } - \mu _ { k } \| ^ { 2 }
$$

K-means solves a least-squares problem the cost $\mathcal { L }$ is called quadratic distortion

Proposition. The K-means algorithm decreases $\mathcal { L } ( \Delta )$ at every step.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_068\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_068\auto

# Optimal Number of Clusters

Elbow method: A heuristic method to determine the optimal number of clusters.

o Steps:

Run k-means clustering for a range of $k$ values (e.g., 1 to 10). 2 Calculate the Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS) for each $k$ . Plot WCSS against $k$ . Look for an ”elbow” point where adding more clusters yields diminishing returns.

• Goal: Balance between minimizing WCSS and avoiding overfitting with too many clusters.

![](images/e6777ec2fa8488073c5dd74c12ad532a0f85a51325a81f9aed51af9745382c23.jpg)  
Figure: Example Elbow Plot

Cons:

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_072\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_072\auto

# Initialization of the Centers

Start with K points at random   
Starts with K data points at random Question: What’s wrong with chosing K data points at random?   
The probability of hitting all $\boldsymbol { K }$ clusters with K samples approaches 0 when $\boldsymbol { \kappa }$ is large   
Start with $\boldsymbol { K }$ data points using Fastest First Traversal (greedy simple approach to spread out centers)   
k-means++ (randomized, theoretically backed approach to spread out centers)   
“K-logK” Initialization (start with enough centers to hit all clusters, then prune down to K )

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_073\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_073\auto

# k-Means++: Smart Initialization for k-Means

# • K-Means++ Algorithm:

1 Choose the first center randomly from the data points.   
2 For each remaining point, compute its squared distance to the nearest existing center.   
3 Select the next center with probability proportional to that squared distance.   
4 Repeat until $\boldsymbol { \kappa }$ centers are chosen.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_074\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_074\auto

# k-Means++: Smart Initialization for k-Means

# • K-Means++ Algorithm:

1 Choose the first center randomly from the data points.   
2 For each remaining point, compute its squared distance to the nearest existing center. Select the next center with probability proportional to that squared distance.   
4 Repeat until $\boldsymbol { \kappa }$ centers are chosen.

Key Idea: Spreads centers by favoring points farther from existing ones, balancing randomness and determinism.

• Advantage: Reduces sensitivity to poor initialization, theoretically guarantees $O ( \log K )$ -competitive solution.

The Bound: $E [ \phi _ { \mathsf { K - M e a n s + + } } ] \leq 8 ( \mathsf { l n } K + 2 ) \cdot \phi _ { \mathsf { O P T } }$

$\star 8 ( \ln K + 2 ) = O ( \log K )$ in big-O terms.   
$\star$ Log factor from sequential covering over $\boldsymbol { \kappa }$ steps.   
$\star$ Ref: D Arthur, S Vassilvitskii. k-means $^ { + + }$ : The advantages of careful seeding

• Similar to k-means but uses actual data points (medoids) as cluster centers.

Initialize $k$ medoids randomly. Assign each point to the nearest medoid. Update medoids to minimize the total cost. 4 Repeat until convergence.

Advantages: ▶ Robust to noise and outliers. ▶ Works with any distance metric.

• Limitations: ▶ Computationally expensive for large datasets.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_078\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_078\auto

# Kernel Tricks

In many cases, we don’t need to compute $\phi ( x )$ but only $\phi ( { \boldsymbol { x } } ) ^ { \top } \phi ( { \boldsymbol { y } } )$ ▶ In SVM, we have

$$
\mathcal { L } ( w , b , \lambda ) = \sum _ { i } \lambda _ { i } - \frac { 1 } { 2 } \sum _ { i } \sum _ { j } \lambda _ { i } \lambda _ { j } y _ { i } y _ { j } ( x _ { i } ^ { \top } x _ { j } )
$$

This can sometimes be computed much efficiently

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \mathbf { x } = \binom { x _ { 1 } } { x _ { 2 } } , \boldsymbol { \phi } ( \mathbf { x } ) = \left( \begin{array} { l } { x _ { 1 } x _ { 1 } } \\ { x _ { 1 } x _ { 2 } } \\ { x _ { 2 } x _ { 1 } } \\ { x _ { 2 } x _ { 2 } } \end{array} \right) } \end{array}
$$

What is the complexity of computing $\phi ( x )  { ? }$

What is the complexity of directly computing $\phi ( x ) ^ { \top } \phi ( y ) ?$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_079\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_079\auto

# Kernel Tricks

In many cases, we don’t need to compute $\phi ( x )$ but only $\phi ( { \boldsymbol { x } } ) ^ { \top } \phi ( { \boldsymbol { y } } )$ ▶ In SVM, we have

$$
\mathcal { L } ( w , b , \lambda ) = \sum _ { i } \lambda _ { i } - \frac { 1 } { 2 } \sum _ { i } \sum _ { j } \lambda _ { i } \lambda _ { j } y _ { i } y _ { j } ( x _ { i } ^ { \top } x _ { j } )
$$

This can sometimes be computed much efficiently

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \mathbf { x } = \binom { x _ { 1 } } { x _ { 2 } } , \boldsymbol { \phi } ( \mathbf { x } ) = \left( \begin{array} { l } { x _ { 1 } x _ { 1 } } \\ { x _ { 1 } x _ { 2 } } \\ { x _ { 2 } x _ { 1 } } \\ { x _ { 2 } x _ { 2 } } \end{array} \right) } \end{array}
$$

What is the complexity of computing $\phi ( x )  { ? }$

What is the complexity of directly computing $\phi ( x ) ^ { \top } \phi ( y ) ?$ $\phi ( x ) ^ { \top } \phi ( y ) = ( x ^ { \top } y ) ^ { 2 } = K ( x , y )$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_080\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_080\auto

# Common Kernel Functions

Linear Kernel: $K ( x , y ) = x ^ { \top } y$ (no transformation). Polynomial Kernel: $K ( x , y ) = ( x ^ { \top } y + c ) ^ { d }$ (degree $d$ , constant $c$ ). Radial Basis Function (RBF) Kernel: $K ( x , y ) = \exp ( - \gamma \| x - y \| ^ { 2 } )$ (parameter $\gamma$ ). Sigmoid Kernel: $K ( x , y ) = \mathsf { t a n h } ( \alpha x ^ { \top } y + c )$ . Note: Choice of kernel depends on the data and problem.

# Kernel SVM: XOR Problem Example

# Problem:

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_082\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_082\auto

# Kernel SVM: XOR Problem Example

# Problem:

Data: XOR points in 2D: (0,0), $( 1 , 1 ) =$ Class 0; (0,1), $( 1 , 0 ) = \mathsf { C l a s s 1 }$ . • Not linearly separable in 2D.

# Solution:

Use a polynomial kernel: $K ( x , y ) \stackrel { \cdot } { = } ( x ^ { \top } y ) ^ { 2 } .$   
Maps to 3D: $\phi ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } ) = ( x _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } , \sqrt { 2 } x _ { 1 } x _ { 2 } , x _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } ) .$   
$( 0 , 1 ) \mapsto ( 0 , 0 , 1 ) ; ( 1 , 0 ) \mapsto ( 1 , 0 , 0 )$   
$\mathbf { \Sigma } _ { \cdot , 1 } ) \mapsto ( 1 , \sqrt { 2 } , 1 ) ; ( 0 , 0 ) \mapsto ( 0 , 0 , 0 )$   
• Now linearly separable in 3D!

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_084\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_084\auto

# Kernel SVM: RBF Kernel Example

# Problem:

● Inner points: Class 0; Outer points: Class 1. Not linearly separable in 2D.

# Solution:

RBF Kernel: $K ( x , y ) = \exp ( - \gamma \| x - y \| ^ { 2 } ) .$

▶ Maps to an infinite-dimensional space: (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ Radial_basis_function_kernel) ▶ Measures similarity based on distance. $\gamma$ controls the ”reach” of the kernel. The decision function will be $\textstyle \sum _ { i } { \alpha _ { i } y _ { i } K ( x , x _ { i } ) } + b$ where $x _ { j }$ are support vectors

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_085\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_085\auto

# Application: Kernel-Based Clustering

Clustering (e.g., Kernel K-Means) assumes linear separability in the original space.

Kernel tricks allow clustering of non-linearly separable data.

Process:

1 Uses a kernel function to compute distances or similarities in the transformed space.   
2 Perform clustering (e.g., K-Means) in that space.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_086\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_086\auto

# Application: Kernel-Based Clustering

Clustering (e.g., Kernel K-Means) assumes linear separability in the original space.

Kernel tricks allow clustering of non-linearly separable data.

Process:

1 Uses a kernel function to compute distances or similarities in the transformed spac   
2 Perform clustering (e.g., K-Means) in that space.   
3 But wait, we don’t have explicit high-dimensional points to calculate the mean

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_087\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_087\auto

# How to Avoid Explicit Means

Centroid in feature space: $\begin{array} { r } { \phi ( m _ { k } ) = \frac { 1 } { | C _ { k } | } \sum _ { x _ { i } \in C _ { k } } \phi ( x _ { i } ) . } \end{array}$ We don’t compute $\phi ( m _ { k } )$ directly—too complex or infinite-dimensional. Instead:

Use kernel values to measure distances to the “virtual” centroid. All calculations stay in the original space using $K ( x _ { i } , x _ { j } )$ . For two points $x _ { j }$ and $x _ { j }$ , we have

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \| \phi ( x _ { i } ) - \phi ( x _ { j } ) \| ^ { 2 } = ( \phi ( x _ { i } ) - \phi ( x _ { j } ) ) ^ { \top } ( \phi ( x _ { i } ) - \phi ( x _ { j } ) ) } \\ & { \qquad = \phi ( x _ { i } ) ^ { \top } \phi ( x _ { i } ) - 2 \phi ( x _ { i } ) ^ { \top } \phi ( x _ { j } ) + \phi ( x _ { j } ) } \\ & { \qquad = K _ { i i } - 2 K _ { i j } + K _ { j j } } \end{array}
$$

Result: Clusters form based on similarity, not explicit coordinates.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_088\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_088\auto

# Kernel K-Means Algorithm

1 Initialize: Randomly assign points to $k$ clusters.

2 Assign: For each point $x _ { j }$ , compute distance to each cluster’s centroid:

$$
\phi ( m _ { k } ) \| ^ { 2 } = 1 - \frac { 2 } { | C _ { k } | } \sum _ { x _ { j } \in C _ { k } } K ( x _ { i } , x _ { j } ) + \frac { 1 } { | C _ { k } | ^ { 2 } } \sum _ { x _ { m } , x _ { n } \in C _ { k } }
$$

Assign xi to the closest cluster.

3 Update: Recompute kernel sums for each cluster based on new assignments.

4 Repeat: Until assignments stabilize.

# Kernel Clustering: Two Moons Example

# Problem:

Data: Two interlocking crescent moons in 2D.   
Standard K-Means fails (linear boundaries).

# Solution:

Use RBF Kernel: $K ( x , y ) = \exp ( - \gamma \| x - y \| ^ { 2 } ) .$   
Maps points to a space where moons are separable.   
• Kernel K-Means assigns points to clusters based on transformed distances.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_090\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_090\auto

# Motivation of Density-based Clustering

# Limitations of K-Means and K-Medoids:

Assume spherical, evenly sized clusters Require pre-specifying $\boldsymbol { \kappa }$ Struggle with noise/outliers and non-convex shapes.

# o Density-Based Perspective:

▶ Clusters as regions of high point density separated by low-density areas.   
▶ No need to assume cluster shape or specify $\boldsymbol { \kappa }$ in advance.

# Key Motivation:

▶ Handle arbitrary cluster shapes (e.g., elongated, irregular).   
Identify noise/outliers naturally as low-density points.   
Adapt to real-world data with varying densities.

Examples: DBSCAN, OPTICS – define clusters by density reachability, not prototypes.

Advantage: More flexible and robust for complex datasets vs. prototype-based methods.

---

# DBSCAN: Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise

A density-based clustering algorithm.

• Key concepts:

▶ $\epsilon$ -neighbors: $N _ { \epsilon } ( X _ { j } ) = \{ x _ { i } \in { \mathcal { D } } | \mathrm { d i s t } ( x _ { i } , x _ { j } ) \leq \epsilon \}$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_092\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_092\auto

# DBSCAN: Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise

A density-based clustering algorithm.

• Key concepts:

$\epsilon$ -neighbors: $N _ { \epsilon } ( X _ { j } ) = \{ x _ { i } \in { \mathcal { D } } | \mathrm { d i s t } ( x _ { i } , x _ { j } ) \leq \epsilon \}$ Core points: Points with at least minPts neighbors within ϵ.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_093\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_093\auto

# DBSCAN: Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise

A density-based clustering algorithm.

• Key concepts:

▶ $\epsilon$ -neighbors: $N _ { \epsilon } ( X _ { j } ) = \{ x _ { i } \in { \mathcal { D } } | \mathrm { d i s t } ( x _ { i } , x _ { j } ) \leq \epsilon \}$ Core points: Points with at least minPts neighbors within ϵ.

▶ $x _ { j }$ is directly density-reachable from $x _ { j }$ if $x _ { j } \in N _ { \epsilon } ( x _ { i } )$ and $x _ { j }$ is a core point ▶ $x _ { j }$ is density-reachable from a core point $x _ { j }$ if there is a chain $q _ { 1 } , q _ { 2 } , \ldots , q _ { n }$ , with $q _ { 1 } = x _ { i }$ , $q _ { n } = x _ { j }$ , $q _ { k + 1 }$ is directly density-reachable from $q _ { k }$ ▶ $x _ { j }$ and $x _ { j }$ are density-connected if there is a $x _ { k }$ such that $x _ { j }$ and $x _ { j }$ are both density-reachable from $x _ { k }$ (cid:)

![](images/149d088f67b441945d25964ae101e4b64496192dc1d65c9b7350e746691c8260.jpg)

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_094\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_094\auto

We can define cluster $C$ based on density-reachability: ▶ Connectivity: $\forall x _ { i } , x _ { j } \in C$ , $x _ { j }$ and $x _ { j }$ are density-connected ▶ Maximality: $\forall x _ { j } , x _ { i } \in C \ \land x _ { j }$ is density-reachable from $x _ { i } \Rightarrow x _ { j } \in C$

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_095\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_095\auto

1 Select an unvisited point.   
2 Retrieve all points within the ϵ-neighborhood.   
3 If there are enough points in the neighborhood (at least minPts), create a new cluster.   
4 Expand the cluster by checking the neighbors of the newly added points.   
Repeat the process for all unvisited points.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_096\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_096\auto

# Pros and Cons of DBSCAN

● Pros:

▶ Does not require the number of clusters to be specified. Can identify clusters of arbitrary shape. Handles noise effectively by identifying outliers.

● Cons:

▶ Performance degrades with high-dimensional data. Sensitive to the choice of $\epsilon$ and minPts. Struggles with clusters of varying densities.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_097\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_097\auto

# Hierarchical Clustering

Builds a hierarchy of clusters.

● Two approaches:

Agglomerative (bottom-up): Start with each point as a cluster and merge.   
Divisive (top-down): Start with all points in one cluster and split.

• Commonly used in biology, social sciences, and data mining.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_098\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_098\auto

# Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering

Start with each data point as a single cluster. Merge the closest pairs of clusters iteratively. Continue until one cluster remains. Keys: How to measure the distance between two clusters?

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_099\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_099\auto

# Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering

Start with each data point as a single cluster.   
Merge the closest pairs of clusters iteratively.   
Continue until one cluster remains.   
Keys: How to measure the distance between two clusters?   
Common linkage methods: ▶ Single linkage ▶ Complete linkage ▶ Average linkage ▶ Ward’s method

---

# Divisive Hierarchical Clustering

Start with all data points in one cluster.   
Split the cluster into smaller clusters iteratively.   
Continue until each data point is in its own cluster.   
Less commonly used than agglomerative clustering. ▶ Much more computationally intensive

# ● Pros

▶ No need to specify the number of clusters a priori.

# Cons

▶ Sensitive to noise and outliers.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L09_Clustering\page_104\DSAA2011-L09_Clustering_page_104\auto

# HDBSCAN: Hierarchical Density-Based Clustering

• Limitations of DBSCAN: ▶ Sensitive to the choice of $\epsilon$ . ▶ Struggles with clusters of varying density.

HDBSCAN builds a hierarchy of clusters based on the density of points in the data.

• It converts the problem into a hierarchical clustering algorithm and then extracts the most persistent clusters.

Advantages:

▶ Can handle clusters of varying densities. Does not require setting an $\epsilon$ value upfront. Robust to noise.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_005\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_005\auto

# Algorithm k-means Clustering

Require: Dataset $X = \{ x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } \}$ , number of clusters K   
Ensure: Cluster assignments for each $x _ { j }$   
1: Initialize centers $\left\{ \mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } , \ldots , \mu _ { K } \right\}$ (e.g., random points from X )   
2: repeat   
3: Assign step: Assign each point $x _ { j }$ to the closest center

$$
r _ { i } = \mathsf { a r g } \operatorname* { m i n } _ { k \in \{ 1 , \ldots , K \} } \| x _ { i } - \mu _ { k } \|
$$

4: Update step: Recompute each center as the mean of all points assigned to it

$$
\mu _ { k } = \frac { \sum _ { i : r _ { i } = k } x _ { i } } { \sum _ { i : r _ { i } = k } 1 }
$$

5: until Stop conditions are met

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_006\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_006\auto

# k-means

● Stop Conditions

▶ Maximum iterations reached Assignments no longer change convergence to local optimum of cost $\mathcal { L }$ (defined next)

Optimal number of cluster: elbow method

1 Run k-means clustering for a range of $k$ values (e.g., 1 to 10).   
2 Calculate the Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS) for each $k$ .   
3 Plot WCSS against $k$ .   
4 Look for an ”elbow” point where adding more clusters yields diminishing returns.

![](images/5ad7669ec611c60964c1ae26597dfa1d0a3fab6722cc26ac3e4d726adf22fac7.jpg)

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_008\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_008\auto

Use kernel functions to calculate the inner product in high-dimensional space   
Enable algorithms to operate in a high-dimensional, implicit feature space without ever computing the coordinates of the data in that space   
• Widely used kernels Linear Kernel: $K ( x , y ) = x ^ { \top } y$ (no transformation). Polynomial Kernel: $K ( x , y ) = ( x ^ { \top } y + c ) ^ { d }$ (degree $d$ , constant $c$ ). ▶ Radial Basis Function (RBF) Kernel: $K ( x , y ) = \exp ( - \gamma \| x - y \| ^ { 2 } )$ (parameter $\gamma$ ). Sigmoid Kernel: $K ( x , y ) = \operatorname { t a n h } ( \alpha x ^ { \top } y + c )$ .

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_009\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_009\auto

# Kernel K-Means Algorithm

1 Initialize: Randomly assign points to $k$ clusters.

2 Assign: For each point $x _ { j }$ , compute distance to each cluster’s centroid:

$$
\phi ( m _ { k } ) \| ^ { 2 } = 1 - \frac { 2 } { | C _ { k } | } \sum _ { x _ { j } \in C _ { k } } K ( x _ { i } , x _ { j } ) + \frac { 1 } { | C _ { k } | ^ { 2 } } \sum _ { x _ { m } , x _ { n } \in C _ { k } }
$$

Assign xi to the closest cluster.

3 Update: Recompute kernel sums for each cluster based on new assignments.

4 Repeat: Until assignments stabilize.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_015\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_015\auto

# Motivation of Density-based Clustering

# Limitations of K-Means and K-Medoids:

Assume spherical, evenly sized clusters Require pre-specifying $\boldsymbol { \kappa }$ Struggle with noise/outliers and non-convex shapes.

# o Density-Based Perspective:

▶ Clusters as regions of high point density separated by low-density areas.   
▶ No need to assume cluster shape or specify $\boldsymbol { \kappa }$ in advance.

# Key Motivation:

▶ Handle arbitrary cluster shapes (e.g., elongated, irregular).   
Identify noise/outliers naturally as low-density points.   
Adapt to real-world data with varying densities.

Examples: DBSCAN, OPTICS – define clusters by density reachability, not prototypes.

Advantage: More flexible and robust for complex datasets vs. prototype-based methods.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_016\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_016\auto

DBSCAN: Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise

Key concepts: ▶ ϵ-neighbors: $N _ { \epsilon } ( X _ { j } ) = \{ x _ { i } \in { \mathcal { D } } | \mathrm { d i s t } ( x _ { i } , x _ { j } ) \leq \epsilon \}$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_017\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_017\auto

# DBSCAN: Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise

Key concepts:

ϵ-neighbors: $N _ { \epsilon } ( X _ { j } ) = \{ x _ { i } \in { \mathcal { D } } | \mathrm { d i s t } ( x _ { i } , x _ { j } ) \leq \epsilon \}$   
Core points: Points with at least minPts neighbors within ϵ.   
Border points: Points within $\epsilon$ of a core point but not core points themselves.   
Noise points: Points that are neither core nor border points, i.e., not reachable from any other point.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_018\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_018\auto

# DBSCAN: Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise

$x _ { j }$ is directly density-reachable from $x _ { j }$ if $x _ { j } \in N _ { \epsilon } ( x _ { i } )$ and $x _ { j }$ is a core point   
$x _ { j }$ is density-reachable from a core point $x _ { j }$ if there is a chain $q _ { 1 } , q _ { 2 } , \ldots , q _ { n }$ , with $q _ { 1 } = x _ { i }$ , $q _ { n } = x _ { j }$ , $q _ { k + 1 }$ is directly density-reachable from $q _ { k }$   
xi and $x _ { j }$ are density-connected if there is a $x _ { k }$ such that $x _ { j }$ and xj are both density-reachable from $x _ { k }$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_019\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_019\auto

Basic idea: try to expand the cluster based on density-reachability

A cluster is a set of density-connected points which is maximal w.r.t. density-reachability.

▶ Connectivity: $\forall x _ { i } , x _ { j } \in C$ , $x _ { j }$ and $x _ { j }$ are density-connected ▶ Maximality: $\forall x _ { i } \in C \land x _ { j }$ is density-reachable from $x _ { i } \Rightarrow x _ { j } \in C$

How to achieve this?

▶ Select an unvisited point

$\star$ If it is a core point, create a new cluster by including all points density-reachable from it $\star$ If it is not a core point, mark it as noisy (temporarily)

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_020\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_020\auto

# Algorithm DBSCAN Algorithm

Require: Dataset $D$ , radius $\epsilon$ , minimum points MinPts

1: Initialize all points as unvisited   
2: for each unvisited point $p \in D$ do   
3: Mark $p$ as visited   
4: $N \gets \mathrm { g e t N e i g h b o r s } ( p , \epsilon )$   
5: if $\vert N \vert < M i n P t s$ then   
6: Label $p$ as noise   
7: else   
8: Create new cluster $C$ , and add $p$ to cluster C   
9: Expand cluster C   
10: end if   
11: end for

▷ Points within $\epsilon$ distance

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_021\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_021\auto

# Algorithm Expand the cluster C

Require: Initial cluster $C = \{ p \}$ , radius ϵ, minimum points MinPts   
1: for each point $q \in C$ do   
2: if $q$ is unvisited then   
3: Mark $q$ as visited   
4: $N \gets$ getNeighbors $( q , \epsilon )$   
5: if $| N | \geq M i n P t s$ then ▷ Core points   
6: $C  C \cup N$   
7: end if   
8: end if   
9: if $q$ is not yet assigned to any cluster then ▷ Mark as noise points before   
10: Add $q$ to cluster C   
11: end if   
12: end for
