## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_022\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_022\auto

# Properties of DBSCAN

Core points are deterministically assigned

Two core points $p$ and $q$ belong to the same cluster if there exists a chain of core points This relation $p \sim q$ is an equivalence relation because it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive ▶ Then we obtain a partition induced by this equivalence relation

Noise points are deterministically assigned ▶ Noise point is not a core point and it is not within the $\epsilon$ -neighborhood of any core point

Border points are non-deterministically assigned ▶ A border point is not a core point but lies within the $\epsilon$ -neighborhood of at least one core point ▶ The assignment depends on the order in which core points are processed

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_023\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_023\auto

# Pros and Cons of DBSCAN

● Pros:

▶ Does not require the number of clusters to be specified. Can identify clusters of arbitrary shape.   
▶ Handles noise effectively by identifying outliers.

● Cons:

▶ Not entirely deterministic   
▶ Performance degrades with high-dimensional data: curse of dimensionality   
▶ Sensitive to the choice of $\epsilon$ and minPts. $\cdot \sf { m i n P t s } = 2 \ F _ { d i m }$ is a good choice, may need to try a larger value for a larger dataset $\star \ \epsilon \mathbf { : }$ plotting the distance to the $k = m i n P t s - 1$ nearest neighbor ordered from the largest to the smallest value $^ { \star }$ Ref: DBSCAN Revisited, Revisited: Why and How You Should (Still) Use DBSCAN

Struggles with clusters of varying densities.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_024\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_024\auto

# Curse of Dimensionality

• The Curse of Dimensionality refers to various phenomena that arise when working in high-dimensional spaces.   
• We focus on how distance metrics behave in high dimensions.   
Assume points are drawn uniformly from a unit hypercube $[ 0 , 1 ] ^ { d }$ ▶ The expected squared Euclidean distance between two random points $\begin{array} { r } { \mathbb { E } [ d ^ { 2 } ] \stackrel { * } { = } \mathbb { E } [ \| \mathbf { x } - \mathbf { \dot { y } } \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } ] = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { D } \mathbb { E } [ ( x _ { i } - y _ { i } ) ^ { 2 } ] = D / 6 } \end{array}$ However, the variances increase in a similar speed $\mathsf { V a r } [ \| \mathbf x - \mathbf y \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } ] = 7 D / 1 8 0$ $\begin{array} { r } { \begin{array} { r } { \succ \mathsf { V a r } [ d ] \approx V a r [ d ^ { 2 } ] ( \frac { 1 } { 2 \sqrt { \mathbb { E } [ d ^ { 2 } ] } } ) ^ { 2 } = \frac { \mathsf { V a r } [ d ^ { 2 } ] } { 4 \mathbb { E } [ d ^ { 2 } ] } = 7 / 1 2 0 } \\ { \vdash \mathsf { R e l a t i v e ~ d i f f e r e n c e } = \frac { d _ { \mathsf { m a x } } - d _ { \mathsf { m i n } } } { d _ { \mathsf { m i n } } } \approx \frac { \mathsf { C o n s t a n t } } { \sqrt { D / 6 } } \to 0 } \end{array} } \end{array}$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_025\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_025\auto

# Curse of Dimensionality

• The volume of a high-dimensional unit ball decrease to 0

$$
V _ { D } = { \frac { \pi ^ { D / 2 } } { \Gamma ( D / 2 + 1 ) } } \to 0
$$

But the volume is concentrated near its surface.

$$
V _ { D } ( 1 - \varepsilon ) / V _ { D } = ( 1 - \varepsilon ) ^ { D } \to 0
$$

Randomly pick 2 vectors, we have $P \left( | \cos \theta _ { x , y } | \geq \sqrt { \frac { - | \log \varepsilon } { D } } \right) < \varepsilon$ Set $\varepsilon = 1 / D$ then

$$
P \left( | \cos \theta _ { x , y } | \geq \sqrt { \frac { \log D } { D } } \right) < \frac { 1 } { D }
$$

Every two vectors are almost orthogonal!

# Key Concepts in OPTICS

• Hyperparameters

ϵ: maximum radius, can set as $\infty$ . A smaller value can make the algorithm run faster ▶ minPts: minimum number of points to form a cluster

Key concepts to achieve adaptive $\epsilon$ ▶ Core Distance cd(p) =  ${ \mathsf { c d } } ( p ) = { \left\{ \begin{array} { l l } { U N D } & { | N _ { \epsilon } ( p ) | < m i n P t s } \\ { d ( p , N _ { \epsilon } ^ { m i n P t s } ( p ) ) } & { | N _ { \epsilon } ( p ) | \geq m i n P t s } \end{array} \right. }$

$\star$ Minimum distance to make a point $p$ to be a core point. $^ { \star }$ “Local density”

Reachability Distance $\mathsf { r d } ( q , p ) = \left\{ \begin{array} { l l } { U N D } & { | N _ { \epsilon } ( p ) | < m i n P t s } \\ { \mathsf { m a x } \{ \mathsf { c d } ( p ) , d ( p , q ) \} } & { | N _ { \epsilon } ( p ) | \geq m i n P t s } \end{array} \right.$ Minimum distance to make $p$ to be a core point and $q$ is directly reachable from $p$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_030\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_030\auto

# Algorithm OPTICS

Require: ϵ, minPts   
1: $k \gets 1 , I \gets \{ 1 , 2 , \dots , N \}$   
2: while $I$ is not empty do   
3: Get an element $i$ from $I$ , and let $I  I \backslash \{ i \}$   
4: if $i$ is unprocessed then   
5: Mark $i$ as processed, $p _ { k }  i , k  k + 1$   
6: if $| N _ { \epsilon } ( p _ { i } ) | \geq m i n P t s$ then   
7: Seeds $=$ empty priority queue   
8: Update( $\left[ N _ { \epsilon } ( i ) \right.$ , i , Seeds, ϵ, minPts)   
9: while Seeds is not empty do   
10: Remove the top element $j$ from Seeds ▷ minimum reachability distance   
11: Mark $j$ as processed, $p _ { k } \gets j$ , $k \gets k + 1$   
12: if $| N _ { \epsilon } ( j ) | \geq m i n P t s$ then   
13: Update $\left[ N _ { \epsilon } ( j )\right.$ , $j$ , Seeds, ϵ, minPts)

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_031\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_031\auto

# Algorithm Update priority queue

Require: $N _ { \epsilon } ( i )$ , i, Seeds, ϵ, minPts   
1: $c _ { I } =$ core distance(i,ϵ,minPts)   
2: for each unprocessed element $j$ in $N _ { \epsilon } ( i )$ do   
3: $\begin{array} { r } { \mathsf { \Pi } _ { j } ^ { \mathsf { n e w } } = \mathsf { m a x } \bigl ( c _ { i } , d ( i , j ) \bigr ) \phantom { x x x x x x x x x x x x x x x x x x x x x x x x x } } \\ { \mathsf { f } \textsf { r } _ { j } = U N D \mathsf { O R } \textsf { r } _ { j } ^ { \mathsf { n e w } } < r _ { j } } \\ { \mathsf { \Pi } _ { j } \gets \mathsf { r } _ { j } ^ { \mathsf { n e w } } } \\ { \mathsf { S e e d s . l n s e r t } ( j , \mathsf { \Pi } _ { j } ^ { \mathsf { n e w } } \bigr ) } \end{array}$   
4: then ▷ Relax rj   
5:   
6: ▷ insert or update point $j$ with priority $r _ { i } ^ { \mathfrak { n } }$ ew   
7: end if   
8: end for

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_034\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_034\auto

# Determine k in OPTICS Results

OPTICS does not explicitly define clusters.   
Clusters are extracted from the hierarchical structure using: ▶ Reachability Plot: Visualize clusters by identifying valleys (low reachability distances). ▶ Xi Method: Automatically detect clusters by steepness in the reachability plot (parameter $\xi$ ). ▶ Cut-off Threshold: Manually set a reachability distance threshold to separate clusters.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_035\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_035\auto

# Pros and Cons of OPTICS

● Pros

Flexible: Detects clusters with varying densities, unlike DBSCAN.   
Hierarchical: Produces a reachability plot for multiple cluster resolutions.   
Robust: Less sensitive to parameter choices than DBSCAN.   
Noise Handling: Effectively identifies outliers.

Cons

Computational Cost: Slower than DBSCAN for large datasets $O ( n ^ { 2 } )$ without indexing).   
Parameter Tuning: Requires setting ϵ and MinPts, which can affect results.   
Interpretation: Reachability plots may need expertise to analyze.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_036\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_036\auto

# Hierarchical Clustering

Builds a hierarchy of clusters.

● Two approaches:

Agglomerative (bottom-up): Start with each point as a cluster and merge.   
Divisive (top-down): Start with all points in one cluster and split.

• Commonly used in biology, social sciences, and data mining.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_038\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_038\auto

# Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering

Start with each data point as a single cluster.   
Merge the closest pairs of clusters iteratively.   
Continue until one cluster remains.   
Keys: How to measure the distance between two clusters?   
Common linkage methods: ▶ Single linkage ▶ Complete linkage ▶ Average linkage ▶ Ward’s method

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_039\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_039\auto

# Comparison of Linkage Methods

<table><tr><td>Linkage Method</td><td>Distance Measure</td><td>Characteristics</td></tr><tr><td>Single Linkage</td><td>Minimum pairwise distance</td><td>Tends tio o lngated   ser,</td></tr><tr><td>Complete Linkage</td><td>Maximum pairwise distance</td><td>Forms compact, spherical clusters; Less sensitive to noise compared to single linkage.</td></tr><tr><td>Average Linkage</td><td>Average of all pairwise distances</td><td>Balances between single and complete linkage; Produces more balanced clusters.</td></tr><tr><td>Ward&#x27;s Method</td><td>Increase in total within-cluster variance when merged</td><td>Produces compact clusters with minimum variance; Efficient in minimizing within-cluster sum of squares.</td></tr></table>

# Table: Comparison of Common Linkage Methods

• Ward’s method: Cost of merge cluster A and B

$$
\mu _ { A \cup B } \| ^ { 2 } - \sum _ { x \in A } \| x - \mu _ { A } \| ^ { 2 } - \sum _ { x \in B } \| x - \mu _ { B } \| ^ { 2 } = { \frac { 2 n _ { A } n _ { i } } { n _ { A } + r } }
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_040\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_040\auto

# Divisive Hierarchical Clustering

Start with all data points in one cluster.   
Split the cluster into smaller clusters iteratively.   
Continue until each data point is in its own cluster.   
Less commonly used than agglomerative clustering. ▶ Much more computationally intensive

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_041\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_041\auto

# Dendrogram

A tree-like diagram that shows the arrangement of clusters.   
Height represents the distance between clusters.   
Useful for visualizing hierarchical clustering results.   
Can be cut at a certain height to determine the number of clusters.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_042\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_042\auto

# HDBSCAN: Hierarchical Density-Based Clustering

Transform the distance space: Similar to OPTICS, it calculates core distance and reachability distance, but $\mathsf { r d } ( p , q ) = \mathsf { m a x } \{ \mathsf { c d } ( p ) , \mathsf { c d } ( q ) , d ( p , q ) \}$ ▶ Mutual reachability distance allows single linkage clustering to more closely approximate the hierarchy of level sets   
Build a minimum spanning tree: connect all the samples while minimizing the sum of mutual reachability distances

![](images/8e5008cdb1ba642b565d9f7df1ee19630ee92653570de27f3dc06cd3f716e1ef.jpg)

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_043\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_043\auto

# HDBSCAN: Hierarchical Density-Based Clustering

Build the dendrogram: Iteratively merges nodes or clusters based on the smallest edge weight to form a binary tree   
Condense the Tree: if both child clusters have enough samples, retain the split; otherwise merge the smaller cluster into its parent   
Extracting the Final Clusters ▶ Compute cluster stability for each cluster: $\begin{array} { r } { S ( C ) = \sum _ { p \in C } ( \lambda _ { p } ^ { \mathrm { d e a t h } } - \lambda _ { p } ^ { \mathrm { b i r t h } } ) , \lambda = 1 / d } \end{array}$ ▶ Traverse the dendrogram bottom-up: $^ \star$ At each node, compare the stability of the parent cluster to the sum of its child clusters’ stabilities. $\star$ Select the parent if $S ( { \mathsf { p a r e n t } } ) > \sum$ S(children); otherwise, select the children and recurse.

![](images/65e7008bae8af6d6d5cc7002882b1a861496d2ae0ce06c941ad9454092503cc0.jpg)

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_044\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_044\auto

# Pros and Cons of Hierarchical Clustering

# ● Pros

▶ No need to specify the number of clusters a priori.   
Provides a visual representation of data structure.

# Cons

▶ Computationally expensive for large datasets.   
▶ Sensitive to noise and outliers.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_045\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_045\auto

Hard clustering assumes that each sample belongs to exactly one cluster.   
Does not allow uncertainty in class membership or for an instance to belong to multiple clusters.   
• Soft clustering gives probabilities that a sample belongs to each of a set of clusters.   
Each sample is assigned a probability distribution across a set of clusters (the sum of probabilities is 1).

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_046\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_046\auto

# What Are Gaussian Mixture Models?

Real-world data is messy and often mixed. A way to describe data that might come from multiple “groups.” It is a “universal approximator” of densities. Any smooth density can be approximated with any specific nonzero amount of error by a GMM with enough components.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_047\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_047\auto

# Recap of Gaussian Distributions

A “bell curve” defined by two things:

▶ Mean $( \mu )$ : Where the peak is. ▶ Variance $( \sigma ^ { 2 } )$ : How wide it is. $f ( x | \mu , \sigma ^ { 2 } ) = { \frac { 1 } { { \sqrt { 2 \pi \sigma ^ { 2 } } } } } \exp \left( - { \frac { ( x - \mu ) ^ { 2 } } { 2 \sigma ^ { 2 } } } \right)$

To deal with this multivariate case: $\begin{array} { l } { { f ( x | \mu , \Sigma ) = \displaystyle \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { ( 2 \pi ) ^ { D } | \Sigma | } } } } \\ { { \displaystyle ~ \exp \left( - \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( x - \mu ) ^ { \intercal } \Sigma ^ { - 1 } ( x - \mu ) \right) } } \end{array}$

# Fitting a Univariate Guassian Distribution

Likelihood

• Log-likelihood

$$
p ( \mathcal { D } | \mu , \boldsymbol { \sigma ^ { 2 } } ) = \prod _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 2 \pi \sigma ^ { 2 } } } \exp { \left( - \frac { ( x _ { i } - \mu ) ^ { 2 } } { 2 \sigma ^ { 2 } } \right) }
$$

$$
\mathcal { L } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \left( - \frac { 1 } { 2 } \log ( 2 \pi \sigma ^ { 2 } ) - \frac { ( x - \mu ) ^ { 2 } } { 2 \sigma ^ { 2 } } \right)
$$

$$
{ \frac { \partial { \mathcal { L } } } { \partial \mu } } = - \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } { \frac { 2 ( x - \mu ) } { 2 \sigma ^ { 2 } } } = 0 \Rightarrow \mu _ { \sf M L } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } x _ { i } / n
$$

$$
= - { \frac { n } { \sigma } } + \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } { \frac { ( x _ { i } - \mu ) ^ { 2 } } { \sigma ^ { 3 } } } = 0 \Rightarrow \sigma ^ { 2 } { \mathsf { M L } } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } { \frac { ( x _ { i } - \mu ) } { n } }
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_054\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_054\auto

# Limitations of Single Gaussian

Single Gaussian may fail to capture complex data, i.e., data with sub-distributions   
• Introduce latent variable $z _ { i }$ to model sub-distributions ▶ $z _ { i } = k$ indicates sample $x _ { j }$ is from the k−th distribution   
Latent variable: the variables you can never observe, can only be inferred indirectly from other observable variables   
An observation $x _ { j }$ is caused by some underlying latent variable   
• • $p ( x , z \mid \theta ) = p ( x \mid z , \theta ) p ( z \mid \theta )$ $\begin{array} { r l } & { p ( x \mid z , \theta ) p ( z \mid \theta ) } \\ & { p ( x , z \mid \theta ) \mathrm { d } z = \sum _ { z } p ( x , z \mid \theta ) } \\ & { \mathsf { a y e s i a n } ) \ P ( A = a | B = b ) = \frac { P ( A = a , B = b ) } { P ( B = b ) } = \frac { \mathsf { 1 } } { \sum } } \end{array}$ P(A = a, B = b)   
(Basics of B x∈A P(A = x, B = b)

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_055\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_055\auto

# (Guassian) Mixture Model

The weighted sum of a number of pdfs where the weights are determined by a distribution

$$
p ( { \pmb x } ) = \pi _ { 1 } f _ { 1 } ( { \pmb x } ) + \pi _ { 2 } f _ { 2 } ( { \pmb x } ) + . . . + \pi _ { K } f _ { K } ( { \pmb x } )
$$

$$
\sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } \pi _ { k } = 1
$$

For GMM, $f _ { i } ( { \pmb x } ) = \mathcal { N } ( { \pmb x } \mid { \pmb \mu } _ { i } , { \pmb \Sigma } _ { i } )$

• Understand GMM using the latent variable model

$$
{ \begin{array} { r l } & { { \mathsf { P a r a m e t e r \ } } \{ \theta = \iota \pi _ { i } , \mu _ { i } , \pm _ { i } ) \} _ { i = 1 } ^ { \cdot } } \\ & { p ( x _ { i } \mid z _ { i } = k , \theta ) = { \mathcal { N } } ( x \mid \mu _ { k } , \Sigma _ { k } ) } \\ & { p ( z _ { i } = k \mid \theta ) = \pi _ { k } } \\ & { p ( x _ { i } \mid \theta ) = \sum _ { z } p ( x _ { i } , z \mid \theta ) = \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } \pi _ { k } { \mathcal { N } } ( x _ { i } \mid \mu _ { k } , \Sigma _ { k } ) } \end{array} }
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_056\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_056\auto

# Fitting a GMM Model

For simplicity we only consider the univariate case

• Likelihood

$$
= \prod _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } \pi _ { k } { \mathcal { N } } ( x _ { i } | \mu _ { k } , \sigma _ { k } ) = \prod _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } \pi _ { k } { \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 2 \pi \sigma ^ { 2 } } } } \exp \qquad 
$$

C Log-likelihood

$$
\mathcal { L } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \log \left( \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } \pi _ { k } \mathcal { N } ( x _ { i } | \mu _ { k } , \sigma _ { k } ) \right)
$$

The summation over the $\mathsf { K }$ components “blocks” our log function Try to take the derivative on $\mu _ { k }$

$$
{ \frac { \partial { \mathcal { L } } } { \partial \mu _ { k } } } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } { \frac { \pi _ { k } { \mathcal { N } } ( x _ { i } | \mu _ { k } , \sigma _ { k } ) } { \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } \pi _ { k } { \mathcal { N } } ( x _ { i } | \mu _ { k } , \sigma _ { k } ) } } { \frac { ( x _ { i } - \mu _ { k } ) } { \sigma _ { k } ^ { 2 } } } = 0
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_057\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_057\auto

# Expectation Maximization (EM) for GMMs

Goal: Iteratively estimate $\theta = \{ \pi _ { i } , \mu _ { i } , \pmb { \Sigma } _ { i } \} _ { i = 1 } ^ { K }$ using unlabeled data.

1 Init: Randomly initialize $\theta$   
2 E-Step: Compute responsibilities

$$
r _ { i k } = \frac { \pi _ { k } \mathcal { N } ( \pmb { x } _ { i } | \pmb { \mu } _ { k } , \pmb { \Sigma } _ { k } ) } { \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } \pi _ { k } \mathcal { N } ( \pmb { x } _ { i } | \pmb { \mu } _ { k } , \pmb { \Sigma } _ { k } ) } , \forall i , k
$$

3 M-Step: Update parameters

$$
= \frac { \sum _ { i } r _ { i k } \pmb { x } _ { i } } { \sum _ { i } r _ { i k } } , \quad \sigma _ { k } ^ { 2 } = \frac { \sum _ { i } r _ { i k } ( \pmb { x } _ { i } - \pmb { \mu } _ { k } ) ^ { 2 } } { \sum _ { i } r _ { i k } } , \quad \pi _ { k } = \frac { \sum } { \pmb { \mu } }
$$

4 Check: Stop if log-likelihood converges or max iterations reached

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_059\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_059\auto

# Why EM works?

Instead of directly handling log $\begin{array} { r } { p ( X | \theta ) = \log \sum _ { Z } p ( X , Z | \theta ) } \end{array}$ , we focus on the expected log-likelihood

The Expectation of the complete-data likelihood w.r.t. to the posterior distribution:

$$
( Z | X , \theta ^ { \circ | \mathrm { d } } ) \log p ( X , Z | \theta ) = \sum _ { Z } p ( Z | X , \theta ^ { \circ | \mathrm { d } } ) \log p ( X , .
$$

This expectation is then Maximized w.r.t. to $\theta$ :

$$
\mathbb { E } _ { p ( Z | X , \theta ^ { \circ | \mathfrak { d } } ) } \log p ( X , Z | \theta ) = { \underset { \theta } { \operatorname { a r g m a x } } } \sum _ { Z } p ( Z | X , \theta ^ { \circ | \mathfrak { d } } )
$$

Therefore, we can solve this problem in alternating steps with one variable fixed at a time: fixed $\theta ^ { \mathrm { o l d } }$ and obtain $p \big ( Z | X , \theta ^ { \mathrm { o l d } } \big )$ , then maximize $\mathbb { E } _ { p ( Z | X , \theta ^ { \circ | \mathsf { d } } ) } \log p ( X , Z | \theta )$ and obtain θnew

# Mathematical model for EM algorithm (Optional)

● What is the relationship between the incomplete-data likelihood log $p ( X \mid \theta )$ and the expectation of the complete-data likelihood w.r.t. to the posterior distribution?

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \log p ( X \mid \theta ) = \log \displaystyle \sum _ { Z } p ( X , Z \mid \theta ) } \\ & { \phantom { = } = \log \displaystyle \sum _ { Z } q ( Z ) \frac { p ( X , Z \mid \theta ) } { q ( Z ) } } \\ & { \phantom { = = } = \log \mathbb { E } _ { q ( Z ) } \frac { p ( X , Z \mid \theta ) } { q ( Z ) } } \\ & { \geq \mathbb { E } _ { q ( Z ) } \log \frac { p ( X , Z \mid \theta ) } { q ( Z ) } \quad \mathrm { ( J e n s e l ~ } } \\ & { = L ( \theta , q ) } \end{array}
$$

We obtain a lower bound $L$ on log $p ( X \mid \theta )$ , which is a function of $\theta$ and $q$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b\page_065\DSAA2011-L10_clustering_b_page_065\auto

# Pros and Cons of GMMs and EM

# Pros:

Easy to implement for uni/multivariate data   
EM converges to a (local) minimum   
Log-likelihood decreases each iteration   
Faster and more stable than gradient descent   
Handles covariance constraints well

# Cons:

Sensitive to parameter initialization Risk of singularities $( \sigma  0 )$ (d) May overfit without validation

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_004\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_004\auto

# Density-based Clustering

Define clusters by density reachability • Handle arbitrary cluster shapes Robust to noise/outliers • Does not require the number of clusters Representatives: DBSCAN, OPTICS

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_005\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_005\auto

Parameters: minPts defines minimum number of samples in a cluster, and $\epsilon$ affects the reachability   
$p$ is a core point if $| N _ { \epsilon } ( p ) | \geq m i n P t s$   
$q$ is directly density-reachable from $p$ if $p$ is a core point and $q \in N _ { \epsilon } ( p )$   
• $q$ is density-reachable from $p$ if there is a chain of directly density-reachable relationship

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_006\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_006\auto

DBSCAN cannot handle clusters with varying densities   
OPTICS allow adaptive ϵ: larger $\epsilon$ for sparse region and smaller $\epsilon$ for dense region   
Core distance: minimum distance to make $p$ a core point   
Reachability distance: minimum distance to make $q$ directly density-reachable from $p$   
Algorithm: ▶ Always process the points with minimum reachability distance (w.r.t. previous points) first Keep updating reachability distances for all unprocessed points

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_007\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_007\auto

# Hierarchical Clustering

Agglomerative (bottom-up): Start with each point as a cluster and merge.   
Divisive (top-down): Start with all points in one cluster and split.   
Widely used metrics ▶ Single linkage: minimum distance Complete linkage: maximum distance Average linkage: average distance Ward’s method: increase in variance

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_008\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_008\auto

# Soft Clustering

Gaussian mixture model • $\begin{array} { r } { \textstyle f ( x ) = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } \pi _ { k } { \mathcal { N } } ( x \mid \mu _ { k } , \Sigma _ { k } ) } \end{array}$ EM algorithm ▶ E-Step: Compute responsibilities

$$
r _ { i k } = \frac { \pi _ { k } \mathcal { N } ( \pmb { x } _ { i } | \pmb { \mu } _ { k } , \pmb { \Sigma } _ { k } ) } { \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } \pi _ { k } \mathcal { N } ( \pmb { x } _ { i } | \pmb { \mu } _ { k } , \pmb { \Sigma } _ { k } ) } , \forall i , k
$$

▶ M-Step: Update parameters

$$
\iota _ { k } = \frac { \sum _ { i } r _ { i k } \pmb { x } _ { i } } { \sum _ { i } r _ { i k } } , \quad \sigma _ { k } ^ { 2 } = \frac { \sum _ { i } r _ { i k } ( \pmb { x } _ { i } - \pmb { \mu } _ { k } ) ^ { 2 } } { \sum _ { i } r _ { i k } } , \quad \pi _ { k } = \frac { \sum _ { i } r _ { i k } } { n }
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_013\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_013\auto

# Why Dimensionality Reduction?

Curse of Dimensionality: High-dimensional data leads to sparsity, computational cost, and overfitting.

● Goals:

▶ Visualization (e.g., 100D to 2D). Noise reduction. Feature extraction.   
▶ Computational efficiency.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_014\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_014\auto

# Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

• Principal Component Analysis is a linear dimensionality reduction technique.

Finds new axes (principal components, linear combinations of existing axes) that capture most important patterns in the data.

▶ Maximize variance: if many samples are collapsed in the new space, we lose information Minimize reconstruction error: we can use lower-dimensional representations to recover the original data $\begin{array} { r } { \pmb { x } _ { i } \approx \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { k } z _ { i j } \pmb { v } _ { j } , \pmb { v } _ { j } } \end{array}$ are the best directions to capture important patterns

![](images/318e5f2c0106f9b2900a084be8615919bd2b9c7fe24bfc22e96ab27459a1df5e.jpg)

### Images:
- data\1. Machine_Learning\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_014\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_014\auto\images\318e5f2c0106f9b2900a084be8615919bd2b9c7fe24bfc22e96ab27459a1df5e.jpg

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_015\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_015\auto

1 Input: $\ b { X } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n \times p }$ (n samples, p features).

2 Standardize the Data: Scale features to zero mean and unit variance: $X _ { k } \gets ( X _ { k } - \mu _ { k } ) / \sigma _ { k }$ or $\pmb { \chi }  ( \pmb { V } ^ { 1 / 2 } ) ^ { - 1 } ( \pmb { X } - \pmb { \mu } )$ .

3 Compute Covariance Matrix: Calculate $\begin{array} { r } { \Sigma = \frac { 1 } { n } X ^ { \prime \top } X ^ { \prime } } \end{array}$ .

4 Eigenvalue Decomposition: Find eigenvectors (principal components) and eigenvalues (variance) of $\boldsymbol { \Sigma }$ .

5 Select Principal Components: Choose top $k$ eigenvectors based on highest eigenvalues (e.g., $9 5 \%$ variance).

6 Project Data: Transform data to lower-dimensional space: $Z = X ^ { \prime } W$ , where W is the matrix of selected eigenvectors.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_016\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_016\auto

# PCA: Mathematics - Variance Maximization

First, consider projecting the data in one-dimensional space We are projecting data onto a unit vector $u \in \mathbb { R } ^ { p }$ : $z = X u$ , and hence $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ .

Variance of projection:

$$
\mathsf { V a r } ( z ) = \mathsf { V a r } ( X u ) = u ^ { T } \mathsf { C o v } ( X ) u = u ^ { T } \Sigma u ,
$$

where $\Sigma = { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { n } } X ^ { T } X$ .

Optimization problem:

max uT Σu, subject to $u ^ { \top } u = 1 .$

or equivalently

$$
\operatorname* { m a x } _ { u } \frac { u ^ { \top } \Sigma u } { u ^ { \top } u }
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_017\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_017\auto

# Reacp of Linear Algebra

# Spectral Decomposition

For a $n \times n$ real symmetric matrix $A$ , we have $\begin{array} { r } { A = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \lambda _ { i } e _ { i } e _ { i } ^ { \top } } \end{array}$ , where $\lambda _ { j }$ is $j .$ -th eigenvalue, and $e _ { j }$ is the corresponding normalized eigenvector. Let $\boldsymbol { \Lambda } = \mathrm { d i a g } \{ \lambda _ { 1 } , . . . , \lambda _ { n } \}$ , $Q = [ e _ { 1 } , \ldots , e _ { n } ]$ , we have $A = Q \Lambda Q ^ { \top }$ , and $A ^ { 1 / 2 } = Q \Lambda ^ { 1 / 2 } Q ^ { \top }$

# Maximization of Quadratic Forms for Points on the Unit Sphere (Rayleigh quotient)

Let $B$ be a positive semi-definite matrix with eigenvalues $\lambda _ { 1 } \geq \lambda _ { 2 } \geq \cdot \cdot \cdot \geq \lambda _ { n } \geq 0$ and associated normalized eigenvectors $e _ { 1 } , \ldots , e _ { n }$ , and $\boldsymbol { u }$ is a unit vector, then

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \underset { u \neq 0 } { \circ } u \times u ^ { \top } B u = \lambda _ { 1 } } \\ & { \circ \underset { u \neq 0 } { \operatorname* { m i n } } u ^ { \top } B u = \lambda _ { n } } \\ & { \circ \underset { u \neq 0 , u \bot \epsilon _ { 1 } , \ldots , \epsilon _ { k } } { \operatorname* { m a x } } u ^ { \top } B u = \lambda _ { k + 1 } } \end{array}
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_019\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_019\auto

# PCA: Mathematics - Eigenvalue Decomposition

# Principal Components

The eigenvectors of the covariance matrix define the principal components.

Covariance matrix: $\Sigma = { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { n } } X ^ { T } X$ is a symmetric matrix.

Eigenvalue decomposition:

$$
\Sigma = U \Lambda U ^ { T } ,
$$

where:

▶ $U \in \mathbb { R } ^ { p \times p }$ : Matrix of eigenvectors (principal components).   
▶ Λ: Diagonal matrix of eigenvalues $\left( \lambda _ { 1 } \geq \lambda _ { 2 } \geq \cdots \geq \lambda _ { p } \right)$ .

• Top $k$ components: Select columns of $U _ { k } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { p \times k }$ corresponding to the $k$ largest eigenvalues.

● Projection: New data in lower dimensions:

$$
Z = X U _ { k } , \quad Z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n \times k } .
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_021\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_021\auto

# PCA: Mathematics - Reconstruction Error Minimization

Data: $\ b { X } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n \times p }$ (n samples, p features).

● Assume we have the projection matrix $U \in \mathbb { R } ^ { p \times k }$ . $U$ contains $k$ orthonormal bases that define the subspace   
The projected points (the coordinates in the subspace): $Z = X U$   
• The reconstructed points: $\hat { X } = Z U ^ { \top } = X U U ^ { \top }$   
By Pythagorean theorem, the reconstruction error

$$
\underbrace { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \lVert x _ { i } - \hat { x } _ { i } \rVert ^ { 2 } } _ { \mathrm { R e c o n s t r u c t i o n ~ e r r o r } } = \underbrace { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \lVert x _ { i } \rVert ^ { 2 } } _ { \mathrm { C o n s t } } - \underbrace { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \lVert \hat { x } _ { i } \rVert ^ { 2 } } _ { \mathrm { V a r i a n c e } }
$$

Minimize the reconstruction error $\Leftrightarrow$ maximize the projected variance!

![](images/c01589895c802e78ae6fcc73be61cdf4aa82fa5b59fb02f65c3ac8acd3d61c68.jpg)

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_023\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_023\auto

# Quick Question

Why do we (usually) need to do standardization

▶ If not centering data around the origin, make sure you use the covariance matrix $( X - \mu ) ( X - \mu ) ^ { \intercal }$ instead of $X X ^ { \top }$ If not scaling each coordinate appropriately, the coordinate with the higher variance will dominate the principal component, then the PCA results will be sensitive to the units of each coordinate (e.g., height in m and cm) Why we use $\begin{array} { r } { \Sigma = \frac { 1 } { \eta } \dot { X } \dot { X ^ { \top } } } \end{array}$ instead of $\scriptstyle { \frac { 1 } { n - 1 } } X X ^ { \dagger }$

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_024\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_024\auto

# Quick Question

Why do we (usually) need to do standardization

▶ If not centering data around the origin, make sure you use the covariance matrix $( X - \mu ) ( X - \mu ) ^ { \intercal }$ instead of $X X ^ { \top }$

▶ If not scaling each coordinate appropriately, the coordinate with the higher variance will dominate the principal component, then the PCA results will be sensitive to the units of each coordinate (e.g., height in m and cm)

Why we use $\begin{array} { r } { \Sigma = \frac { 1 } { n } \dot { X } X ^ { \top } } \end{array}$ instead of $\scriptstyle { \frac { 1 } { n - 1 } } X X ^ { \dagger }$

▶ It does not matter, the eigenvalue is the same.

What is the difference between linear regression and PCA? Both of them have concepts like projection matrix, best subspace, etc.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_025\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_025\auto

# Quick Question

Why do we (usually) need to do standardization ▶ If not centering data around the origin, make sure you use the covariance matrix $( X - \mu ) ( X - \mu ) ^ { \intercal }$ instead of $X X ^ { \top }$

▶ If not scaling each coordinate appropriately, the coordinate with the higher variance will dominate the principal component, then the PCA results will be sensitive to the units of each coordinate (e.g., height in m and cm)

Why we use $\begin{array} { r } { \Sigma = \frac { 1 } { n } \dot { X } X ^ { \top } } \end{array}$ instead of $\scriptstyle { \frac { 1 } { n - 1 } } X X ^ { \dagger }$

It does not matter, the eigenvalue is the same.

What is the difference between linear regression and PCA? Both of them have concepts like projection matrix, best subspace, etc.

▶ In PCA, all dimensions are treated equally. In linear regression, $y$ is special In PCA, we minimize the sum of the squared perpendicular distances after projecting X into the subspace spanned by PC. In linear regression, we minimize the sum of squared errors after projecting $y$ into the subspace spanned by $X$

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_026\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_026\auto

# Kernel PCA (Optional)

Recall that in linear PCA, we have $\begin{array} { r } { \Sigma = \frac { 1 } { n } X ^ { \top } X = \frac { 1 } { n } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } x _ { i } x _ { i } ^ { \top } } \end{array}$   
• Using kernel trick, we have $\begin{array} { r } { \Sigma = \frac { 1 } { n } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \phi ( x _ { i } ) \phi ( x _ { i } ) ^ { \top } } \end{array}$ , and we need to compute its   
eigenvalues and eigenvectors using kernels $K _ { i j } = \phi ( x _ { i } ) ^ { \top } \phi ( x _ { j } )$   
● The eigenvector should satisfy $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { n } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \phi ( x _ { i } ) \phi ( x _ { i } ) ^ { \top } v = \lambda v } \end{array}$   
• Since $\phi ( \boldsymbol { x } _ { i } ) ^ { \top } \boldsymbol { v }$ is a scalar, we knows that $v$ is a linear combination of $\phi ( x _ { i } )$ , i.e.,   
$\boldsymbol { v } = [ \phi ( x _ { 1 } ) , \phi ( x _ { 2 } ) , \ldots , \phi ( x _ { n } ) ] \alpha = \phi ( X ) \alpha$   
C Let $K = \phi ( X ) ^ { \top } \phi ( X )$ , we can have $K ^ { 2 } \alpha = n \lambda K \alpha$   
So we can solve the Eigenvalue problem for $K \alpha = \eta \lambda \alpha$ , and the solution will also   
satisfy $K ^ { 2 } \alpha = n \lambda K \alpha$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_027\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_027\auto

# Summary of PCA

# Pros:

Linear method, simpler to implement ● Computationally efficient for large datasets Reduces multi-collinearity effectively

# Cons:

Assumes linear relationships in data Less effective for preserving local structure • May lose critical information if variance is not representative item Sensitive to outliers (variants: robust PCA)

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_028\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_028\auto

# Multidimensional Scaling (MDS)

The proximity matrix, such as similarity matrix, distance matrix, and dissimilarity matrix, is unchanged by shifting, rotation, or reflection.   
MDS aims to preserve the proximity matrix in lower dimensions.   
Classical MDS: Based on Euclidean distances, assumes data is metric.   
Metric MDS: Generalized classical MDS that works with another metric.   
Non-metric MDS: Uses rank order of distances, suitable for non-metric data.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_029\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_029\auto

Input: Proximity matrix $\pmb { D } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n \times n }$ , where $d _ { i j }$ is the distance between samples $i$ and $j$ .

• Goal: Find $\boldsymbol { X } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n \times k }$ s.t. $\lVert x _ { i } - x _ { j } \rVert \approx d _ { i j }$ .

Our MDS takes two steps:

1 $D  B$ : the matrix $B$ can be computed from proximity matrix $D$ by using double centering   
2 $B \to E \bar { \Lambda } E ^ { \top } = X X ^ { \top }$ : the coordinate matrix $X$ can be derived by eigenvalue decomposition from $B$

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_030\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_030\auto

1 Compute the squared proximity matrix $D ^ { ( 2 ) } = \big ( d _ { i j } ^ { 2 } \big )$   
2 Compute the inner product matrix $B$ using double centering: $B = - \frac { 1 } { 2 } J D ^ { ( 2 ) } J ,$ , where $\begin{array} { r } { J = J - \frac { 1 } { n } \mathbf { 1 1 } ^ { \top } , } \end{array}$   
3 Compute the $k$ largest eigenvalues $\lambda _ { 1 } , \ldots , \lambda _ { k }$ and corresponding eigenvectors $u _ { 1 } , \ldots , u _ { k }$ of $B$   
4 Obtain the coordinates $X = E _ { k } \Lambda _ { k } ^ { 1 / 2 }$ , where $E _ { k } = [ e _ { 1 } , \ldots , e _ { k } ] \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n \times k }$ and $\Lambda _ { m } ^ { 1 / 2 } = \mathsf { d i a g } ( \sqrt { \lambda _ { 1 } } , \ldots , \sqrt { \lambda _ { k } } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { k \times k }$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_033\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_033\auto

# Strain Function in MDS

The quality of the MDS solution is evaluated using a strain function:

$$
\mathsf { S t r a i n } ( x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n } ) = \sqrt { \sum _ { i < j } ( b _ { i j } - x _ { i } ^ { \top } x _ { j } ) ^ { 2 } / \sum _ { i < j } b _ { i j } ^ { 2 } }
$$

Lower strain indicates a better fit. Classical MDS provides the closed-form solution for minimizing strain

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_034\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_034\auto

# Metric MDS

In classical MDS, we aim to find $x _ { j }$ that gives $d _ { i j } \approx \hat { d } _ { i j } = \lVert \boldsymbol { x } _ { i } - \boldsymbol { x } _ { j } \rVert _ { 2 }$ by matching the inner product

▶ This assumes that the distance $d _ { i j }$ should be Euclidean distance (or at least “look lik Euclidean distance.   
▶ When $d _ { i j }$ is more general (dissimilarity), such a modeling will be improper   
▶ Does not support different weights

We directly match the distance by optimizing

$$
\mathfrak { c } _ { 1 } , \dots , \pmb { \mathscr { x } } _ { n } ) = \sqrt { \sum _ { i < j } w _ { i j } ( d _ { i j } - \| \pmb { x } _ { i } - \pmb { x } _ { j } \| ^ { 2 } ) / \sum _ { i < j } \| \pmb { x } _ { i } - \pmb { x } _ { i } \| ^ { 2 } }
$$

or sometimes

$$
\Im \mathrm { t r e s s } ( x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n } ) = \sqrt { \sum _ { i < j } ( d _ { i j } - | | x _ { i } - x _ { j } | | ^ { 2 } ) / \sum _ { i < j } { \cal { C } } _ { i } }
$$

No closed-form solution. Solved using iterative algorithms Also called Stress majorization

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_035\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_035\auto

# Non-Metric MDS

In some cases, the dissimilarities $d _ { i j }$ are qualitative   
We only focus on their rank: the ordering results of dissimilarity in low-dimensional space should be consistent with the high-dimensional space

$$
\mathfrak { s } ( \boldsymbol { x } _ { 1 } , \dots , \boldsymbol { x } _ { n } , f ) = \sqrt { \sum _ { i < j } ( f ( d _ { i j } ) - \| \boldsymbol { x } _ { i } - \boldsymbol { x } _ { j } \| ^ { 2 } ) / \sum _ { i < j } }
$$

▶ $f$ is a monotonically increasing function, i.e., $d _ { i j } < d _ { k I } \Leftrightarrow f ( d _ { i j } ) < f ( d _ { k I } )$ ▶ Algorithm:

$\star$ Use monotonic regression to found optimal $f$ to best minimizing the stress function   
$\star$ Optimize $x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n }$ to best minimizing the stress function   
$^ { \star }$ Repeat these two steps alternatively

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_036\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_036\auto

# Summary of MDS

# Pros:

Preserves pairwise distances (Euclidean or other metrics) as closely as possible. ● Flexible: Works with any dissimilarity matrix, not just Euclidean distances.

# Cons:

• Assumes linear relationships, failing to capture nonlinear manifold structures.   
Computationally intensive for large datasets (e.g., eigenvalue decomposition).   
Sensitive to noise and outliers in the dissimilarity matrix.   
Results depend on the choice of distance metric and initialization.

---

# PCA:

• Maximize the projected variance Compute covariance matrix

# MDS:

• Preserve proximity matrix Compute inner product matrix

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_040\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_040\auto

1 Construct Neighborhood Graph: Build a graph where each data point is connected to its $k$ nearest neighbors or points within radius ϵ.

2 Compute Geodesic Distances: Estimate geodesic distances between all pairs of points using shortest paths (e.g., Dijkstra’s algorithm).

3 Apply MDS: Use classical MDS to embed the data into a lower-dimensional space, preserving geodesic distances.

4 Output: Low-dimensional coordinates that reflect the manifold’s geometry.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_041\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_041\auto

# Summary of Isomap

# Pros:

Captures nonlinear manifold structures effectively.   
● Preserves global geometric properties via geodesic distances.

# Cons:

• Sensitive to the choice of $k$ or $\epsilon$ for neighborhood graph.   
Computationally expensive for large datasets (shortest path calculations).   
• Assumes data lies on a single, well-sampled manifold.   
May fail if the manifold has holes or is noisy.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_043\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_043\auto

1 Given a dataset $D \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n \times p }$ and the associated class labels $\pmb { \gamma }$ of $C$ classes   
2 Compute $\begin{array} { r } { S _ { w } = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { C } \sum _ { i \in C _ { j } } ( x - m _ { j } ) ( x - m _ { j } ) ^ { \top } } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { S _ { b } = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { C } { n } _ { j } ( { m } _ { j } - m ) ( { m } _ { j } - m ) ^ { \top } , } \end{array}$ , where $C _ { j }$ is the set of index belong to class $j , n _ { j } = | C _ { j } |$ is the number of samples belong to class $j$ , $\begin{array} { r } { m _ { j } = \frac { 1 } { n _ { j } } \sum _ { i \in C _ { j } } x _ { j } } \end{array}$ is the mean of samples in class $j$ , and $\begin{array} { r } { m = \frac { 1 } { n } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } x _ { i } } \end{array}$ is the mean of all samples   
3 Solve the generalized eigenvalue problem $S _ { b } v = \lambda S _ { w } v$ to find all eigenvalues and their associated eigenvectors $V = [ v _ { 1 } , \ldots , v _ { k } ]$   
4 Project the data $Y = X V \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n \times k }$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_053\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_053\auto

# Multiclass extension

When we have $C \geq 3$ classes, how can we measure their separation? ▶ Each class center should be far away from each other

$$
\sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { C } n _ { j } ( \mu _ { j } - \mu ) ^ { 2 } , \quad { \mathrm { w h e r e ~ } } \mu = { \frac { 1 } { n } } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { C } n _ { j } \mu _ { j }
$$

$$
\sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { C } n _ { j } ( \mu _ { j } - \mu ) ^ { 2 } = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { C } n _ { j } v ^ { \top } ( m _ { j } - m ) ( m _ { j } - m ) ^ { \top } v = v ^ { \top } .
$$

▶ Each class should be as compact as possible

$$
\sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { C } s _ { j } ^ { 2 } = v ^ { \top } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { C } S _ { j } v = v ^ { \top } S _ { w } v
$$

Similarly, we solve a generalized eigenvalue problem $\begin{array} { r } { S _ { b } v = \lambda S _ { w } v } \end{array}$ Now Ra $\mathsf { i } \mathsf { n } \mathsf { k } ( S _ { b } ) \leq c - 1$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_057\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_057\auto

# Summary of LDA

Pros:

▶ Effectively leverage label information to maximize class separability ▶ Effective for classification tasks

Cons:

▶ At most $C - 1$ feature projections Assumes linear class boundaries Assume Gaussian-distributed data with equal covariance matrix   
▶ It assumes that different classes are identifiable through the mean

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_058\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_058\auto

# Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA)

Extending Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) for non-linearly separable data. Key Difference from LDA: Assume each class has its own covariance matrix, allowing quadratic decision boundaries. How it Works: Models each class as a multivariate Gaussian with class-specific mean and covariance, then assigns points based on maximum posterior probability.

---

• Preserves topological properties of the input space.   
Application: data visualization, clustering, dimensionality reduction.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_060\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_060\auto

# Input $\ b X \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n \times p }$

1 Randomly initialize weight vectors $\in \mathbb { R } ^ { p }$ for each neuron on the grid.   
2 Randomly select an input vector from the dataset.   
1 Find Best Matching Unit (BMU): Identify the neuron with the closest weight vector to the input.   
2 Update Weights: Adjust the BMU and its neighbors’ weight vectors to become closer to the input vector.   
3 Iterate until convergence, gradually reducing the learning rate and neighborhood size.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_061\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_061\auto

# SOM: Mathematics - Weight Update

For an input sample $\pmb { \times }$ , the Best Matching Unit (BMU) is the neuron $i ^ { * }$ with the smallest distance: $\boldsymbol { i } ^ { * } = \arg \operatorname* { m i n } _ { i } d ( \mathbf { x } , \mathbf { w } _ { i } )$ • Weight vectors of the BMU and its neighbors are updated using:

$$
{ \bf w } _ { i } ( t + 1 ) = { \bf w } _ { i } ( t ) + \alpha ( t ) \cdot h _ { i , i ^ { * } } ( t ) \cdot ( { \bf x } - { \bf w } _ { i } ( t ) )
$$

where:

$\alpha ( t )$ : Learning rate, decreases over time (e.g., $\alpha ( t ) = \alpha _ { 0 } e ^ { - t / \tau } )$ . $h _ { i , i ^ { * } } ( t )$ : Neighborhood function, typically Gaussian:

$$
h _ { i , i ^ { * } } ( t ) = \mathrm { e x p } \left( - \frac { \| \mathbf { r } _ { i } - \mathbf { r } _ { i ^ { * } } \| ^ { 2 } } { 2 \sigma ^ { 2 } ( t ) } \right)
$$

$\boldsymbol { \mathsf { r } } _ { i } , \boldsymbol { \mathsf { r } } _ { j ^ { \ast } }$ : Positions of neurons $j$ and BMU on the grid.   
$\sigma ( t )$ : Neighborhood radius, decreases over time.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_062\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_062\auto

# SOM: Mathematics - Neighborhood Function

The Gaussian neighborhood function controls the influence of the BMU on neighboring neurons:

$$
h _ { i , i ^ { * } } ( t ) = \exp { \left( - \frac { \| \mathbf { r } _ { i } - \mathbf { r } _ { i ^ { * } } \| ^ { 2 } } { 2 \sigma ^ { 2 } ( t ) } \right) }
$$

$\sigma ( t )$ shrinks over time, reducing the neighborhood size:

$$
\sigma ( t ) = \sigma _ { 0 } e ^ { - t / \tau }
$$

• This ensures early global ordering and later fine-tuning of the map.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_063\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_063\auto

# Summary of SOM

# Pros:

Effective for visualizing high-dimensional data in 2D/3D.   
Preserves topological relationships in data.   
Unsupervised, no need for labeled data.   
Robust to noise and missing data.

# Cons:

• Computationally intensive for large datasets.   
Sensitive to initialization and hyperparameters (e.g., learning rate, neighborhood size).   
Fixed grid size may not suit all datasets.   
No guaranteed convergence to global optimum.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_064\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_064\auto

# Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (SNE)

Goal: Preserve the neighborhood information of high-dimensional data in a low-dimensional embedding.   
Idea: Model pairwise similarities as probabilities in both high- and low-dimensional spaces.

Key steps:

Compute conditional probabilities $p _ { j \vert j }$ in high-dimensional space.   
Define similar probabilities $q _ { j \vert j }$ in low-dimensional space.   
Minimize divergence between $p _ { j | i }$ and $q _ { j \vert j }$ .

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_065\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_065\auto

# SNE: Mathematics

High-dimensional similarity (jump from $j$ to $i$ in the original space):

$$
p _ { j | i } = \frac { \exp { \left( - \| x _ { i } - x _ { j } \| ^ { 2 } / 2 \sigma _ { i } ^ { 2 } \right) } } { \sum _ { k \neq i } { \exp { \left( - \| x _ { i } - x _ { k } \| ^ { 2 } / 2 \sigma _ { i } ^ { 2 } \right) } } }
$$

$\blacktriangleright \ p _ { i | i } = 0$ $\vdash \sigma _ { i }$ is a bandwidth parameter, representing the “size” of the neighborhood Search $\sigma _ { i }$ such that $\begin{array} { r } { H ( P _ { i } ) = - \sum _ { j } p _ { j | i } \log p _ { j | i } = \log \mathsf { P e r p l e x i t } . } \end{array}$ y)

Low-dimensional similarity (jump from $j$ to $i$ in the embedded space):

$$
q _ { j | i } = \frac { \exp { \left( - \| \pmb { y } _ { i } - \pmb { y } _ { j } \| ^ { 2 } \right) } } { \sum _ { k \neq i } \exp { \left( - \| \pmb { y } _ { i } - \pmb { y } _ { k } \| ^ { 2 } \right) } }
$$

▶ qi |i = 0 $\sigma _ { j }$ is set uniformly to $1 / \sqrt { 2 }$ for all samples Reduce the computational complexity Avoids overfitting to the high-dimensional structure.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_066\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_066\auto

Objective: Minimize Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence:

$$
C = \sum _ { i } \mathsf { K L } ( P _ { i } | | Q _ { i } ) = \sum _ { i } \sum _ { j } p _ { j | i } \log { \frac { p _ { j | i } } { q _ { j | i } } }
$$

Optimized via gradient descent:

$$
\frac { \partial C } { \partial { \pmb { y } } _ { i } } = 2 \sum _ { j } ( { \pmb { y } } _ { i } - { \pmb { y } } _ { j } ) ( p _ { i | j } - q _ { i | j } + p _ { j | i } - q _ { j | i } )
$$

Each sample $i$ is connecting with other samples via springs   
Force direction: y − y   
Force magnitude: $p _ { i | j } - q _ { i | j } + p _ { j | i } - q _ { j | i }$ , mismatch between high-dimensional similarity   
and low-dimensinal similarity

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_067\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_067\auto

# Symmetric SNE

In SNE, $p _ { i \mid j }$ and $q _ { i \vert j }$ is asymmetric   
For a symmetric one, pij = pji , qij = qji   
● $\begin{array} { l } { { \subseteq = K L ( P \ | \ | \ Q ) = \sum _ { i } \sum _ { j } p _ { i j } \frac { p _ { i j } } { q _ { i j } } } } \\ { { \mathrm { ~ } } } \\ { { \mathrm { ~ } } } \\ { { \mathrm { ~ } } } \\ { { \mathit { l i j } = \frac { \exp ( - \| \mathbf { y } _ { i } - \mathbf { y } _ { j } \| ^ { 2 } ) } { \sum _ { k \neq l } \exp ( - \| \mathbf { y } _ { k } - \mathbf { y } _ { l } \| ^ { 2 } ) } } } \\ { { \mathrm { ~ } } } \\ { { \mathit { N e } \ \mathrm { d o } \ \mathrm { n o t } \ \mathrm { u s e } \ p _ { i j } = \frac { \exp ( - \| \mathbf { x } _ { i } - \mathbf { x } _ { j } \| ^ { 2 } / 2 \sigma ^ { 2 } ) } { \sum _ { k \neq l } \exp ( - \| \mathbf { x } _ { k } - \mathbf { x } _ { l } \| ^ { 2 } / 2 \sigma ^ { 2 } ) } } } \end{array}$   
because for a outlier $x _ { i } , p _ { i j }$ are extremely small for all $j$ , so $\pmb { y } _ { j }$ has little effect on the cost function   
Instead, we use $p _ { i j } = ( p _ { i | j } + p _ { j | i } ) / 2 n$ , which ensures that $\sum _ { j } p _ { i j } > 1 / 2 n$   
C ${ \frac { \partial C } { \partial { \pmb { y } } _ { i } } } = 4 \sum _ { j } ( p _ { i j } - q _ { i j } ) ( { \pmb { y } } _ { i } - { \pmb { y } } _ { j } )$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_068\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_068\auto

# SNE: Strengths and Limitations

Strengths: ▶ Preserves local structure effectively. ▶ Flexible framework for extensions.

● Limitations:

▶ Crowding problem: Points clump in low-dimensional space.   
▶ Computationally expensive for large datasets.   
Sensitive to perplexity parameter.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_069\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_069\auto

# Crowding Problem

Fact 1: Assume we can have 11 samples that are mutually equidistant in a 10-dimensional space, there is no way to model this faithfully in a two-dimensional map.   
Fact 2: the distribution of pairwise distances in high-D space and low-dimensional space is totally different: the volume of sphere $V ( r ) \propto r ^ { D }$ , indicating that we don’t have much room to place “neighbors” in low-D space   
Samples with medium distance with sample $i$ will be placed too far away (i.e., $p _ { i j } > q _ { i j } )$ , contributing to a large number of very small attractive forces. Thus, sample $i$ will be placed at the center of the map

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_070\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_070\auto

# Crowding Problem

Fact 1: Assume we can have 11 samples that are mutually equidistant in a 10-dimensional space, there is no way to model this faithfully in a two-dimensional map.   
Fact 2: the distribution of pairwise distances in high-D space and low-dimensional space is totally different: the volume of sphere $V ( r ) \propto r ^ { D }$ , indicating that we don’t have much room to place “neighbors” in low-D space   
o Samples with medium distance with sample $i$ will be placed too far away (i.e., $p _ { i j } > q _ { i j } )$ , contributing to a large number of very small attractive forces. Thus, sample i will be placed at the center of the map   
• Solution: increase $q _ { i j }$ for distant points: we use $t { \mathrm { . } }$ -distribution instead of the Gaussian distribution in the low-dimensional space.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_071\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_071\auto

# t-distrbution

• A long-tail distribution to convert distances into probabilities

This allows a moderate distance in the high-dimensional space to be faithfully modeled by a much larger distance on the map   
It eliminates the unwanted attractive forces between map points that represent moderately dissimilar datapoints.

![](images/09cd01fbe9ef43f16af3dd5307b0c33f0c3077431739a5f0a1d0bd56ba71341c.jpg)

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_072\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_072\auto

# t-Distributed SNE (t-SNE)

Introduced by van der Maaten and Hinton (2008).

An improvement over SNE to address its limitations.

● Key changes:

Uses a heavier-tailed Student’s t-distribution in low-dimensional space.   
Symmetrizes the objective function.

Widely used for visualizing high-dimensional data (e.g., MNIST, single-cell RNA-seq).

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_073\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_073\auto

# t-SNE: Mathematical Foundation

High-dimensional similarity (symmetrized):

$$
p _ { i j } = \frac { p _ { j | i } + p _ { i | j } } { 2 n }
$$

• Low-dimensional similarity (t-distribution, 1 degree of freedom):

$$
q _ { i j } = \frac { \left( 1 + \| y _ { i } - y _ { j } \| ^ { 2 } \right) ^ { - 1 } } { \sum _ { k \neq I } \left( 1 + \| y _ { k } - y _ { I } \| ^ { 2 } \right) ^ { - 1 } }
$$

Objective: Minimize KL divergence:

$$
C = \mathsf { K L } ( P | | Q ) = \sum _ { i \neq j } p _ { i j } \log \frac { p _ { i j } } { q _ { i j } }
$$

Optimization: Gradient descent with tricks (e.g., early exaggeration).

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_074\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_074\auto

# Early Exaggeration in t-SNE

• Technique to enhance cluster formation.   
Basic idea: multiplies high-dimensional similarities by a factor initially.

Purpose: ▶ Helps form tight, distinct clusters early in the optimization.

# ● Process:

Start with exaggerated similarities to pull similar points closer.   
After ${ \sim } 1 0 0$ iterations, use true similarities to fine-tune positions.

Results in clearer, more interpretable visualizations with well-defined clusters.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_075\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_075\auto

# How to use t-sne Effectively

● Check this page: https://distill.pub/2016/misread-tsne/

Those hyperparameters really matter

![](images/3b979af717d8ae1467e8784826daa58c73cb93d48831376f5927f7729549f6a1.jpg)

Perplexity: controls the balance between local and global structure

$^ { \star }$ The effective number of neighbors used to compute conditional probabilities.   
$\star$ Low perplexity (e.g., 5–10): Emphasizes local structure, producing tight, fine-grained clusters but potentially missing global relationships.   
$\star$ High perplexity (e.g., 30–50): Captures more global structure, spreading out points and potentially merging nearby clusters.

▶ Learning rates: Determines the step size during gradient descent optimization of the KL divergence,

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_077\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_077\auto

# Summary of t-SNE

# Pros:

Excellent for visualizing clusters. Mitigates crowding problem via t-distribution. Robust to different datasets.

# Cons:

Non-convex optimization (sensitive to initialization). Does not preserve global structure well. • Computationally intensive for large datasets. (hours for 10k points) No easy way to embed new points

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_078\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_078\auto

# Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP)

Learn the manifold structure and perform the projection

Assumptions:

There exists a manifold on which the data would be uniformly distributed. The underlying manifold of interest is locally connected. ▶ Preserving the topological structure of this manifold is the primary goal

Key features:

▶ Faster and more scalable than t-SNE. Preserves more global structure. Flexible for various distance metrics. ▶ Can embed new points

pip install umap-learn

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_079\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_079\auto

# UMAP: Learn the manifold structure

C Constructs a weighted k-neighbour graph. For each sample xi

We identify $k$ neareset neighbors $N _ { k } ( x _ { i } )$   
▶ σi $\rho _ { i } = \mathsf { m i n } \{ d ( x _ { i } , x _ { j } ) \mid x _ { j } \in N _ { k } ( x _ { i } ) \}$ $\sigma _ { j }$ $\begin{array} { r l } & { \mathsf { \varepsilon } \nabla ^ { \mathsf { A } } \mathsf { \varepsilon } ^ { \mathsf { A } } ^ { \mathsf { J } } \mathsf { J } ^ { \mathsf { J } } } \\ & { \mathsf { \varepsilon } \nabla \left( - \frac { d \left( x _ { i } , x _ { j } \right) - \rho _ { i } } { \sigma _ { i } } \right) = \mathsf { l o g } _ { 2 } k } \\ & { \mathsf { g h b o u r \ g r a p h \ v } _ { j \mid i } = \mathsf { e x p } \left( - \frac { d \left( x _ { i } , x _ { j } \right) - \rho _ { i } } { \sigma _ { i } } \right) \mathsf { f o r } \ x _ { j } \in N _ { k } { \mathsf { I } } } \end{array}$ $v _ { j | j } = 0$ otherwise   
▶ Symmetric weighted k-neighbour graph: $B = A + A ^ { \top } - A \circ A ^ { \top }$ , where $A$ is the weighted   
adjacency matrix of the graph, i.e., $v _ { i j } = v _ { i | j } + v _ { j | i } - v _ { i | j } v _ { j | i }$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_080\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_080\auto

# UMAP: Perform the projection

• Minimize cross entropy

$$
C _ { \mathsf { U M A P } } = \sum _ { i \neq j } v _ { i j } \log \frac { v _ { i j } } { w _ { i j } } + ( 1 - v _ { i j } ) \log \frac { 1 - v _ { i j } } { 1 - w _ { i j } }
$$

$V _ { I j }$ is the similarity in high-D space and define before   
$\begin{array} { r } { \dot { w _ { i j } } = ( 1 + a \| y _ { i } - y _ { j } \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 b } ) ^ { - 1 } } \end{array}$ is the similarity in low-D space   
Can be solved using a force directed graph layout algorithm to project the graph   
Iteratively applying attractive and repulsive forces at each edge or vertex Attractive force: take derivative on vij log vijwij ▶

$$
- { \frac { 2 a b \| { \pmb y } _ { i } - { \pmb y } _ { j } \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 b - 2 } } { 1 + \| { \pmb y } _ { i } - { \pmb y } _ { j } \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } } } w ( x _ { i } , x _ { j } ) ( { \pmb y } _ { i } - { \pmb y } _ { j } )
$$

▶ Repulsive force: take derivative on $\begin{array} { r } { \left( 1 - v _ { i j } \right) \log \frac { 1 - v _ { i j } } { 1 - w _ { i j } } } \end{array}$

$$
\frac { 2 n } { ( \varepsilon + \| \pmb { y } _ { i } - \pmb { y } _ { j } \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } ) ( 1 + \| \pmb { y } _ { i } - \pmb { y } _ { j } \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } ) } ( 1 - w ( x _ { i } , x _ { j } ) ) ( \pmb { y } _ { i } - \pmb { y } _ { j } )
$$

Optimized via stochastic gradient descent.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_081\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_081\auto

# Project unseen data

● UMAP allows for the projection of unseen data

1 Query the $k$ nearest neighbors for the input $x$   
2 Calculate the weights Use the weighted average on low-dimensional space $\sum w _ { i } y _ { i } / \sum w _ { i }$ as the initial values   
2 Optimize the position of new points while keeping other points fixed

Why t-SNE does not support it?

The loss function $K L ( P | | Q )$ relies on all sample pairs   
After adding new points, $p _ { i j }$ changes due to the changes in normalizing factors   
If we fixed the positions of existing samples, $p _ { i j }$ decrease while $q _ { i j }$ remains unchanged,   
making the optimization fail

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_082\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_082\auto

# Hyperparameters of UMAP

n neighbors: the number of nearest neighbors used to approximate the local manifold structure.

It is analogous to perplexity in t-SNE. ▶ But directly specifies the neighbor count.

min dist: minimum distance apart that points are allowed to be in the low-dimensional representation.

Lower values allow points to cluster closely, producing compact, well-separated groups. ▶ Larger values will prevent UMAP from packing points together and will focus on the preservation of the broad topological structure instead.

Check this page umap-learn for more details and visualization examples

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction\page_083\DSAA2011-L11_dimensionality_reduction_page_083\auto

# Summary of UMAP

# Strengths:

• Fast and scalable.   
Preserves global and local structure.

# Limitations:

• Sensitive to hyperparameters.   
May overfit to noise in some cases.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_004\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_004\auto

# Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

• Key Idea: Find principal components (linear combinations of existing dimensions) that capture the most variance in the data (and equivalently, minimize reconstruction error).

● Steps:

Standardize the data $X _ { k } \gets ( X _ { k } - \mu _ { k } ) / \sigma _ { k }$ Compute covariance matrix of data: $\begin{array} { r } { \dot { \Sigma } = \frac { 1 } { n } X ^ { \top } X } \end{array}$ . Eigenvalue decomposition: $\Sigma = U \Lambda U ^ { T }$ . ▶ Project data onto top- $k$ eigenvectors (principle components): $Y = X U _ { k }$ , where $U _ { k } = [ e _ { 1 } , \ldots , e _ { k } ] \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n \times k }$ .

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_005\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_005\auto

# Classical Multidimensional Scaling (MDS)

Key Idea: Preserves pairwise Euclidean distances between data points in a lower-dimensional space.

• Steps:

▶ Compute squared distance matrix $D ^ { ( 2 ) }$ .   
▶ Compute inner product matrix through double centering: $\begin{array} { r } { B = - \frac { 1 } { 2 } J D ^ { ( 2 ) } J } \end{array}$ , where $\begin{array} { r } { J = \dot { I } - \frac { 1 } { n } \mathbf { 1 } \mathbf { 1 } ^ { T } } \end{array}$ .   
▶ Eigenvalue decomposition: $B = U \Lambda U ^ { T }$ .   
▶ Obtain the coordinates $X = U _ { k } \Lambda _ { k } ^ { 1 / 2 }$ , where $U _ { k } = [ e _ { 1 } , \ldots , e _ { k } ] \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n \times k }$ and $\textstyle \bigwedge _ { k } ^ { 1 / 2 } = \operatorname { d i a g } ( \sqrt { \lambda _ { 1 } } , \dotsc , \sqrt { \lambda _ { k } } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { k \times k }$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_006\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_006\auto

# Metric MDS & Non-metric MDS

Metric MDS: Generalization of classical MDS that directly minimizes a stress function to preserve distances.

▶ Stres $\begin{array} { r l } & { \texttt { s f u n c t i o n : } \mathrm { S t r e s s } ( x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n } ) = \sqrt { \sum _ { i < j } ( d _ { i j } - \| x _ { i } - x _ { j } } } \\ & {  { ( d _ { i j } - \| x _ { i } - x _ { j } \| ) ^ { 2 } } / \sum _ { i < j } \| x _ { i } - x _ { j } \| ^ { 2 } . } \end{array}$ ∥)2 or qP ▶ Optimize using gradient descent or iterative methods.

• Non-metric MDS: Preserves the rank order of dissimilarities rather than their exact values.

• Use monotonic regression to match dissimilarities in low-dimensional space.

Stress $\frac  \mathsf { f u n c t i o n : } \mathsf { S t r e s s } ( x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n } , f ) = \sqrt { \sum _ { i < j } ( f ( d _ { i j } ) - \| x _ { i } - }$ x j ∥)2 or   
qPi<   
▶ Alternatively optimize $f$ and $\pmb { x } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \pmb { x } _ { n }$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_007\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_007\auto

# Isometric Mapping (Isomap)

• Key Idea: Use shortest paths on a nearest-neighbor graph to approximate geodesic distances on a manifold.

● Steps:

Construct $k$ -NN (or $\epsilon$ -NN) graph. Compute pairwise shortest path distances on the graph (e.g., Dijkstra or Floyd-Warshall algorithm) ▶ Apply MDS to obtain the low-dimensional representation

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_008\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_008\auto

# Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)

Key Idea: Project data to maximize between-class scatter and minimize within-class scatter.

● Steps:

▶ Compute within-class scatter $\begin{array} { r } { S _ { w } = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { C } \sum _ { i \in C _ { j } } ( x - m _ { j } ) ( x - m _ { j } ) ^ { \top } } \end{array}$ and between-class scatter $\begin{array} { r } { S _ { b } = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { C } { n } _ { j } ( { m } _ { j } - m ) ( { m } _ { j } - m ) ^ { \top } } \end{array}$ .   
Solve generalized eigenvalue problem: $\begin{array} { r } { S _ { b } v = \lambda S _ { w } b } \end{array}$ .   
Project data onto top eigenvectors (at most $C - 1 )$ .

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_009\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_009\auto

# Self-Organizing Map (SOM)

Key Idea: Neural network-based method that organizes data points on a grid while preserving topology.

Steps:

▶ Initialize the node weight vectors in a map   
▶ Randomly select an input sample $\star$ Find the best matching unit (BMU) $\star$ Update the weight of BMU and its neighbors: ${ \bf w } _ { i } ( t + 1 ) = { \bf w } _ { i } ( t ) + \alpha ( t ) \cdot h _ { i , i ^ { * } } ( t ) \cdot ( { \bf x } - { \bf w } _ { i } ( t ) )$ . $\star \textit { h } _ { c i }$ is a neighborhood function; $\eta$ is learning rate.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_010\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_010\auto

# Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (SNE)

Key Idea: Match probability distributions of pairwise similarities in high- and low-dimensional spaces.

Steps:

High-dimensional similarity: pj|i = $\begin{array} { r l } & { p _ { j | i } = \frac { \exp ( - | | x _ { i } - x _ { j } | | ^ { 2 } / 2 \sigma _ { i } ^ { 2 } ) } { \sum _ { k \ne i } \exp ( - | | x _ { i } - x _ { k } | | ^ { 2 } / 2 \sigma _ { i } ^ { 2 } ) } . } \\ & { q _ { j | i } = \frac { \exp ( - | | y _ { i } - y _ { j } | | ^ { 2 } ) } { \sum _ { k \ne i } \exp ( - | | y _ { i } - y _ { k } | | ^ { 2 } ) } . } \end{array}$ ▶ Low-dimensional similarity: qj|i = ▶ Minimize KL divergence between $P$ and low-dimensional $Q$ .

$$
C = \sum _ { i } \mathsf { K L } ( P _ { i } | | Q _ { i } ) = \sum _ { i } \sum _ { j } p _ { j | i } \log { \frac { p _ { j | i } } { q _ { j | i } } }
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_011\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_011\auto

# t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE)

● Description: Handles the crowding problem by using a t-distribution for low-dimensional similarities.

Steps:

▶ High-dimensional similarity: $\begin{array} { r l } & { p _ { i j } = \big ( p _ { j | i } + p _ { j | i } \big ) / 2 n . } \\ & { q _ { i j } = \cfrac { \big ( 1 + \| y _ { i } - y _ { j } \| ^ { 2 } \big ) ^ { - 1 } } { \sum _ { k \ne I } \big ( 1 + \| y _ { k } - y _ { I } \| ^ { 2 } \big ) ^ { - 1 } } . } \end{array}$ Low-dimensional similarity: Minimize KL divergence using gradient descent.

$$
C = \mathsf { K L } ( P | | Q ) = \sum _ { i \neq j } p _ { i j } \log \frac { p _ { i j } } { q _ { i j } }
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_012\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_012\auto

# Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP)

• Key Idea: Construct a weighted neighborhood graph and preserve graph structure in the low-dimensional representation

● Steps:

High-dimensional similarity based on nearest neighbors: pi |j $\begin{array} { r l } & { = \exp \left( - \frac { d \left( x _ { i } , x _ { j } \right) - { \bar { \rho _ { i } } } } { \sigma _ { i } } \right) \quad p _ { i j } = p _ { i | j } + p _ { j | i } - p _ { i | j } p _ { j | i } } \\ & { { \sf d i m e n s i o n a l ~ s i m i l a r i t y ~ } q _ { i j } = ( 1 + a \cdot \| y _ { i } - y _ { j } \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 b } ) ^ { - 1 } } \end{array}$ LowCross-entropy loss to optimize low-dimensional coordinates.

$$
C = \sum _ { i \neq j } p _ { i j } \log { \frac { p _ { i j } } { q _ { i j } } } + \left( 1 - p _ { i j } \right) \log \left( { \frac { 1 - p _ { i j } } { 1 - q _ { i j } } } \right)
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_021\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_021\auto

# Introduction to Probabilistic Graphical Models

• Graphical frameworks for representing probability distributions Nodes represent random variables, edges represent dependencies Model complex joint probability distributions compactly

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_022\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_022\auto

# Components of PGMs

Nodes: Random variables (discrete or continuous) Edges: Probabilistic dependencies Factors: Conditional probabilities or potentials Joint Probability $P ( X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n } )$ are encoded via factorization

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_023\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_023\auto

# Types of PGMs

# ● Bayesian Networks:

▶ Directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) Conditional dependencies For directed dependencies

# Markov Random Fields:

▶ Undirected graphs Potential functions over cliques For cyclic or mutual dependencies

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_024\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_024\auto

# Static Bayesian Network

• For directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) with $d$ nodes representing random variables $X _ { 1 : d } = ( X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { d } )$ • The joint probability distribution is factorized as $\begin{array} { r } { P ( X _ { 1 : d } ) = \prod _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } P ( X _ { i } \mid \mathsf { p a } ( X _ { i } ) ) , } \end{array}$ where $\mathsf { p a } ( X _ { i } )$ is the set of nodes that point to $X _ { i }$ (parents).

![](images/ccd0b123db543e22eab80cd5aeaefb9d1d6bfcaae00f66bf204d2a786b8a3a51.jpg)

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_032\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_032\auto

# d-separation

A, B , $C$ are arbitrary non-intersecting sets of nodes. C can be empty   
We wish to know whether A⊥⊥ $B \mid C$ holds or not.   
Construct all possible (undirected) paths from any node in A to any node in B.   
A path is blocked by $C$ if ▶ The path contains a chain $i  j  k$ or a fork $i \left. j \right. k$ such that the middle node $j$ is in C ▶ The path contains a v-structure $i \to j  k$ such that the $j$ (and all the descendants) is not in C   
If all paths from A to $B$ are blocked, then $A$ is d-separated from $B$ by C

# Theorem 1

(d-separation) If A is $d .$ -separated from $B$ by C , then the joint distribution over all the variables in the graph will satisfy A⊥⊥B | C

# Static Bayesian Network: IID Bernoulli Samples

Consider $n$ i.i.d. samples from a Bernoulli distribution with parameter $\theta$ .

Variables:

▶ $\theta$ : Probability of success (latent), $\theta \sim \mathsf { U n i f } ( 0 , 1 )$ ▶ $X _ { j }$ : Outcome of the $j .$ -th trial (Observed, $i = 1 , \ldots , N )$

Joint Probability Distribution: $\begin{array} { r } { P ( \theta , X _ { 1 : N } ) = P ( \theta ) \prod _ { i = 1 } ^ { N } P ( X _ { i } \mid \theta ) } \end{array}$

![](images/ca02f9ee7afb296d9f316a111a357b28ba6b4b3b79952b7e82c538dc5ab8bced.jpg)

![](images/7641942d0c72ab90b43c8937d791c8b9fad6f22e2b7e35690f0bb4ade6d638ab.jpg)

Plate notation

The plate encloses variables that are repeated $n$ times.   
The edges inside the plate are replicated for each instance.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_037\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_037\auto

A statistical method to uncover hidden topics based on word co-occurrence patterns in a collection of documents.

Key concepts:

Word: A basic unit   
Document: A bag of words, do not consider the order of words   
Topic: A distribution over words that represent a coherent theme. For example, “game,” “team,” “score” will have higher frequency in the topic “sports”   
Assumption: Documents are generated by sampling words from a mixture of topics.

Goal: Automatically discover topic-word distributions and document-topic distributions from observed words.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_038\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_038\auto

# Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA)

• One of the most famous generative probabilistic models for topic modeling Notations

We have $\boldsymbol { K }$ topics, $D$ documents, and a dictionary containing $d$ words The collections of documents $\pmb { W } = \{ \pmb { w } _ { 1 } , \dots , \pmb { w } _ { D } \}$ , each document ${ \pmb w } _ { t } \in \mathbb { N } ^ { d }$ is a word frequency vector ▶ The topics $\{ \beta _ { 1 } , \ldots , \beta _ { K } \}$ , each topic $\beta _ { k } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ is a word probability vector

Assumption

▶ Assumes each document is a mixture of topics $\theta _ { t } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { k }$ , where $\theta _ { t , k }$ is the Each topic is a distribution over words. Uses Dirichlet distributions to model topic and word distributions.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_039\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_039\auto

# Why Dirichlet Distribution

Revisit the IID Bernoulli Samples: $\theta \sim \mathsf { U n i f } ( 0 , 1 ) , X _ { i } \sim \mathsf { B e r n o u l l i } ( \theta )$

Let $\begin{array} { r } { y = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } X _ { i } } \end{array}$ be the count of 1. The posterior distribution of $\theta$ will be

$$
p ( \theta \mid X _ { 1 : n } ) \propto p ( \theta ) \prod _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } p ( x _ { i } \mid \theta ) \propto \theta ^ { y } ( 1 - \theta ) ^ { ( n - y ) }
$$

What happen if we change the prior $p ( \theta ) ?$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_040\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_040\auto

# Why Dirichlet Distribution

Revisit the IID Bernoulli Samples: $\theta \sim \mathsf { U n i f } ( 0 , 1 ) , X _ { i } \sim \mathsf { B e r n o u l l i } ( \theta )$

Let $\begin{array} { r } { y = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } X _ { i } } \end{array}$ be the count of 1. The posterior distribution of $\theta$ will be

$$
p ( \theta \mid X _ { 1 : n } ) \propto p ( \theta ) \prod _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } p ( x _ { i } \mid \theta ) \propto \theta ^ { y } ( 1 - \theta ) ^ { ( n - y ) }
$$

$\theta \mid X _ { 1 : n } \sim \mathsf { B e t a } ( y + 1 , n - y + 1 )$

What happen if we change the prior $p ( \theta ) ?$

Conjugate prior: the prior and posterior distributions are in the same distribution family   
Example: $p ( \theta ) \sim \mathsf { B e t a } ( a , b )$ , i.e., $p ( \theta ) \propto \theta ^ { a - 1 } ( 1 - \theta ) ^ { b - 1 }$   
● The posterior will be $p ( \theta \mid X _ { 1 : n } ) \propto \theta ^ { a - 1 + y } ( 1 - \theta ) ^ { b - 1 + ( n - y ) }$ , i.e., $\theta \mid X _ { 1 : n } \sim \mathsf { B e t a } ( a + y , b + n - y )$   
Benefits of using conjugate prior: ▶ Efficient to update the distribution of $\theta$ ▶ The posterior distribution can be regarded as prior for the following data (online Bayesian) Interpreted as pseudo-observations
