## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_041\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_041\auto

# Why Dirichlet Distribution

• Dirichlet Distribution $\mathsf { D i r } ( K , \alpha )$ is the generalization of the Beta distribution

$$
f ( \theta ; a , b ) = \frac { \Gamma ( a + b ) } { \Gamma ( a ) \Gamma ( b ) } \theta ^ { a - 1 } ( 1 - \theta ) ^ { b - 1 } , \quad 0 \leq x \leq
$$

$$
\mathbf { \bar { \rho } } ( \pmb { p } ; \alpha ) = \frac { \Gamma ( \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } \alpha _ { k } ) } { \prod _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } \Gamma ( \alpha _ { k } ) } \prod _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } p _ { k } ^ { \alpha _ { k } - 1 } , \quad \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } p _ { k } = 1 , 0 \leq
$$

Dirichlet Distribution is the conjugate prior distribution of the categorical distribution $\mathsf { C a t } ( K , \pmb { p } )$

$\mathsf { c a t } _ { K } ( \pmb { p } ) : \quad f ( \pmb { c } \mid \pmb { p } ) \propto \prod _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } p _ { k } ^ { c _ { k } } , \quad c _ { i } \mathrm { i s \ t h e \ n u m b e r }$ of occurrences of category k

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \pmb { p } \vert \pmb { c } ) \propto \prod _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } p _ { k } ^ { c _ { k } + \alpha _ { k } - 1 } , \mathrm { i . e . , } \pmb { p } \vert \pmb { c } \sim \mathrm { D i r } _ { K } ( \pmb { \alpha } + \pmb { c } ) } \end{array}
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_043\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_043\auto

# LDA Generative Process

![](images/fe5bfe00499715f0442df3d47352743f2ad2b03b4158c7e094926941db55f239.jpg)

1 For each topic $k$ :

▶ Draw a distribution over words $\phi _ { k } \sim \mathsf { D i r i c h l e t } ( \beta )$ .

2 For each document $d$ :

▶ Draw a topic proportion $\theta _ { d } \sim \mathsf { D i r i c h l e t } ( \alpha )$ .

▶ For each word $W _ { d , n }$ in document $d$

![](images/61fe582b7c688b52247c8d3c0d372bb1a3d5187b848b314907a257edab903ec2.jpg)

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_044\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_044\auto

# Inference in LDA

• Goal: Infer Topic-word distributions $\phi _ { k }$ and Document-topic distributions $\theta _ { d }$ from observed words.

# ● Challenges:

▶ Exact inference is computationally intractable.   
▶ Approximate methods are used.

Solution: Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method (more specifically, collapsed Gibbs Sampling) ▶ “Top 10 algorithms in the 20th century”

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_045\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_045\auto

# Dynamic Bayesian Network

# Limitation of Static Bayesian Networks:

Model relationships among variables at a single time point. ▶ Cannot capture temporal dynamics or evolving dependencies.

# Need for Temporal Modeling:

▶ Real-world systems (e.g., speech recognition, robotics, financial markets) involve variables that change over time. ▶ Require models that represent time-series dependencies and state transitions.

# Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs):

▶ Extend Bayesian networks to model temporal processes. Represent variables and their dependencies across multiple time steps. Enable efficient inference and prediction in dynamic systems.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_046\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_046\auto

# Markov Chain

• A Markov Chain is a mathematical model for systems that transition from one state to another.   
It consists of a set of states and transition probabilities between them.   
Key property: The Markov Property — the future state depends only on the current state, not on the sequence of past states.

$$
\mathbf { \Phi } _ { + 1 } = s _ { j } \mid X _ { t } = s _ { i } , X _ { t - 1 } , \dotsc , X _ { 0 } ) = P ( X _ { t + 1 } = s _ { j } \mid X
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_047\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_047\auto

# Components of a Markov Chain

States: A finite or countable set of possible states, e.g., {Sunny, Rainy}.

Transition Probabilities: Probability of moving from state $s _ { i }$ to state $s _ { j }$ , denoted $P ( s _ { i } \to s _ { j } )$ .

Transition Matrix: A matrix $P$ where $P _ { i j } = P ( s _ { i } \to s _ { j } )$ , and each row sums to 1.

Initial Distribution $\pi _ { 0 } = ( P ( X _ { 0 } = s _ { 1 } )$ , $P ( X _ { 0 } = s _ { 2 } ) , \ldots , P ( X _ { 0 } = s _ { n } ) )$ : Probability distribution over states at time $t = 0$ .

Stationary Distribution $\pi ^ { * }$ : Probability distribution that satisfy $\pi ^ { * } P = \pi ^ { * }$ ● Example:

▶ Transition probabilities:

$\star$ Sunny Sunny: 0.8, Sunny Rainy: 0.2   
$^ { \star }$ Rainy Sunny: 0.4, Rainy Rainy: 0.6

▶ Transition matrix:

$$
P = { \binom { 0 . 8 \quad 0 . 2 } { 0 . 4 \quad 0 . 6 } }
$$

P ( X _ { 1 : T } , Z _ { 1 : T } ) = P ( X _ { 1 } ) \prod _ { t = 2 } ^ { T } P ( X _ { t } \mid X _ { t - 1 } ) \prod _ { t = 1 } ^ { T } P ( Z _ { t } \mid

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_049\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_049\auto

# Dynamic Bayesian Network: Hidden Markov Model

Consider a more concrete model with a discrete state space and observation space • Parameters of HMM $\lambda$ contains three parts $[ A , B , \pi ]$ :

Set of hidden states $\mathcal { S } = \{ s _ { 1 } , s _ { 2 } , \ldots , s _ { n } \}$ , $X _ { t } \in S$ .   
Set of observable values $\mathcal { O } = \{ o _ { 1 } , o _ { 2 } , \dots , o _ { m } \}$ , $Z _ { t } \in \mathcal { O }$   
Transition Probabilities $A = \{ a _ { i j } \} _ { n \times n }$ , where $a _ { i j } = P ( x _ { t + 1 } = s _ { j } \mid x _ { t } = s _ { i } ) .$ Emission Probabilities $B = \{ b _ { i j } \} _ { n \times m }$ , where $b _ { i j } = P ( z _ { t } = o _ { j } \mid x _ { t } = s _ { i } )$ . Initial State Distribution: $\pi = ( \pi _ { 1 } , . . . , \pi _ { n } ) \pi _ { i } = P ( x _ { 1 } = s _ { i } )$ .

We can use HMM to solve these questions

▶ Likelihood: Given the model parameter $\lambda$ and the observation sequence $O$ , calculate $P ( O \mid \lambda )$   
▶ Decoding: Given the model parameter $\lambda$ and the observations $O$ , infer the hidden state sequence $S$   
▶ Learning:Given the observations $O$ , learn the model parameters $\lambda$ that maximize the likelihood $P ( O \mid \lambda )$

For concrete algorithms you may refer to this note [Link]

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_052\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_052\auto

# Markov Random Field

A probabilistic model for representing joint distributions over a set of variables.   
Defined on an undirected graph, where nodes represent random variables and edges represent mutual dependencies.   
C Satisfies the (Local) Markov property: A variable is conditionally independent of all others given its neighbors.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_053\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_053\auto

# Key Components of an MRF

Graph Structure $G = ( V , E ) )$ : ▶ V : Set of nodes (random variables). ▶ E : Set of undirected edges (dependencies).

Cliques: Subsets of nodes that every pair is directly connected (complete subgraphs).

Maximal Clique: A clique that is not a subset of any other clique.

Potential Functions $( \psi _ { C } )$ : Assign non-negative values to configurations of clique C . Joint Probability:

$$
P ( X ) = \frac { 1 } { Z } \prod _ { C \in \mathsf { m a x } \mathsf { c l i q u e s } } \psi _ { C } ( X _ { C } )
$$

where Z = Px QC ∈cliques $\psi _ { C } ( X _ { C } )$ is the normalizing constant.

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_056\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_056\auto

# Markov Property in MRFs

Local Markov property A variable is conditionally independent of all other variables given its neighbors in the graph.

Let $v$ be a node, $n ( v )$ be its neighbor nodes, and $n ^ { * } ( v ) = \{ v \} \cup n ( v )$ we have $x _ { v } \bot \bot x _ { V \setminus n ^ { * } ( v ) } \mid x _ { n ( v ) }$

Global Markov Property: Variables in non-adjacent nodes are independent given a separating set.

▶ Let $A , B , C$ be three sets of nodes, and all paths connecting nodes in $A$ and $B$ must pass nodes in $B$ , we say $C$ is the separating set.   
▶ $x _ { A } \bot \bot x _ { B } \mid x _ { C }$

Pairwise Markov Property: Non-adjacent variables are conditionally independent given all others.

▶ Let $u , v$ be two non-adjacent nodes (i.e., $\langle u , v \rangle \not \in E )$ , we have $x _ { u } \bot \bot x _ { v } \mid x _ { V \setminus \{ u , v \} }$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model\page_057\DSAA2011-L12_graphical_model_page_057\auto

# Conditional Random Field (CRF)

MRF is a generative model that models the joint probability distribution $P ( X )$ CRF is a special case of MRF

▶ Observation $\mathsf { X }$ and output variables Y are disjoint nodes in the graph ▶ The conditional probability obeys the Markov property:

$$
P ( Y _ { v } | X , Y _ { V \setminus v } ) = P ( Y _ { v } \mid X , y _ { n ( v ) } )
$$

▶ Focuses on modeling the conditional probability distribution $P ( y \mid X )$ (i.e., discriminative model)

# Examplar Application of CRF: POS Tagging

• Sentence: “The cat runs.”   
• Goal: Assign Part-of-speech (POS) tags to each word: ▶ “The” Determiner (DET) “cat” Noun (NN) ▶ “runs” Verb (VB)

• Task: Model the probability of the tag sequence [DET, NN, VB] given the word sequence [The, cat, runs].

Input (Observations): Word sequence ${ \pmb u } =$ [The, cat, runs]. Output (Labels): Tag sequence $\mathbf { t } = [ \mathsf { D E T } , \mathsf { N N } , \mathsf { V B } ]$ . Model: Linear-chain CRF

$t _ { 1 } ( N N , D E T , \pmb { x } , 1 ) = 1$ for the transition DET → NN. • $t _ { 2 } ( V B , N N , { \pmb x } , 2 ) = 1$ for the transition ${ \mathsf { N N } } \to { \mathsf { V B } }$ . • $s _ { 1 } ( D E T , x , 1 ) = 1$ if $x _ { 1 } =$ “The” and $y _ { 1 } = \mathsf { D }$ ET $s _ { 2 } ( N N , x , 2 ) = 1$ if $x _ { 2 } { = } " { \mathsf { c a t } } ^ { \prime \prime }$ and $y _ { 1 } { = } { \mathsf { N N } }$ $s _ { 3 } ( V B , x , 3 ) = 1$ if $x _ { 3 } =$ “runs” and $y _ { 3 } { = } \mathsf { V B }$ The CRF computes the probability of [DET, NN, VB] by summing the weighted features and normalizing by $Z ( x )$ Goal: Find the most likely tag sequence $\mathbf { t } ^ { * }$ :

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_005\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_005\auto

# d-separation

A, B , $C$ are arbitrary non-intersecting sets of nodes. C can be empty   
We wish to know whether A⊥⊥ $B \mid C$ holds or not.   
Construct all possible (undirected) paths from any node in A to any node in B.   
A path is blocked by $C$ if ▶ The path contains a chain $i  j  k$ or a fork $i \left. j \right. k$ such that the middle node $j$ is in C ▶ The path contains a v-structure $i \to j  k$ such that the $j$ (and all the descendants) is not in C   
If all paths from A to $B$ are blocked, then $A$ is d-separated from $B$ by C

# Theorem 1

(d-separation) If A is $d .$ -separated from $B$ by C , then the joint distribution over all the variables in the graph will satisfy A⊥⊥B | C

# Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA)

![](images/b7beeec0eb59641de99470ba8f3509099a86be6d57357251ebca42aeaa404d1d.jpg)

$\beta$ : parameter of the Dirichlet prior to generate word distributions for each topic   
$\phi _ { k }$ : word distribution for topic $k$ , $1 \leq k \leq K$   
• $\alpha$ : parameter of the Dirichlet prior to generate topic distributions for each document   
$\theta _ { d }$ : topic distribution for document $d$ , $1 \leq d \leq D$   
• ${ \cal Z } _ { d , n }$ : indicates the topic for $n$ -th word in document $d$   
$w _ { d , n }$ : the $n$ -th word in document $d$ (the only observable variables)

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_007\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_007\auto

# Dynamic Bayesian Network: Hidden Markov Model

• Variables at time $t$ :

▶ $X _ { t }$ : Hidden state in $\boldsymbol { S } = \{ s _ { 1 } , \ldots , s _ { n } \}$ (latent) $Z _ { t }$ : Observation in $\mathcal { O } = \{ o _ { 1 } , \ldots , o _ { m } \}$ (observed) Transition Probabilities $A = \{ a _ { i j } \} _ { n \times n }$ , where $a _ { i j } = P ( x _ { t + 1 } = s _ { j } \mid x _ { t } = s _ { i } ) .$ Emission Probabilities $B = \{ b _ { i j } \} _ { n \times m }$ , where $b _ { i j } = P ( z _ { t } = o _ { j } \mid x _ { t } = s _ { i } )$ . Initial State Distribution: $\pi = ( \pi _ { 1 } , \ldots , \pi _ { n } )$ (d:) $\pi _ { i } = P ( x _ { 1 } = s _ { i } ) $ . Joint Probability Distribution

$$
^ { \circ } ( X _ { 1 : T } , Z _ { 1 : T } ) = P ( X _ { 1 } ) \prod _ { t = 2 } ^ { T } P ( X _ { t } \mid X _ { t - 1 } ) \prod _ { t = 1 } ^ { T } P ( Z _ { t } \mid X _ { t - 1 } )
$$

![](images/fd59d6c3bce6d2ef327a61e520bf8d7edd9eab57bdec263cf0ec77630f22f970.jpg)

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_008\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_008\auto

# Markov Random Field

Use undirected graph to model the joint distribution.

C Satisfies the (Local) Markov property: A variable is conditionally independent of all others given its neighbors.

Joint Probability:

$$
P ( X ) = \frac { 1 } { Z } \prod _ { C \in \mathsf { m a x } \mathsf { c l i q u e s } } \psi _ { C } ( X _ { C } )
$$

where $Z = \textstyle \sum _ { x } \prod _ { C \in { } }$ liques $\psi _ { C } ( X _ { C } )$ is the normalizing constant.

The potential functions are used to model the interactions between variables

▶ Since it should be non-negative, usually we model it as $\psi _ { C } ( X _ { C } ) = \exp ( { - H _ { Q } ( X _ { Q } ) } )$ ▶ $H _ { Q }$ is a real function, usually defined as

$$
H _ { Q } ( x _ { Q } ) = \sum _ { u \in Q } \alpha _ { u } x _ { u } + \sum _ { u , v \in Q , u \neq v } \beta _ { u v } x _ { u } x _ { v }
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_009\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_009\auto

# Conditional Random Field (CRF)

MRF is a generative model that models the joint probability distribution $P ( X )$ CRF is a special case of MRF

▶ Observation $\mathsf { X }$ and output variables Y are disjoint nodes in the graph ▶ The conditional probability obeys the Markov property:

$$
P ( Y _ { v } | X , Y _ { V \setminus v } ) = P ( Y _ { v } \mid X , Y _ { n ( v ) } )
$$

Focuses on modeling $P ( Y \mid X )$ (i.e., discriminative model)

Linear-Chain CRFs

P( $\begin{array} { l } { { \displaystyle \gamma _ { i } | X , y _ { 1 } , . . . , y _ { i - 1 } , y _ { i + 1 } , . . . , y _ { n } ) = P ( y _ { i } | X , y _ { i - 1 } , y _ { i + 1 } ) } } \\ { { \displaystyle \prime | x ) = \frac 1 { Z ( x ) } \exp \left( \sum _ { k } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n - 1 } \lambda _ { k } t _ { k } ( y _ { i + 1 } , y _ { i } , x , i ) + \sum _ { I } \sum _ { i } ^ { n } \right. } } \end{array}$ n=1 µl sl (yi , x , i )

![](images/f72a40149b6c0ab660c2a344a28ec99cc5d0a51619316d8c9c78236c0f53bfc8.jpg)

$$
X = ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } )
$$

# Factor Graph

A bipartite graph representing the factorization of a function.

Can describe both Bayesian Network and Markov Random Fields   
More effective for some inference algorithms, e.g., sum-product algorithm ▶ Variable nodes (circles) Factor nodes (squares) Edges represent dependencies

# Transform BN/MRF to Factor Graph

Each conditional and marginal distribution in a Bayesian Network becomes a factor

![](images/49fc89852da7dde0d0189fb75c1dbd9e02a77c439d24a8dd75eafd35e98281dd.jpg)

$P ( X ) = P ( A ) P ( B ) P ( C | A , B )$ $P ( X ) = \psi _ { A } \psi _ { B } \psi _ { A , B , C }$

Each clique in a Markov Random Field becomes a factor

![](images/39fcf4d1beccf2c86f7fe14c43486a7621e37053c32878edc94799309ef39c97.jpg)

$$
P ( X ) = \frac { 1 } { Z } \psi _ { A , B } \psi _ { B , C } \psi _ { C , D } \psi _ { D , A }
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_016\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_016\auto

# Motivation for Active Learning

Unlabeled data is abundant, but labels are time-consuming/expensive Active learning allows for intelligent choices of which instances to label Goal: aims to achieve high accuracy using as few labeled instances as possible, thereby reducing the cost of obtaining labeled data

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_017\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_017\auto

# Active Learning Process

Start with small labeled and large unlabeled sets. 2 Train model on labeled data. Select instances using a query strategy. 4 Query oracle, update labeled set, retrain. 5 Repeat until stopping criterion met.

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_018\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_018\auto

# Comparison with Passive Learning

# Semi-supervised learning

Design a predictor based on i.i.d. unlabeled instances and a few randomly labeled instances   
Assumption: Knowledge of marginal density can simplify prediction, e.g. similar instances have similar labels   
● Label Acquisition: Automatic (inferred)   
Still a “passive” learner

![](images/1d85c4b9ab29acf6e6fca839bee2fcc743a72efb3a1f4bec2b017d2bb6be6d63.jpg)

# Active learning

Design a predictor based on i.i.d. unlabeled and selectively labeled instances   
• Assumption: Some unlabeled instances are more informative than others for prediction   
Label Acquisition: Human/Oracle Queries   
An “active” learner!

![](images/db904906e102a51265cd431c8db5700dfe13ff7ba634f2756579e689c51cc977.jpg)

(Source: Active Learning Literature Survey)

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_019\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_019\auto

# Two Scenarios in Active Learning

Pool-based: Chooses from a large unlabeled pool.

Stream-based: Decides per instance in a sequence.

Assumption: unlabeled instance arrives sequentially   
First sample an unlabeled instance   
Then decide whether to query its label or to ignore it ▶ Informativeness measure: more informative instances are more likely to be queried ▶ Region of uncertainty: only query instances that fall within it   
Assumption: a large pool of unlabeled instances is available   
Rank samples in order of informativeness   
Query the labels for the most informative samples

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_020\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_020\auto

# Comparison between stream-based and pool-based

• The stream-based scenario scans through the data sequentially and makes query decisions individually   
The pool-based scenario evaluates and ranks the entire collection before selecting the best query   
The pool-based scenario appears to be more common in applications   
Sometimes stream-based active learning could be more appropriate. For example, when memory or processing power may be limited, as with mobile and embedded devices

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_021\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_021\auto

# Query Strategy Frameworks

All types of active learning require a query selection strategy

▶ Uncertainty Sampling Query-By-Committee (QBC) Expected Model Change Expected Error Reduction Variance Reduction Density-based Sampling

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_022\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_022\auto

# Uncertainty Sampling

Query samples that the current model is the most uncertain about

0 Often used in probabilistic models (e.g., logistic regression, neural networks).

● Various ways to measure uncertainty

▶ Least Confident: $x _ { L C } ^ { * } = \arg \operatorname* { m a x } _ { x } 1 - P _ { \theta } ( \hat { y } | x )$ , where $\hat { y } = \arg \operatorname* { m a x } _ { y } P _ { \theta } ( \hat { y } | x )$   
▶ Smallest Margin: $x _ { S M } ^ { * } = \arg \mathsf { m a x } _ { x } P _ { \theta } ( \hat { y } _ { 1 } | x ) - P _ { \theta } ( \hat { y } _ { 2 } | x )$ , where $\hat { y } _ { 1 } , \hat { y } _ { 2 }$ are the two most probable labels for $x$   
▶ Label Entropy: $\begin{array} { r } { x _ { L E } ^ { * } = \arg \mathsf { m a x } _ { x } - \sum _ { y } P _ { \theta } \big ( y | x \big ) \log P _ { \theta } \big ( y | x \big ) } \end{array}$

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_023\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_023\auto

# Query-By-Committee (QBC)

Uses an ensemble of models (committee) $C = \{ \theta _ { 1 } , \ldots , \theta _ { K } \}$ to identify instances with maximum disagreement

All models trained using the currently available labeled data $\mathcal { L }$ The instances with maximum disagreement on their predictions are chosen for labeling ▶ Vote Entropy: let $V ( y )$ is the number of votes received to label y

$$
X _ { V E } ^ { * } = \mathop { \sf a r g m a x } _ { x } - \sum _ { y } \frac { V ( y ) } { K } \log \frac { V ( y ) } { K }
$$

KL divergence: let $P _ { \theta _ { i } }$ be the prediction of the model $\theta _ { j }$ and $P _ { C }$ be the prediction of th ensemble model

$$
X _ { K L } ^ { * } = \underset { x } { \arg \operatorname* { m a x } } \frac { 1 } { C } { \sf K L } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { K } ( P _ { \theta _ { i } } | | P _ { C } )
$$

Each model in the committee is re-trained after including the new instance(s)

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_024\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_024\auto

# Effect of Outliers

A instance may be uncertain or controversial simply because it is an outlier   
Querying outliers is not likely to help us reduce error on more typical data   
Other robust query selection methods exist to deal with outliers ▶ Density Weighting ⋆ Weight the uncertainty of an instance by its density w.r.t. the pool U. $\star$ For example, multiple a term $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { \vert U \vert } \sum _ { u } \sin ( x , u ) } \end{array}$

▶ Estimate model performance

⋆ Select samples that reduce the expected generalization error the most, measured w.r.t. the remaining unlabeled samples (representative of the test distribution) $\star$ Minimize the expected uncertainty over the set of unlabeled samples $\mathcal { U }$

$$
x ^ { * } = \underset { x } { \arg \operatorname* { m i n } } \sum _ { u \in \mathcal { U } } \sum _ { y } P _ { \theta } \big ( y | x \big ) \big ( 1 - P _ { \theta ^ { + } \langle x , y \rangle } \big ( \hat { y } | u \big ) \big )
$$

where $\theta ^ { + \langle x , y \rangle }$ refers to the new model after it has been re-trained with the training tuple $\langle x , y \rangle$ added

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_025\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_025\auto

# Expected Model Change

• Query the instance that would impart the greatest change to the current model Since we don’t know the label, we need to compute the expectation • Expected gradient length: let $\nabla { \mathcal { L } } _ { \boldsymbol { \theta } } \big ( \langle x , y _ { i } \rangle \big )$ be the gradient after adding training samples $\langle x , y _ { i } \rangle$

$$
x _ { E G L } ^ { * } = \underset { x } { \arg \operatorname* { m i n } } \sum _ { y } P _ { \theta } { \left( y | x \right) } { \left\| \nabla \mathcal { L } _ { \theta } { \left( \left. x , y _ { i } \right. \right) } \right\| }
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_026\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_026\auto

# Expected Error Reduction

Estimate generalization error after adding the query x   
Computationally expensive because ▶ Estimate the expected error over $\mathcal { U }$ is costly ▶ Re-train model is costly

Solutions

▶ Use models that naturally support incremental training Use sampling to reduce the $| \boldsymbol { \mathcal { U } } |$ when estimating error Use approximate training techniques

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_027\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_027\auto

Select samples that reduce the model variance the most

Minimizing the variance minimizes the future generalization error

$$
{ \mathbb E } [ ( \hat { y } - y ) ^ { 2 } | x ] = { \mathsf { b i a s } } ^ { 2 } + { \mathsf { v a r i a n c e } } + { \mathsf { n o i s e } }
$$

The Fisher information sets a lower bound on the variance (Cramer-Rao inequality) Maximize Fisher information

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_028\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_028\auto

# Density-based Methods

Identify the core-set that well represents the distribution of the original dataset   
Known as coreset selection, prototype learning, e.t.c.   
Several ideas ▶ Farthest first traversal Distance-based weighting Reduce the probability of selecting neighbors (of selected samples) Solve the facility location problem $\begin{array} { r } { S ^ { * } = \arg \operatorname* { m i n } _ { \cal S } \sum _ { u \in \mathcal { U } } \operatorname* { m i n } _ { p \in \mathcal { U } } d ( u , p ) } \end{array}$ Minimize reconstruction error: assume the dataset can be represented as a combination of several samples

https://github.com/PatrickZH/DeepCore

# ACM A.M. Turing Award Honors Two Researchers Who Led the Development of Cornerstone AI Technology

Andrew Barto and Richard Sutton Recognized as Pioneers of Reinforcement Learning

ACM has named Andrew G. Barto  and Richard S. Sutton  as the recipients of the 2024 ACM A.M. Turing Award for developing the conceptual and algorithmic foundations of reinforcement learning. In a series of papers beginning in the 1980s, Barto and Sutton introduced the main ideas, constructed the mathematical foundations, and developed important algorithms for reinforcement learning—one of the most important approaches for creating intelligent systems.

Barto is Professor Emeritus of Information and Computer Sciences at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst. Sutton is a Professor of Computer Science at the University of Alberta, a Research Scientist at Keen Technologies, and a Fellow at Amii (Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute).

# Example: grid world

• A maze-like problem

The agent lives in a grid

Walls block the agent’s path • Noisy movement: actions do not always go as planned

• $80 \%$ of the time, the action North takes the agent North (if there is no wall there)   
$10 \%$ of the time, North takes the agent West; $10 \%$ East   
If there is a wall in the direction the agent would have been taken, the agent stays

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_049\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_049\auto

# Markov Decision Processes

• An MDP is defined by:

A set of states $s \in { \mathcal { S } }$

A set of actions $a \in { \mathcal { A } }$

A transition function $T ( s , a , s ^ { \prime } )$

▶ Probability that a from $s$ leads to $s ^ { \prime }$ , i.e., $P ( s ^ { \prime } | s , a )$

▶ Also called the model or the dynamics

A reward function $R ( s , a , s ^ { \prime } )$ ▶ Sometimes just $R ( s , a ) , R ( s )$ or $R ( s ^ { \prime } )$

A start state

● Maybe a terminal state

![](images/bceb5c63f4852aff3dd35f2c2df96e015c4b62f88bf3e454810afee6bc4ffede.jpg)

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_057\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_057\auto

# Visualizing discounting

• How to discount?

Each time we descend a level, we multiply in the discount once

• Why discount?

Sooner rewards probably do have higher utility than later rewards Also helps our algorithms converge

# • Example: discount of 0.5

$U ( [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] ) = 1 \times 1 + 0 . 5 \times 2 + 0 . 2 5 \times 3$ $U ( [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] ) < U ( [ 3 , 2 , 1 ] )$

![](images/589690441025ffc2311b9724058ffb3377e5e6fa880f167f5e9459f2156a8c5a.jpg)

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_058\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_058\auto

# Stationary preference (Optional)

• Theorem: if we assume stationary preference:

$$
[ a _ { 1 } , a _ { 2 } , . . . ] \succ [ b _ { 1 } , b _ { 2 } , . . . ]
$$

$$
[ r , a _ { 1 } , a _ { 2 } , . . . ] \succ [ r , b _ { 1 } , b _ { 2 } , . . . ]
$$

• Then: there are only two ways to define utilities

Additive utility: $U ( [ r _ { 0 } , r _ { 1 } , r _ { 2 } , \ldots ] ) = r _ { 0 } + r _ { 1 } + r _ { 2 } + \ldots .$ Discounted utility: $U ( [ r _ { 0 } , r _ { 1 } , r _ { 2 } , \dots ] ) = r _ { 0 } + \gamma r _ { 1 } + \gamma ^ { 2 } r _ { 2 } + \dots .$

![](images/1573e4761b6c27a556000de5fb2f1425c9b324ebdd150cf53c36e6f7d357fd76.jpg)

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_060\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_060\auto

# Infinite utilities?!

• Problem: What if the game lasts forever? Do we get infinite rewards?

• Solutions:

Finite horizon: (similar to depth-limited search) ▶ Terminate episodes after a fixed $\tau$ steps (e.g. life) ▶ Gives nonstationary policies ( $\pi$ depends on time left)

![](images/7da8da20ab82af1c149c0137a1385762bfa6dee3c415f8a0683d59ee9a8c1be8.jpg)

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_061\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_061\auto

# Infinite utilities?!

• Problem: What if the game lasts forever? Do we get infinite rewards?

# • Solutions:

Finite horizon: (similar to depth-limited search) ▶ Terminate episodes after a fixed $\tau$ steps (e.g. life) ▶ Gives nonstationary policies ( $\pi$ depends on time left)

Discounting: use $0 < \gamma < 1$

![](images/d88c20fa103eb45f96ddd9b2cac9c22aeb72b3341f4ea790a8c9679a7b7e1778.jpg)

$$
U ( [ r _ { 0 } , \dots , r _ { \infty } ] ) = \sum _ { t = 0 } ^ { \infty } \gamma ^ { t } r _ { t } \le R _ { \sf m a x } / ( 1 - \gamma )
$$

▶ Smaller $\gamma$ means smaller “horizon” – shorter term focus

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_062\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_062\auto

# Infinite utilities?!

• Problem: What if the game lasts forever? Do we get infinite rewards?

# • Solutions:

Finite horizon: (similar to depth-limited search)

▶ Terminate episodes after a fixed $\tau$ steps (e.g. life) ▶ Gives nonstationary policies ( $\pi$ depends on time left)

Discounting: use $0 < \gamma < 1$

![](images/420eb20030aded1cf780b069270e8424e71c7e26e0321348ce4b2539acbfbc12.jpg)

$$
U ( [ r _ { 0 } , \dots , r _ { \infty } ] ) = \sum _ { t = 0 } ^ { \infty } \gamma ^ { t } r _ { t } \le R _ { \sf m a x } / ( 1 - \gamma )
$$

▶ Smaller $\gamma$ means smaller “horizon” – shorter term focus

Absorbing state: guarantee that for every policy, a terminal state will eventually be reached (like “overheated” for racing)

Policy $=$ Choice of action for each state

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_065\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_065\auto

# Optimal quantities

• The value (utility) of a state s:

• V ∗(s) = expected utility starting in s and acting optimally

• The value (utility) of a $q \cdot$ -state (s, a): :

$Q ^ { * } ( s , a ) =$ expected utility starting out having taken action a from state s and (thereafter) acting optimally

# • The optimal policy:

$\pi ^ { * } ( s ) =$ optimal action from state s

![](images/6752b5756b4f908e1bc1fb8600f1644993f6e623470839262748f0df517ac068.jpg)

s is a state

$( s , a )$ is a $q$ -state

$( s , a , s ^ { \prime } )$ is a transition

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_066\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_066\auto

# Values of states

• Fundamental operation: compute the (expectimax) value of a state

Expected utility under optimal action Average sum of (discounted) rewards (Optimal) This is just what expectimax computed!

• Recursive definition of value:

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { { \cal V } ^ { * } = \displaystyle \mathsf { m a x } Q ^ { * } ( s , a ) } } \\ { { { \cal Q } ^ { * } ( s , a ) = \displaystyle \sum _ { s ^ { \prime } } T ( s , a , s ^ { \prime } ) [ R ( s , a , s ^ { \prime } ) + \gamma V ^ { * } ( s ^ { \prime } ) ] } } \\ { { { \cal V } ^ { * } = \displaystyle \mathsf { m a x } \sum _ { a } T ( s , a , s ^ { \prime } ) [ R ( s , a , s ^ { \prime } ) + \gamma V ^ { * } ( s ^ { \prime } ) ] } } \end{array}
$$

![](images/c2a50a377a5084a72373a5eeb47c1a36d0b4f35538089327440b879716c4cc8e.jpg)

# Recap: definition of MDP

• An MDP is defined by:

Set of states $s \in { \mathcal { S } }$   
Start state $s _ { 0 }$   
Set of actions $a \in { \mathcal { A } }$   
Transition function $P ( s ^ { \prime } | s , a )$ or $T ( s , a , s ^ { \prime } )$ Rewards $R ( s , a , s ^ { \prime } )$ (and discount $\gamma$ )

• MDP quantities so far:

Policy $=$ Choice of action for each state   
Utility $=$ sum of (discounted) rewards   
Values $=$ expected future utility from a state (max node)   
$Q$ -Values $=$ expected future utility from a $q \cdot$ -state (chance node)

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_069\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_069\auto

# The Bellman equations

• Definition of “optimal utility” via expectimax recurrence gives a simple one-step lookahead relationship amongst optimal utility values

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { V ^ { * } = \displaystyle { \sf m a x } Q ^ { * } ( s , a ) } } \\ { { Q ^ { * } ( s , a ) = \displaystyle \sum _ { s ^ { \prime } } T ( s , a , s ^ { \prime } ) [ R ( s , a , s ^ { \prime } ) + \gamma V ^ { * } ( s ^ { \prime } ) ] } } \\ { { V ^ { * } = \displaystyle { \sf m a x } \sum _ { a } T ( s , a , s ^ { \prime } ) [ R ( s , a , s ^ { \prime } ) + \gamma V ^ { * } ( s ^ { \prime } ) ] } } \end{array}
$$

![](images/dc21545d005f07404557dd59a0b3ecc76e241a42a959235c9800541517d19b2c.jpg)

### Images:
- data\1. Machine_Learning\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_069\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_069\auto\images\89ad34e3655e22729e0b69ab2cde74075955c194fa404ffb24fc18c5cc247612.jpg
- data\1. Machine_Learning\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_069\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_069\auto\images\dc21545d005f07404557dd59a0b3ecc76e241a42a959235c9800541517d19b2c.jpg

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_070\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_070\auto

# The Bellman equations

• Definition of “optimal utility” via expectimax recurrence gives a simple one-step lookahead relationship amongst optimal utility values

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { { \cal V } ^ { * } = \displaystyle { \sf m a x } Q ^ { * } ( s , a ) } } \\ { { { \cal Q } ^ { * } ( s , a ) = \displaystyle \sum _ { s ^ { \prime } } T ( s , a , s ^ { \prime } ) [ R ( s , a , s ^ { \prime } ) + \gamma V ^ { * } ( s ^ { \prime } ) ] } } \\ { { { \cal V } ^ { * } = \displaystyle { \sf m a x } \sum _ { a } T ( s , a , s ^ { \prime } ) [ R ( s , a , s ^ { \prime } ) + \gamma V ^ { * } ( s ^ { \prime } ) ] } } \end{array}
$$

• These are the Bellman equations, and they characterize optimal values in a way we’ll use over and over

![](images/54d562b29a31f5b6e40cfb466a94d014175e119b70a2c7a5cdf0c073267fc216.jpg)

# Continuous action space

![](images/8afbef955e7ca08d7b54ef893c04a7e46372114ec8d18d652372b1100f79a60d.jpg)

$$
\mathcal { A } = [ 0 , 3 6 0 ] \times [ 0 , 1 8 0 ]
$$

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_077\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_077\auto

# Discretization

![](images/438fa2c1a55b5ba666ff7a50b4c13d54418736b41784c278eb43c7de3acd73b4.jpg)

Discretize the action space (draw a grid)   
Number of actions is the number of grid points   
Problem: curse of dimensionality   
◦ Let $d$ be the degree of freedom

$$
\left. \begin{array} { r } { a _ { 1 } \in [ 0 , 3 6 0 ] } \\ { a _ { 2 } \in [ 0 , 1 8 0 ] } \end{array} \right\} d = 2
$$

◦ Number of actions grows exponentially with $d$

# Model-based vs model-free RL

• One of the most important branching points in an RL algorithm is the question of whether the agent has access to (or learns) a model of the environment

Model of the environment: a function which predicts state transitions and rewards

Yes: model-based model-based value iteration No: model-free TD learning

◦ Reference: webpage by OpenAI

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_086\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_086\auto

# Target policy vs Behavior policy

• Target policy is the policy that an agent is trying to learns (e.g., agent is learning the value function for this policy)

◦ Used to Update $Q$ -Value → Training

Behaviour policy is the policy that is being used by an agent for action select. (i.e., agent follows this policy to interact with the environment)

◦ Used to Execute the Actions → Data Collection

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_088\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_088\auto

# Prediction vs Control

# Prediction task

We have a policy Fix policy, evaluate the future

◦ Goal is to evaluate policy by estimating the state-value or $Q$ -value of running actions of given policy

# Control task

We don’t have a policy Adapt policy, optimize the future ◦ Goal is to find the optimal policy aiming to collect maximum rewards

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_091\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_091\auto

# Ensemble Learning

Bagging: Aggregate multiple “independent” learners.

Trains multiple learners on random subsets of data Random forest: Further decorrelate learners by limiting the number of features ▶ Reduce variance

Boosting: Sequentially trains learners to correct errors of the previous.

▶ Gradient Boosting: Adding learners that approximate the gradient Adaptive Boosting: Adjusts weights of misclassified samples Reduce bias

● Feature selection

Filter Methods: Select features based on statistical correlation Wrapper Methods: Evaluate feature subsets using model performance. ▶ Embedded Methods: Integrate feature selection into the model training process

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_092\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_092\auto

● Clustering Metrics

▶ External: compared to ground truth labels $^ { \star }$ Purity $^ { \star }$ (Adjusted) Rand index, Fowlkes-Mallows index ⋆ (Normalized) Mutual Information, V-measure   
▶ Internal: use cluster structure $\star$ Silhouette Coefficient $^ { \star }$ Calinski-Harabaz Index (Variance Ratio Criterion) $^ { \star }$ Davies-Bouldin Index $^ { \star }$ Dunn index

Prototype-based Clustering: define clusters based on prototype

▶ k-means (algorithm, stopping condition, initialization)   
▶ k-medoids kernel k-means

---

## Lecture: DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning\page_093\DSAA2011-L13_active_learning_reinforcement_learning_page_093\auto

Density-based Clustering: define clusters by density reachability ▶ DBSCAN ▶ OPTICS: allows adaptive $\epsilon$ for different region   
• Hierarchical Clustering ▶ Agglomerative v.s. Divisive ▶ Single/Complete/Average Linkage, Ward’s method   
Soft clustering: Gaussian Mixture Model ▶ Formulation ▶ EM Algorithm

# Probabilistic Graphical Model

Bayesian Network (directed acyclic graph)

$\begin{array} { r } { P ( X _ { 1 : d } ) = \prod _ { i = 1 } ^ { d } P ( X _ { i } \mid \mathsf { p a } ( X _ { i } ) ) } \end{array}$   
Chain Structure, Common Cause (fork), Common Effect (Collider, v-structure)   
d-separation

Markov Random Field (undirected graph) ▶ $\begin{array} { r } { P ( X ) = \frac { 1 } { Z } \prod _ { C \in \mathsf { m a x } } } \end{array}$ cliques $\psi _ { C } ( X _ { C } )$

● Examples

Topic Modeling (LDA) Hidden Markov Model ▶ Conditional Markov Field
